paragraphs: This paper approaches learning from examples as a problem of approximating a multidimensional function. Each example helps specify a relationship between inputs and outputs, and learning constructs a function that represents that relationship. This viewpoint makes function approximation the mathematical setting for understanding the network's task.

The supplied abstract connects this formulation to regularization theory. It recalls an earlier equivalence between regularization and a class of three-layer architectures called regularization networks. That connection gives the network representation a theoretical foundation: the architecture can be understood through the same framework used to formulate a regularized approximation problem.

The title identifies outliers and negative examples as the subjects of the extension. These broaden the focus to the kinds of evidence a learning formulation must accommodate. However, the supplied abstract ends just as it begins introducing the new methods. The supported contribution is therefore an announced extension of the regularization-network framework in those directions; the available text establishes its starting point but does not state the extension's construction or findings.
summary.tldr: The paper extends a regularization-based view of neural function approximation toward outliers and negative examples.

title: Extensions of a Theory of Networks for Approximation and Learning: Outliers and Negative Examples

abstract: We present a fast algorithm for non-linear dimension reduction. The algorithm builds a local linear model of the data by merging PCA with clustering based on a new distortion measure. Exper(cid:173) iments with speech and image data indicate that the local linear algorithm produces encodings with lower distortion than those built by five layer auto-associative networks. The local linear algorithm is also more than an order of magnitude faster to train.

Exper(cid:173) iments with speech and image data indicate that the local linear algorithm produces encodings with lower distortion than those built by five layer auto-associative networks. The local linear algorithm is also more than an order of magnitude faster to train.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a fast method for reducing the dimension of data while capturing nonlinear structure. It builds a locally linear description by combining principal component analysis with clustering. The key organizational choice is to describe different portions of the data with local models, allowing the overall representation to go beyond a single linear description.

A new distortion measure connects the clustering process with the construction of those local models. Distortion expresses how much the encoding loses or alters the data under the method's criterion. Bringing clustering and linear modeling together makes the grouping of examples part of the representation-learning procedure, rather than treating the two operations as unrelated tasks.

Experiments on speech and image data compare the method with five-layer auto-associative networks. The local linear approach produces encodings with lower distortion and trains more than an order of magnitude faster. The reported advantage therefore concerns both representation quality and training effort in those experiments, supporting local linear modeling as a practical approach to nonlinear dimension reduction.
summary.tldr: Combining clustering with local PCA yields lower-distortion encodings and substantially faster training than the tested five-layer auto-associative networks.

title: Fast Non-Linear Dimension Reduction

paragraphs: This paper investigates fluctuations in individual neural activities within a large stochastic recurrent network containing excitatory and inhibitory populations. Population averages can describe overall activity while concealing how individual units fluctuate together. The authors therefore calculate correlation functions, which characterize relationships between activity fluctuations across neurons and across time.

In a stationary state, correlations between different neurons are weak relative to a neuron's correlation with itself. Their relative amplitude scales as one divided by the size of the interacting population. This result has a stated exception: it breaks down near bifurcations, where the network approaches a transition from stationary to changing activity.

Near such a transition, correlations between neurons grow to order-one amplitude, and their decay time diverges. The network consequently retains correlated fluctuations for increasingly long periods, resembling critical slowing down near equilibrium phase transitions. Near a Hopf bifurcation, the correlations also show damped oscillations. These results make local fluctuations informative about collective network dynamics and provide quantities for comparing theoretical models with observed cortical activity.
summary.tldr: Neural correlations are weak in stationary networks but grow stronger and persist longer near transitions to nonstationary activity.

title: Correlation Functions in a Large Stochastic Neural Network

abstract: This paper studies the problem of diffusion in Markovian models, such as hidden Markov models (HMMs) and how it makes very difficult the task of learning of long-term dependencies in sequences. Using results from Markov chain theory, we show that the problem of diffusion is reduced if the transition probabilities approach 0 or 1. Under this condition, standard HMMs have very limited modeling capabilities, but input/output HMMs can still perform interesting computations.
originalAbstract: This paper studies the problem of diffusion in Markovian models, such as hidden Markov models (HMMs) and how it makes very difficult the task of learning of long-term dependencies in sequences. Using results from Markov chain theory, we show that the problem of diffusion is reduced if the transition probabilities approach 0 or 1. Under this condition, standard HMMs have very limited modeling capabilities, but input/output HMMs can still perform interesting computations.

paragraphs: The paper examines why Markovian sequence models can struggle to learn relationships between events separated by long intervals. Its focus is diffusion: as transitions accumulate, the information needed to connect later outcomes to earlier states becomes dispersed. That makes assigning learning credit across a long sequence difficult, including in hidden Markov models.

Using results from Markov chain theory, the authors show that diffusion decreases when transition probabilities approach zero or one. Such transitions are closer to definite choices than uncertain branching. The result identifies a structural condition that can help preserve the distinctions needed to learn dependencies over longer spans.

That condition has different consequences for different model families. Standard hidden Markov models have very restricted modeling capabilities when their transitions become nearly deterministic. Input/output hidden Markov models can still perform useful computations in this regime. The paper therefore identifies both a way to reduce diffusion and a tradeoff: preserving temporal credit can constrain what a model expresses, with the severity depending on its architecture.
summary.tldr: Nearly deterministic transitions reduce credit diffusion, but their effect on modeling capacity differs between standard and input/output HMMs.

title: Diffusion of Credit in Markovian Models

abstract: Dual-Route and Connectionist Single-Route models of reading have been at odds over claims as to the correct explanation of the reading process. Recent Dual-Route models predict that subjects should show an increased naming latency for irregular words when the irregularity is earlier in the word (e.g. chef is slower than glow) - a prediction that has been confirmed in human experiments. Since this would appear to be an effect of the left-to-right reading process, Coltheart & Rastle (1994) claim that Single-Route parallel connectionist models cannot account for it. A refutation of this claim is presented here, consisting of network models which do show the interaction, along with orthographic neighborhood statistics that explain the effect.

paragraphs: This paper examines a dispute about what the timing of reading aloud reveals about the reading process. Human experiments show increased naming latency for irregular words when the irregularity occurs earlier in the word. Dual-route models predict this effect, and it has been interpreted as evidence for a left-to-right component of reading.

The disputed claim is that a single-route connectionist model processing information in parallel cannot reproduce that position-dependent effect. The authors present network models that do show the interaction. Their result provides a counterexample to the claim that this particular behavioral pattern is unavailable to parallel single-route models.

The paper also uses orthographic neighborhood statistics—the patterns among words with related spellings—to explain the effect. This connects naming latency to the structure of the word relationships represented by the models. The finding matters for interpreting behavioral evidence: an effect that appears to reflect serial processing can also arise in a parallel connectionist account through the organization of spelling neighborhoods.
summary.tldr: Parallel single-route reading networks reproduce an irregularity-position effect previously claimed to require serial processing.

title: Serial Order in Reading Aloud: Connectionist Models and Neighborhood Structure

abstract: Massive transaction data sets are recorded in a routine manner in telecommunications, retail commerce, and Web site management. In this paper we address the problem of inferring predictive in- dividual proﬂles from such historical transaction data. We de- scribe a generative mixture model for count data and use an an approximate Bayesian estimation framework that eﬁectively com- bines an individual’s speciﬂc history with more general population patterns. We use a large real-world retail transaction data set to illustrate how these proﬂles consistently outperform non-mixture and non-Bayesian techniques in predicting customer behavior in out-of-sample data.

paragraphs: The paper asks how historical transaction records can be turned into predictive profiles for individuals. Such records arise routinely in retail, telecommunications, and website management. The task is to use a person's recorded behavior to anticipate future behavior, while also drawing on regularities found across the wider population.

The authors build a generative mixture model for count data and estimate it using an approximate Bayesian framework. The mixture represents population patterns, while the Bayesian estimation combines those patterns with an individual's own history. The resulting profile therefore incorporates both sources of information within one predictive modeling approach.

A large real-world retail dataset provides the demonstration. On transactions held out from fitting, the profiles consistently outperform the non-mixture and non-Bayesian techniques considered. This means their advantage concerns predictions on unseen data, rather than only descriptions of past records. The findings support combining population structure and individual evidence when constructing customer profiles in the studied retail setting.
summary.tldr: Bayesian mixture profiles combine individual histories with population patterns and improve held-out customer-behavior predictions on a large retail dataset.

title: Bayesian Predictive Profiles With Applications to Retail Transaction Data

abstract: Recently proposed algorithms for nonlinear dimensionality reduction fall broadly into two categories which have different advantages and disad- vantages: global (Isomap [1]), and local (Locally Linear Embedding [2], Laplacian Eigenmaps [3]). We present two variants of Isomap which combine the advantages of the global approach with what have previ- ously been exclusive advantages of local methods: computational spar- sity and the ability to invert conformal maps.
originalAbstract: Recently proposed algorithms for nonlinear dimensionality reduction fall broadly into two categories which have different advantages and disad- vantages: global (Isomap [1]), and local (Locally Linear Embedding [2], Laplacian Eigenmaps [3]). We present two variants of Isomap which combine the advantages of the global approach with what have previ- ously been exclusive advantages of local methods: computational spar- sity and the ability to invert conformal maps.

paragraphs: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction seeks a lower-dimensional representation of data whose structure need not be captured by a linear transformation. The paper organizes existing approaches into two broad groups: global methods, represented by Isomap, and local methods, represented by Locally Linear Embedding and Laplacian Eigenmaps. Each group offers different advantages and disadvantages.

The authors present two variants of Isomap intended to combine benefits from these groups. They retain advantages of the global approach while incorporating computational sparsity and the ability to invert conformal maps. These are the two properties that the abstract identifies as previously exclusive advantages of local methods.

The importance of the result is that choosing a global approach need not exclude those particular local-method benefits. Computational sparsity concerns how much of the relevant computation must be represented or carried out, while conformal-map inversion concerns the kinds of mappings the method can handle. The contribution is a pair of algorithmic variants that narrow this specific divide between global and local dimensionality reduction.
summary.tldr: Two Isomap variants combine global-method advantages with computational sparsity and the ability to invert conformal maps.

title: Global Versus Local Methods in Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: We present a method to distinguish direct connections between two neu- rons from common input originating from other, unmeasured neurons. The distinction is computed from the spike times of the two neurons in response to a white noise stimulus. Although the method is based on a highly idealized linear-nonlinear approximation of neural response, we demonstrate via simulation that the approach can work with a more re- alistic, integrate-and-ﬁre neuron model. We propose that the approach exempliﬁed by this analysis may yield viable tools for reconstructing stimulus-driven neural networks from data gathered in neurophysiology experiments.
originalAbstract: We present a method to distinguish direct connections between two neu- rons from common input originating from other, unmeasured neurons. The distinction is computed from the spike times of the two neurons in response to a white noise stimulus. Although the method is based on a highly idealized linear-nonlinear approximation of neural response, we demonstrate via simulation that the approach can work with a more re- alistic, integrate-and-ﬁre neuron model. We propose that the approach exempliﬁed by this analysis may yield viable tools for reconstructing stimulus-driven neural networks from data gathered in neurophysiology experiments.

paragraphs: Similar activity in two neurons can reflect a direct connection or input that both receive from other neurons. The paper presents a method for distinguishing these explanations even when the neurons supplying common input are unmeasured. It uses the spike times of two recorded neurons responding to a white-noise stimulus.

The method is derived from a highly idealized linear-nonlinear approximation of neural responses. This assumption provides the analytical basis for separating direct interaction from shared input. The authors then test whether the approach can work beyond that idealized response description by simulating a more realistic integrate-and-fire neuron model.

The simulations demonstrate that the approach can work with that model. This supports the possibility that the analysis could inform practical tools for reconstructing stimulus-driven neural networks from physiological recordings. The evidence establishes feasibility in simulation, and the abstract presents experimental reconstruction as a prospective use. The key contribution is a stimulus-based way to address an ambiguity that otherwise complicates inference from paired neural spike activity.
summary.tldr: A spike-time method distinguishes direct neural connections from shared hidden input, with feasibility demonstrated in integrate-and-fire simulations.

title: Reconstructing Stimulus-Driven Neural Networks from Spike Times

abstract: nspired by events ranging from 9/11 to the collapse of the accounting ﬁrm Arthur Ander- sen, economists Kunreuther and Heal [5] recently introduced an interesting game-theoretic model for problems of interdependent security (IDS), in which a large number of players must make individual investment decisions related to security — whether physical, ﬁnan- cial, medical, or some other type — but in which the ultimate safety of each participant may depend in a complex way on the actions of the entire population. A simple example is the choice of whether to install a ﬁre sprinkler system in an individual condominium in a large building. While such a system might greatly reduce the chances of the owner’s prop- erty being destroyed by a ﬁre originating within their own unit, it might do little or nothing to reduce the chances of damage caused by ﬁres originating in other units (since sprinklers can usually only douse small ﬁres early). If “enough” other unit owners have not made the investment in sprinklers, it may be not cost-effective for any individual to do so.

If “enough” other unit owners have not made the investment in sprinklers, it may be not cost-effective for any individual to do so.

paragraphs: The supplied abstract introduces interdependent security as a problem in which people make separate protective investments, but their eventual safety depends on what others do. The relevant decisions can concern physical, financial, medical, or other forms of security. The key issue is that an individual’s protection cannot always be evaluated independently of the surrounding population.

A condominium sprinkler system illustrates the reasoning. Installing sprinklers may greatly reduce damage from a fire that starts inside the owner’s unit. The same installation may provide little protection against a fire that has already grown elsewhere in the building, because sprinklers can usually extinguish only small fires at an early stage.

This dependence changes the incentive to invest. If sufficiently many neighbors leave their units unprotected, outside fire risk may make an individual installation no longer cost-effective. The example explains why a protective measure can be useful against a local hazard yet unattractive as an individual purchase. It motivates studying security investment as an interacting set of decisions across a population.
summary.tldr: Interdependent security models explain how other people’s choices can make an individually protective investment no longer cost-effective.

title: Algorithms for Interdependent Security Games

abstract: Dopamine exerts two classes of effect on the sustained neural activity in prefrontal cortex that underlies working memory. Direct release in the cortex increases the contrast of prefrontal neurons, enhancing the ro- bustness of storage. Release of dopamine in the striatum is associated with salient stimuli and makes medium spiny neurons bistable; this mod- ulation of the output of spiny neurons affects prefrontal cortex so as to indirectly gate access to working memory and additionally damp sensi- tivity to noise. Existing models have treated dopamine in one or other structure, or have addressed basal ganglia gating of working memory ex- clusive of dopamine effects. In this paper we combine these mechanisms and explore their joint effect. We model a memory-guided saccade task to illustrate how dopamine’s actions lead to working memory that is se- lective for salient input and has increased robustness to distraction.

paragraphs: Working memory depends on sustained activity in prefrontal cortex, and this paper combines two ways dopamine influences that activity. Dopamine released directly in cortex increases neuronal contrast and strengthens storage. Dopamine released in the striatum affects access to working memory through a different route involving medium spiny neurons.

In the striatal mechanism, dopamine associated with salient stimuli makes these neurons bistable, allowing two stable activity states. Changes in their output indirectly gate access to prefrontal working memory and reduce sensitivity to noise. The model brings this mechanism together with dopamine’s direct cortical effects, which previous models had considered separately or without the full dopamine contribution.

The authors explore the combined mechanisms using a memory-guided saccade task, in which remembered information guides an eye movement. The model illustrates how dopamine’s joint actions can favor salient inputs while making maintained information more resistant to distraction. Its contribution is a unified account of how selecting what enters memory and stabilizing what remains there can work together.
summary.tldr: A combined cortical and striatal dopamine model illustrates how working memory can select salient input and resist distraction.

title: Dopamine Modulation in a Basal Ganglio-Cortical Network of Working Memory

abstract: We present a novel method for learning with Gaussian process regression in a hierarchical Bayesian framework. In a first step, kernel matrices on a fixed set of input points are learned from data using a simple and efficient EM algorithm. This step is nonparametric, in that it does not require a parametric form of covariance function. In a second step, kernel functions are fitted to approximate the learned covariance matrix using a generalized Nyström method, which results in a complex, data driven kernel. We evaluate our approach as a recommendation engine for art images, where the proposed hierarchical Bayesian method leads to excellent prediction performance.

In a first step, kernel matrices on a fixed set of input points are learned from data using a simple and efficient EM algorithm. This step is nonparametric, in that it does not require a parametric form of covariance function. In a second step, kernel functions are fitted to approximate the learned covariance matrix using a generalized Nyström method, which results in a complex, data driven kernel. We evaluate our approach as a recommendation engine for art images, where the proposed hierarchical Bayesian method leads to excellent prediction performance.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian approach to learning kernels for Gaussian-process regression. A kernel describes relationships among inputs, so learning it from data makes those relationships part of the estimation task. The authors divide this process into learning a covariance matrix and then constructing a function that approximates it.

The first stage uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to learn kernel matrices on a fixed collection of input points. This stage is nonparametric in the specific sense that it does not require a prescribed parametric covariance-function form. The authors describe the learning algorithm as simple and efficient, allowing the matrix structure to be driven by data.

The second stage fits kernel functions to the learned matrix using a generalized Nyström method. This turns the matrix-level result into a complex, data-driven kernel. The approach is evaluated as an art-image recommendation engine, where the authors report excellent prediction performance. That evaluation supports the usefulness of the two-stage construction in the recommendation setting studied.
summary.tldr: A two-stage hierarchical Bayesian method learns covariance matrices and fits data-driven Gaussian-process kernels, with strong reported art-recommendation performance.

title: Learning Gaussian Process Kernels via Hierarchical Bayes

abstract: A non–linear dynamic system is called contracting if initial conditions are for- gotten exponentially fast, so that all trajectories converge to a single trajectory. We use contraction theory to derive an upper bound for the strength of recurrent connections that guarantees contraction for complex neural networks. Speciﬁ- cally, we apply this theory to a special class of recurrent networks, often called Cooperative Competitive Networks (CCNs), which are an abstract representation of the cooperative-competitive connectivity observed in cortex. This speciﬁc type of network is believed to play a major role in shaping cortical responses and se- lecting the relevant signal among distractors and noise. In this paper, we analyze contraction of combined CCNs of linear threshold units and verify the results of our analysis in a hybrid analog/digital VLSI CCN comprising spiking neurons and dynamic synapses.
originalAbstract: A non–linear dynamic system is called contracting if initial conditions are for- gotten exponentially fast, so that all trajectories converge to a single trajectory. We use contraction theory to derive an upper bound for the strength of recurrent connections that guarantees contraction for complex neural networks. Speciﬁ- cally, we apply this theory to a special class of recurrent networks, often called Cooperative Competitive Networks (CCNs), which are an abstract representation of the cooperative-competitive connectivity observed in cortex. This speciﬁc type of network is believed to play a major role in shaping cortical responses and se- lecting the relevant signal among distractors and noise. paragraphs: A contracting dynamical system progressively loses the influence of its starting conditions: differences between trajectories shrink exponentially until they converge to a common trajectory. This paper uses contraction theory to analyze recurrent neural networks. It derives an upper bound on recurrent connection strength that is sufficient to guarantee this behavior.

The analysis focuses on cooperative competitive networks, whose connectivity abstracts patterns of cooperation and competition observed in cortex. Such networks are believed to help shape cortical responses and select relevant signals amid distractors and noise. A contraction guarantee provides a way to reason about whether recurrent interactions will forget initial conditions, rather than preserve different trajectories indefinitely.

The authors analyze combinations of these networks using linear threshold units, then verify their analytical results in a hybrid analog and digital VLSI implementation containing spiking neurons and dynamic synapses. This connects a mathematical condition to a physical neural-network circuit. The bound supplies a sufficient condition for contraction; the abstract does not characterize it as a necessary boundary for all contracting networks.
summary.tldr: Contraction theory yields a sufficient bound on recurrent connection strength, verified in a spiking-neuron hardware network.

title: Contraction Properties of VLSI Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks of Spiking Neurons

abstract: With the increased availability of data for complex domains, it is desirable to learn Bayesian network structures that are sufficiently expressive for generalization while also allowing for tractable inference. While the method of thin junction trees can, in principle, be used for this purpose, its fully greedy nature makes it prone to overfitting, particularly when data is scarce. In this work we present a novel method for learning Bayesian networks of bounded treewidth that employs global structure modifications and that is polynomial in the size of the graph and the treewidth bound. At the heart of our method is a triangulated graph that we dynamically update in a way that facilitates the addition of chain structures that increase the bound on the model's treewidth by at most one. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our ``treewidth-friendly'' method on several real-life datasets. Importantly, we also show that by using global operators, we are able to achieve better generalization even when learning Bayesian networks of unbounded treewidth.

While the method of thin junction trees can, in principle, be used for this purpose, its fully greedy nature makes it prone to overfitting, particularly when data is scarce. In this work we present a novel method for learning Bayesian networks of bounded treewidth that employs global structure modifications and that is polynomial in the size of the graph and the treewidth bound. At the heart of our method is a triangulated graph that we dynamically update in a way that facilitates the addition of chain structures that increase the bound on the model's treewidth by at most one. paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves balancing expressive structure against the cost of inference. Bounding treewidth helps keep inference tractable, but learning within that restriction can be difficult. The paper highlights that the fully greedy thin-junction-tree approach can overfit, especially with limited data, and proposes learning through more global changes to network structure.

The method maintains a triangulated graph and updates it dynamically to permit the addition of chain structures. These additions increase the treewidth bound by at most one. The resulting learning procedure is polynomial in both graph size and the treewidth bound, combining controlled structural growth with a computationally manageable search procedure.

Experiments on several real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. The authors also report better generalization from global operators when learning networks without a treewidth restriction. That additional finding suggests that the benefit of their structural changes extends beyond enforcing tractable inference: the way the search modifies a network can also improve the learned model's generalization in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Global structural updates enable efficient learning of bounded-treewidth Bayesian networks and improve generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Learning Bounded Treewidth Bayesian Networks

abstract: Our setting is a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process with continuous state, observation and action spaces. Decisions are based on a Particle Filter for estimating the belief state given past observations. We consider a policy gradient approach for parameterized policy optimization. For that purpose, we investigate sensitivity analysis of the performance measure with respect to the parameters of the policy, focusing on Finite Difference (FD) techniques. We show that the naive FD is subject to variance explosion because of the non-smoothness of the resampling procedure. We propose a more sophisticated FD method which overcomes this problem and establish its consistency.
originalAbstract: Our setting is a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process with continuous state, observation and action spaces. Decisions are based on a Particle Filter for estimating the belief state given past observations. We consider a policy gradient approach for parameterized policy optimization. For that purpose, we investigate sensitivity analysis of the performance measure with respect to the parameters of the policy, focusing on Finite Difference (FD) techniques. We show that the naive FD is subject to variance explosion because of the non-smoothness of the resampling procedure. We propose a more sophisticated FD method which overcomes this problem and establish its consistency.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making when the true state is only partially observed and states, observations, and actions are continuous. A particle filter estimates the belief state from past observations, and decisions depend on that estimate. The goal is to improve a parameterized policy by measuring how its performance changes with its parameters.

The authors focus on finite differences, which estimate sensitivity by comparing performance under small parameter changes. They show that a naive implementation suffers from exploding variance. The source is the non-smooth resampling operation inside the particle filter: this internal step makes straightforward sensitivity estimation unstable even though the ultimate target is policy performance.

They propose a more sophisticated finite-difference method that overcomes this problem and prove its consistency. The contribution addresses the interaction between state estimation and policy optimization, rather than treating the particle filter as an inconsequential component. It provides a theoretically supported way to estimate policy sensitivity in the stated continuous, partially observed setting.
summary.tldr: A consistent finite-difference method avoids the variance explosion caused by particle-filter resampling during policy optimization.

title: Particle Filter-based Policy Gradient in POMDPs

abstract: This paper considers the problem of combining multiple models to achieve a prediction accuracy not much worse than that of the best single model for least squares regression. It is known that if the models are mis-specified, model averaging is superior to model selection. Specifically, let $n$ be the sample size, then the worst case regret of the former decays at the rate of $O(1/n)$ while the worst case regret of the latter decays at the rate of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$. In the literature, the most important and widely studied model averaging method that achieves the optimal $O(1/n)$ average regret is the exponential weighted model averaging (EWMA) algorithm. However this method suffers from several limitations. The purpose of this paper is to present a new greedy model averaging procedure that improves EWMA. We prove strong theoretical guarantees for the new procedure and illustrate our theoretical results with empirical examples.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine candidate models for least-squares regression so that predictions are not much worse than those of the best individual candidate. The relevant quantity is regret: the additional prediction error relative to that best model. This comparison remains useful when the candidates are misspecified, meaning none necessarily describes the data correctly.

The abstract highlights an established distinction between averaging and selecting models. Under misspecification, the worst-case regret for averaging decreases at order 1/n, whereas selecting one model has a rate of order 1/sqrt(n). Exponentially weighted model averaging is an important existing method that achieves the optimal 1/n average-regret rate, but the authors identify it as having limitations.

The proposed contribution is a new greedy averaging procedure intended to improve on exponential weighting. The authors prove strong theoretical guarantees and illustrate their results empirically. The significance is a new procedure for obtaining reliable combined predictions within a setting where averaging already has a favorable theoretical advantage over choosing a single candidate.
summary.tldr: A greedy model-averaging procedure offers theoretically supported improvements over exponential weighting for least-squares regression.

title: Greedy Model Averaging

abstract: We present an asymptotic analysis of Viterbi Training (VT) and contrast it with a more conventional Maximum Likelihood (ML) approach to parameter estimation in Hidden Markov Models. While ML estimator works by (locally) maximizing the likelihood of the observed data, VT seeks to maximize the probability of the most likely hidden state sequence. We develop an analytical framework based on a generating function formalism and illustrate it on an exactly solvable model of HMM with one unambiguous symbol. For this particular model the ML objective function is continuously degenerate. VT objective, in contrast, is shown to have only finite degeneracy. Furthermore, VT converges faster and results in sparser (simpler) models, thus realizing an automatic Occam's razor for HMM learning. For more general scenario VT can be worse compared to ML but still capable of correctly recovering most of the parameters.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models explain observed sequences through underlying states that are not directly visible. This paper compares two ways to estimate their parameters. Maximum likelihood locally maximizes the likelihood of the observations, while Viterbi training pursues the probability of the most likely hidden-state sequence. Those different objectives can favor different fitted models.

The authors develop an asymptotic analysis using generating functions and apply it to an exactly solvable model containing one unambiguous symbol. In this model, the maximum-likelihood objective has a continuous degeneracy, meaning a continuum of equivalent solutions. The Viterbi objective instead has only finite degeneracy, narrowing the corresponding set of alternatives.

The analysis also finds faster convergence and sparser models for Viterbi training, giving it an automatic preference for simpler explanations in the studied setting. These benefits do not establish universal superiority: in a more general scenario, Viterbi training can perform worse than maximum likelihood while still recovering most parameters correctly. The paper thus explains both an attraction of Viterbi training and a qualification to that attraction.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic comparison shows why Viterbi training can favor simpler HMMs, while also identifying settings where maximum likelihood performs better.

title: Comparative Analysis of Viterbi Training and Maximum Likelihood Estimation for HMMs

abstract: Loopy belief propagation performs approximate inference on graphical models with loops. One might hope to compensate for the approximation by adjusting model parameters. Learning algorithms for this purpose have been explored previously, and the claim has been made that every set of locally consistent marginals can arise from belief propagation run on a graphical model. On the contrary, here we show that many probability distributions have marginals that cannot be reached by belief propagation using any set of model parameters or any learning algorithm. We call such marginals `unbelievable.' This problem occurs whenever the Hessian of the Bethe free energy is not positive-definite at the target marginals. All learning algorithms for belief propagation necessarily fail in these cases, producing beliefs or sets of beliefs that may even be worse than the pre-learning approximation. We then show that averaging inaccurate beliefs, each obtained from belief propagation using model parameters perturbed about some learned mean values, can achieve the unbelievable marginals.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation approximates probabilities in graphical models containing loops. A natural response to its errors is to adjust the model parameters until its answers match desired marginal probabilities. The paper shows that this strategy has a fundamental obstacle: many target marginals cannot be reached by belief propagation, regardless of the parameters or learning algorithm used.

The authors call these targets unbelievable marginals. They identify a condition under which this problem occurs: the Hessian of the Bethe free energy at the target is not positive-definite. In those cases, learning cannot make belief propagation attain the target, and the resulting beliefs may even be worse than the approximation obtained before learning.

The paper also demonstrates a way to reach such targets through averaging. Belief propagation is run using parameters perturbed around learned mean values, and the resulting inaccurate beliefs are combined. Their average can achieve marginals that an individual run cannot. This distinguishes the limitations of learning a single parameter setting from the possibilities created by aggregating several approximate outputs.
summary.tldr: Some marginal probabilities are unreachable by belief propagation under any parameter setting, but averaging beliefs from perturbed models can achieve them.

title: Learning unbelievable probabilities

abstract: We present a novel method in the family of particle MCMC methods that we refer to as particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling (PG-AS). Similarly to the existing PG with backward simulation (PG-BS) procedure, we use backward sampling to (considerably) improve the mixing of the PG kernel. Instead of using separate forward and backward sweeps as in PG-BS, however, we achieve the same effect in a single forward sweep. We apply the PG-AS framework to the challenging class of non-Markovian state-space models. We develop a truncation strategy of these models that is applicable in principle to any backward-simulation-based method, but which is particularly well suited to the PG-AS framework. In particular, as we show in a simulation study, PG-AS can yield an order-of-magnitude improved accuracy relative to PG-BS due to its robustness to the truncation error. Several application examples are discussed, including Rao-Blackwellized particle smoothing and inference in degenerate state-space models.

paragraphs: Particle Gibbs is a sampling method for inference in models with hidden states. This paper introduces particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling, or PG-AS, to improve mixing: how effectively successive samples move through the possibilities represented by the model. It targets the improvement previously obtained by particle Gibbs with backward simulation, or PG-BS.

The main algorithmic change is to obtain that backward-sampling effect within a single forward sweep. PG-BS instead uses separate forward and backward sweeps. The authors apply this framework to non-Markovian state-space models, where dependencies extend beyond the immediately preceding state, and develop a truncation strategy for handling those dependencies.

The truncation strategy is applicable in principle to other methods based on backward simulation, but the authors find it particularly suitable for PG-AS. In a simulation study, PG-AS can achieve an order-of-magnitude accuracy improvement over PG-BS because it is more robust to truncation error. This is a qualified empirical finding, tied to the approximation being used. The paper also discusses particle smoothing and inference in degenerate state-space models.
summary.tldr: Ancestor sampling gives particle Gibbs a backward-sampling benefit in one forward sweep and can improve robustness to truncated dependencies.

title: Ancestor Sampling for Particle Gibbs

abstract: Recent approaches to collaborative filtering have concentrated on estimating an algebraic or statistical model, and using the model for predicting missing ratings. In this paper we observe that different models have relative advantages in different regions of the input space. This motivates our approach of using stagewise linear combinations of collaborative filtering algorithms, with non-constant combination coefficients based on kernel smoothing. The resulting stagewise model is computationally scalable and outperforms a wide selection of state-of-the-art collaborative filtering algorithms.
originalAbstract: Recent approaches to collaborative filtering have concentrated on estimating an algebraic or statistical model, and using the model for predicting missing ratings. This motivates our approach of using stagewise linear combinations of collaborative filtering algorithms, with non-constant combination coefficients based on kernel smoothing. The resulting stagewise model is computationally scalable and outperforms a wide selection of state-of-the-art collaborative filtering algorithms.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering predicts missing ratings using patterns in observed ratings. The paper starts from the observation that different prediction models have different strengths in different regions of the input space. A model that works well for one part of the prediction problem may therefore be less suitable for another part.

The proposed approach builds a stagewise linear combination of collaborative filtering algorithms. Its combination coefficients are not constant: they vary across the input space using kernel smoothing. This gives the combined predictor a way to adjust how much it relies on each component according to where a prediction is being made. The underlying observation about local strengths is thus reflected directly in the combination mechanism.

The authors report that the resulting model is computationally scalable and outperforms a wide selection of state-of-the-art collaborative filtering algorithms. The stated result supports combining existing predictors in a locally adaptive way. The contribution centers on how models are assembled and weighted, making their differing areas of strength useful within a single rating predictor.
summary.tldr: A scalable stagewise recommender combines collaborative filtering algorithms with weights that adapt across the input space.

title: Automatic Feature Induction for Stagewise Collaborative Filtering

abstract: With simultaneous measurements from ever increasing populations of neurons, there is a growing need for sophisticated tools to recover signals from individual neurons. In electrophysiology experiments, this classically proceeds in a two-step process: (i) threshold the waveforms to detect putative spikes and (ii) cluster the waveforms into single units (neurons). We extend previous Bayesian nonparamet- ric models of neural spiking to jointly detect and cluster neurons using a Gamma process model. Importantly, we develop an online approximate inference scheme enabling real-time analysis, with performance exceeding the previous state-of-the- art. Via exploratory data analysis—using data with partial ground truth as well as two novel data sets—we find several features of our model collectively contribute to our improved performance including: (i) accounting for colored noise, (ii) de- tecting overlapping spikes, (iii) tracking waveform dynamics, and (iv) using mul- tiple channels. We hope to enable novel experiments simultaneously measuring many thousands of neurons and possibly adapting stimuli dynamically to probe ever deeper into the mysteries of the brain.

paragraphs: Electrophysiology recordings contain signals from multiple neurons. A traditional analysis first thresholds waveforms to identify possible spikes and then clusters those waveforms into individual neurons. This paper combines detection and clustering within a Gamma process model, extending earlier Bayesian nonparametric approaches to neural spiking.

The authors develop an online approximate inference procedure that enables real-time analysis and reports performance beyond the previous state of the art. Their model accounts for colored noise, detects overlapping spikes, tracks changes in waveforms, and uses multiple recording channels. These features address several aspects of the recorded signals within the same inference framework.

Exploratory analyses use data with partial ground truth and two new datasets. The authors find that the listed model features collectively contribute to improved performance, supporting their combined use rather than attributing the gains to a single feature. They present experiments measuring thousands of neurons and dynamically adapting stimuli as future possibilities they hope to enable, rather than capabilities already demonstrated by the reported analysis.
summary.tldr: An online Gamma process model jointly detects and clusters neural spikes, enabling real-time analysis with improved reported performance.

title: Real-Time Inference for a Gamma Process Model of Neural Spiking

abstract: Patch-based methods have been widely used for noise reduction in recent years. In this paper, we propose a general statistical aggregation method which combines image patches denoised with several commonly-used algorithms. We show that weakly denoised versions of the input image obtained with standard methods, can serve to compute an efficient patch-based aggregated estimd aggregation (EWA) estimator. The resulting approach (PEWA) is based on a MCMC sampling and has a nice statistical foundation while producing denoising results that are comparable to the current state-of-the-art. We demonstrate the performance of the denoising algorithm on real images and we compare the results to several competitive methods.

We show that weakly denoised versions of the input image obtained with standard methods, can serve to compute an efficient patch-based aggregated estimd aggregation (EWA) estimator. The resulting approach (PEWA) is based on a MCMC sampling and has a nice statistical foundation while producing denoising results that are comparable to the current state-of-the-art. We demonstrate the performance of the denoising algorithm on real images and we compare the results to several competitive methods.

paragraphs: PEWA addresses image denoising by combining the outputs of several existing algorithms at the patch level. Its starting point is that different denoised versions of an image can supply material for a statistical aggregate. The paper proposes a general aggregation method, making the combination of those outputs the central contribution.

The authors show that even weakly denoised versions produced by standard methods can be used to compute an efficient patch-based estimator. The approach uses exponentially weighted aggregation and relies on MCMC sampling. This gives the combination a statistical foundation and provides a computational method for forming the resulting denoised estimate.

Experiments on real images compare PEWA with several competitive denoising methods. The authors report results comparable to the state of the art, rather than claiming that aggregation consistently exceeds every alternative. The finding is that a statistically grounded combination of patches from existing denoisers can itself be competitive. It also establishes that the intermediate denoised images need not already be strong final solutions to serve as useful inputs to the aggregation.
summary.tldr: PEWA statistically aggregates patches from existing denoisers using MCMC, achieving results reported as comparable to the state of the art.

title: PEWA: Patch-based Exponentially Weighted Aggregation for image denoising

abstract: We propose a two-layer spiking network capable of performing approximate inference and learning for a hidden Markov model. The lower layer sensory neurons detect noisy measurements of hidden world states. The higher layer neurons with recurrent connections infer a posterior distribution over world states from spike trains generated by sensory neurons. We show how such a neuronal network with synaptic plasticity can implement a form of Bayesian inference similar to Monte Carlo methods such as particle filtering. Each spike in the population of inference neurons represents a sample of a particular hidden world state. The spiking activity across the neural population approximates the posterior distribution of hidden state. The model provides a functional explanation for the Poisson-like noise commonly observed in cortical responses. Uncertainties in spike times provide the necessary variability for sampling during inference. Unlike previous models, the hidden world state is not observed by the sensory neurons, and the temporal dynamics of the hidden state is unknown. We demonstrate how this network can sequentially learn the hidden Markov model using a spike-timing dependent Hebbian learning rule and achieve power-law convergence rates.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a two-layer spiking neural network that approximately infers and learns a hidden Markov model. Sensory neurons receive noisy measurements of an unobserved world state. A recurrent upper layer uses their spike trains to infer a probability distribution over possible states, allowing the model to represent uncertainty.

Each spike in the inference population acts as a sample of a particular hidden state. Activity across the population approximates the posterior distribution through a process similar to Monte Carlo methods such as particle filtering. Variability in spike timing supplies the randomness needed for sampling, offering a functional explanation for Poisson-like variability in cortical responses.

The network does not require sensory neurons to observe the hidden state directly, and the state's temporal dynamics are initially unknown. The authors demonstrate sequential learning of the hidden Markov model through a spike-timing-dependent Hebbian rule, with power-law convergence rates. The result links approximate probabilistic inference and learning to a common mechanism built from spikes, recurrent connections, and synaptic plasticity.
summary.tldr: A two-layer spiking network uses spikes as samples to approximately infer hidden states and learn their unknown dynamics.

title: Neurons as Monte Carlo Samplers: Bayesian ￼Inference and Learning in Spiking Networks

abstract: Semantic matching is of central importance to many natural language tasks \cite{bordes2014semantic,RetrievalQA}. A successful matching algorithm needs to adequately model the internal structures of language objects and the interaction between them. As a step toward this goal, we propose convolutional neural network models for matching two sentences, by adapting the convolutional strategy in vision and speech. The proposed models not only nicely represent the hierarchical structures of sentences with their layer-by-layer composition and pooling, but also capture the rich matching patterns at different levels. Our models are rather generic, requiring no prior knowledge on language, and can hence be applied to matching tasks of different nature and in different languages. The empirical study on a variety of matching tasks demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed model on a variety of matching tasks and its superiority to competitor models.

paragraphs: The paper addresses semantic matching between two sentences. A useful matcher must account for the structure within each sentence and the interactions between the sentences. The authors propose convolutional neural network architectures that bring these two requirements together, adapting a modeling strategy already used in vision and speech to sentence pairs.

The models build sentence representations through successive layers of composition and pooling. This layered construction represents hierarchical structure while also capturing matching patterns at different levels. The approach therefore treats sentence matching as more than a comparison of two undifferentiated inputs: the representations and their relationships can reflect multiple levels of sentence organization.

The architectures are presented as generic and do not require prior language knowledge, supporting their application to different kinds of matching tasks and different languages. Experiments across a variety of matching tasks demonstrate effectiveness and report stronger results than the competitor models evaluated. The contribution is an architecture for learning sentence structure and cross-sentence relationships together, with empirical support across several matching settings.
summary.tldr: Convolutional sentence-matching models learn hierarchical sentence structure and interactions at multiple levels, outperforming evaluated competitors across varied matching tasks.

title: Convolutional Neural Network Architectures for Matching Natural Language Sentences

abstract: The goal of precipitation nowcasting is to predict the future rainfall intensity in a local region over a relatively short period of time. Very few previous studies have examined this crucial and challenging weather forecasting problem from the machine learning perspective. In this paper, we formulate precipitation nowcasting as a spatiotemporal sequence forecasting problem in which both the input and the prediction target are spatiotemporal sequences. By extending the fully connected LSTM (FC-LSTM) to have convolutional structures in both the input-to-state and state-to-state transitions, we propose the convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) and use it to build an end-to-end trainable model for the precipitation nowcasting problem. Experiments show that our ConvLSTM network captures spatiotemporal correlations better and consistently outperforms FC-LSTM and the state-of-the-art operational ROVER algorithm for precipitation nowcasting.

paragraphs: Precipitation nowcasting asks how rainfall intensity will change across a local region over a short period. This paper represents the task as predicting a sequence of spatial observations from an earlier sequence. That formulation makes both the arrangement of rainfall across space and its evolution through time central to the learning problem.

The authors introduce a convolutional LSTM by replacing fully connected structures with convolutional structures in two places: the transition from input to internal state and the transition between successive states. The resulting recurrent model is designed to represent spatial relationships while carrying information through time. They use this component to construct a model that can be trained end to end for rainfall prediction.

In the reported experiments, ConvLSTM captures spatial and temporal correlations better and consistently outperforms both a fully connected LSTM and the operational ROVER forecasting algorithm. These findings support the architectural choice of incorporating convolution into both transitions. The contribution is a forecasting formulation and a matching recurrent architecture, with empirical evidence that their combination improves precipitation nowcasting.
summary.tldr: ConvLSTM uses convolutional input and recurrent transitions to model rainfall sequences and outperforms FC-LSTM and ROVER in the reported experiments.

title: Convolutional LSTM Network: A Machine Learning Approach for Precipitation Nowcasting

abstract: How can one find a subset, ideally as small as possible, that well represents a massive dataset? I.e., its corresponding utility, measured according to a suitable utility function, should be comparable to that of the whole dataset. In this paper, we formalize this challenge as a submodular cover problem. Here, the utility is assumed to exhibit submodularity, a natural diminishing returns condition preva- lent in many data summarization applications. The classical greedy algorithm is known to provide solutions with logarithmic approximation guarantees compared to the optimum solution. However, this sequential, centralized approach is imprac- tical for truly large-scale problems. In this work, we develop the first distributed algorithm – DISCOVER – for submodular set cover that is easily implementable using MapReduce-style computations. We theoretically analyze our approach, and present approximation guarantees for the solutions returned by DISCOVER. We also study a natural trade-off between the communication cost and the num- ber of rounds required to obtain such a solution. In our extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several applications, includ- ing active set selection, exemplar based clustering, and vertex cover on tens of millions of data points using Spark.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to choose a small subset that preserves utility comparable to an entire massive dataset. It formulates this as submodular cover, assuming that utility exhibits diminishing returns: an additional item contributes less when much relevant information is already present. This assumption captures a useful structure in many summarization tasks.

A classical greedy algorithm offers a logarithmic approximation guarantee, but its sequential, centralized operation becomes impractical at very large scales. The authors introduce DISCOVER, a distributed algorithm that fits MapReduce-style computation. They analyze the quality of its returned solutions and provide approximation guarantees, connecting distributed execution with a formal account of summary quality.

The paper also investigates the tradeoff between communication costs and the number of computational rounds. Experiments using Spark demonstrate the approach on tens of millions of datapoints across active set selection, exemplar-based clustering, and vertex cover. The contribution is a way to make submodular cover usable at substantial scale while retaining theoretical guarantees about the solutions.
summary.tldr: DISCOVER distributes submodular cover computation to summarize massive datasets with approximation guarantees.

title: Distributed Submodular Cover: Succinctly Summarizing Massive Data

abstract: In the recent years, a number of parameter-free algorithms have been developed for online linear optimization over Hilbert spaces and for learning with expert advice. These algorithms achieve optimal regret bounds that depend on the unknown competitors, without having to tune the learning rates with oracle choices. We present a new intuitive framework to design parameter-free algorithms for both online linear optimization over Hilbert spaces and for learning with expert advice, based on reductions to betting on outcomes of adversarial coins. We instantiate it using a betting algorithm based on the Krichevsky-Trofimov estimator. The resulting algorithms are simple, with no parameters to be tuned, and they improve or match previous results in terms of regret guarantee and per-round complexity.

We present a new intuitive framework to design parameter-free algorithms for both online linear optimization over Hilbert spaces and for learning with expert advice, based on reductions to betting on outcomes of adversarial coins. paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make decisions repeatedly and are judged by regret: how much worse they perform than a comparison strategy. Choosing a learning rate can be difficult when the best choice depends on an unknown competitor. Parameter-free methods seek strong regret guarantees without requiring that information to tune their updates.

This paper develops a common design framework for online linear optimization over Hilbert spaces and learning with expert advice. It reduces these tasks to betting on adversarial coin outcomes. The betting formulation provides a way to construct learning algorithms through another sequential decision problem, rather than choosing learning rates using unavailable knowledge.

The authors instantiate the framework with a betting algorithm based on the Krichevsky–Trofimov estimator. The resulting learning algorithms are simple and require no parameter tuning. Their regret guarantees and computational cost per round improve on or match previous results. The contribution is therefore both a reusable construction and concrete algorithms that retain competitive theoretical guarantees without oracle-selected learning rates.
summary.tldr: Reducing online learning to adversarial coin betting yields simple algorithms with competitive regret bounds and no tuning parameters.

title: Coin Betting and Parameter-Free Online Learning

abstract: We present a novel framework, called GRAB (GRaphical models with overlApping Blocks), to capture densely connected components in a network estimate. GRAB takes as input a data matrix of p variables and n samples, and jointly learns both a network among p variables and densely connected groups of variables (called `blocks'). GRAB has four major novelties as compared to existing network estimation methods: 1) It does not require the blocks to be given a priori. 2) Blocks can overlap. 3) It can jointly learn a network structure and overlapping blocks. 4) It solves a joint optimization problem with the block coordinate descent method that is convex in each step. We show that GRAB reveals the underlying network structure substantially better than four state-of-the-art competitors on synthetic data. When applied to cancer gene expression data, GRAB outperforms its competitors in revealing known functional gene sets and potentially novel genes that drive cancer.
originalAbstract: We present a novel framework, called GRAB (GRaphical models with overlApping Blocks), to capture densely connected components in a network estimate. GRAB takes as input a data matrix of p variables and n samples, and jointly learns both a network among p variables and densely connected groups of variables (called `blocks'). GRAB has four major novelties as compared to existing network estimation methods: 1) It does not require the blocks to be given a priori. 2) Blocks can overlap. 3) It can jointly learn a network structure and overlapping blocks. 4) It solves a joint optimization problem with the block coordinate descent method that is convex in each step. We show that GRAB reveals the underlying network structure substantially better than four state-of-the-art competitors on synthetic data. When applied to cancer gene expression data, GRAB outperforms its competitors in revealing known functional gene sets and potentially novel genes that drive cancer.

paragraphs: When estimating a network from observations, densely connected groups can be an important part of its structure. GRAB learns both a network among measured variables and the dense groups within that network. It takes a matrix of variables and samples as input, without requiring those groups to be supplied in advance.

A central feature is that the groups, called blocks, can overlap. A variable can therefore participate in more than one densely connected component. The method learns this organization jointly with the network itself. Its optimization uses block coordinate descent, with each individual step forming a convex problem; the abstract makes this stepwise convexity claim rather than a claim that the entire joint problem is convex.

On synthetic data, GRAB recovers underlying network structure substantially better than four state-of-the-art competitors. On cancer gene-expression data, it better reveals known functional gene sets and potentially novel cancer-driving genes. The latter are candidate discoveries, while the recovery of known sets provides evidence that the learned overlapping organization captures biologically relevant structure.
summary.tldr: GRAB jointly learns a sparse network and overlapping dense groups, improving structural recovery in synthetic and cancer gene-expression studies.

title: Learning Sparse Gaussian Graphical Models with Overlapping Blocks

abstract: For an autonomous system to be helpful to humans and to pose no unwarranted risks, it needs to align its values with those of the humans in its environment in such a way that its actions contribute to the maximization of value for the humans. We propose a formal definition of the value alignment problem as cooperative inverse reinforcement learning (CIRL). A CIRL problem is a cooperative, partial- information game with two agents, human and robot; both are rewarded according to the human’s reward function, but the robot does not initially know what this is. In contrast to classical IRL, where the human is assumed to act optimally in isolation, optimal CIRL solutions produce behaviors such as active teaching, active learning, and communicative actions that are more effective in achieving value alignment. We show that computing optimal joint policies in CIRL games can be reduced to solving a POMDP, prove that optimality in isolation is suboptimal in CIRL, and derive an approximate CIRL algorithm.

Both participants receive rewards according to the human's reward function, but the robot initially does not know that function. The resulting game combines a common objective with unequal information about what achieving that objective means.

This formulation changes how human behavior should be understood. Classical inverse reinforcement learning assumes that the human acts optimally in isolation. In the cooperative setting, actions can also teach the robot, seek information, or communicate intent. The paper shows that optimal isolated behavior is suboptimal in CIRL, making the interaction itself part of the alignment problem.

The authors show that finding optimal joint policies can be reduced to solving a partially observable Markov decision process, and they derive an approximate CIRL algorithm. The contribution is a formal framework in which teaching and learning can emerge from pursuing a shared reward. Its conclusions depend on that cooperative setup, including the assumption that both agents are rewarded according to the human's preferences.
summary.tldr: CIRL models value alignment as cooperation under uncertainty, making teaching, learning, and communication part of the shared decision problem.

title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural networks (NN) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various applications. Unfortunately in applications where training data is insufficient, they are often prone to overfitting. One effective way to alleviate this problem is to exploit the Bayesian approach by using Bayesian neural networks (BNN). Another shortcoming of NN is the lack of flexibility to customize different distributions for the weights and neurons according to the data, as is often done in probabilistic graphical models. To address these problems, we propose a class of probabilistic neural networks, dubbed natural-parameter networks (NPN), as a novel and lightweight Bayesian treatment of NN. NPN allows the usage of arbitrary exponential-family distributions to model the weights and neurons. Different from traditional NN and BNN, NPN takes distributions as input and goes through layers of transformation before producing distributions to match the target output distributions. As a Bayesian treatment, efficient backpropagation (BP) is performed to learn the natural parameters for the distributions over both the weights and neurons. The output distributions of each layer, as byproducts, may be used as second-order representations for the associated tasks such as link prediction. Experiments on real-world datasets show that NPN can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Natural-parameter networks address two concerns about neural networks: overfitting when training data is scarce and limited flexibility in choosing probability distributions for weights and neurons. The authors propose a lightweight Bayesian network family that allows arbitrary distributions from the exponential family to represent these quantities, making distributional choices part of the model design.

The network receives distributions as inputs, transforms them through its layers, and produces distributions intended to match the target outputs. Training uses efficient backpropagation to learn the natural parameters that specify distributions over both weights and neurons. The approach therefore carries distributional representations through the network rather than restricting its internal computations to single-valued activations.

The distributions produced at intermediate layers also provide representations that may be useful for associated tasks, including link prediction. The authors describe these as second-order representations. Experiments on real-world datasets show that the method can achieve state-of-the-art performance. These findings support the proposed combination of flexible probabilistic modeling and neural-network training, without making performance a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Natural-parameter networks propagate and learn exponential-family distributions over weights and neurons, providing a lightweight Bayesian neural-network approach.

title: Natural-Parameter Networks: A Class of Probabilistic Neural Networks

abstract: We provide new results for noise-tolerant and sample-efficient learning algorithms under $s$-concave distributions. The new class of $s$-concave distributions is a broad and natural generalization of log-concavity, and includes many important additional distributions, e.g., the Pareto distribution and $t$ distribution. This class has been studied in the context of efficient sampling, integration, and optimization, but much remains unknown about the geometry of this class of distributions and their applications in the context of learning. The challenge is that unlike the commonly used distributions in learning (uniform or more generally log-concave distributions), this broader class is not closed under the marginalization operator and many such distributions are fat-tailed. In this work, we introduce new convex geometry tools to study the properties of $s$-concave distributions and use these properties to provide bounds on quantities of interest to learning including the probability of disagreement between two halfspaces, disagreement outside a band, and the disagreement coefficient. We use these results to significantly generalize prior results for margin-based active learning, disagreement-based active learning, and passive learning of intersections of halfspaces. Our analysis of geometric properties of $s$-concave distributions might be of independent interest to optimization more broadly.

paragraphs: This paper extends efficient, noise-tolerant learning theory to s-concave distributions, a broader family than log-concave distributions. The family includes important additional examples such as Pareto and t distributions. Studying it enlarges the range of distributional settings for which learning methods can receive sample-efficiency and computational guarantees.

The extension introduces geometric difficulties. Many distributions in the family have heavy tails, and the family is not closed under marginalization. The authors develop convex geometry tools to handle these properties. They bound quantities describing how often two halfspaces disagree, how much disagreement occurs outside a band, and the disagreement coefficient.

These bounds support generalizations of earlier results for margin-based active learning, disagreement-based active learning, and passive learning of intersections of halfspaces. The contribution is therefore both geometric and algorithmic: properties of a broader distribution family become tools for proving learning guarantees. The authors also suggest that their geometric analysis may be useful in optimization, presenting this as a possible further application.
summary.tldr: New geometric tools extend efficient learning guarantees to the broader, potentially heavy-tailed family of s-concave distributions.

title: Sample and Computationally Efficient Learning Algorithms under S-Concave Distributions

abstract: We propose a rank-k variant of the classical Frank-Wolfe algorithm to solve convex optimization over a trace-norm ball. Our algorithm replaces the top singular-vector computation (1-SVD) in Frank-Wolfe with a top-k singular-vector computation (k-SVD), which can be done by repeatedly applying 1-SVD k times. Alternatively, our algorithm can be viewed as a rank-k restricted version of projected gradient descent. We show that our algorithm has a linear convergence rate when the objective function is smooth and strongly convex, and the optimal solution has rank at most k. This improves the convergence rate and the total time complexity of the Frank-Wolfe method and its variants.

paragraphs: This paper considers convex optimization over a trace-norm ball, a matrix constraint, and modifies the classical Frank-Wolfe algorithm for that setting. Its central idea is to use information from the top k singular vectors at each update, replacing the single leading singular-vector computation used by standard Frank-Wolfe.

The larger singular-vector computation can be carried out by repeating the single-vector procedure k times. The authors also give another interpretation of the method: it is projected gradient descent restricted to rank k. These two views connect the proposed algorithm to familiar optimization approaches while making the role of the rank parameter explicit.

The convergence guarantee depends on concrete conditions. The objective must be smooth and strongly convex, and the optimal solution must have rank no greater than k. Under those conditions, the method converges linearly, improving both the convergence rate and total time complexity over Frank-Wolfe and its variants. The result shows how matching the update rank to the solution's rank can support faster optimization.
summary.tldr: A rank-k Frank-Wolfe variant converges linearly for smooth, strongly convex objectives when the optimum has rank at most k.

title: Linear Convergence of a Frank-Wolfe Type Algorithm over Trace-Norm Balls

abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of learning from peers in an online multitask setting. Instead of always requesting a label from a human oracle, the proposed method first determines if the learner for each task can acquire that label with sufficient confidence from its peers either as a task-similarity weighted sum, or from the single most similar task. If so, it saves the oracle query for later use in more difficult cases, and if not it queries the human oracle. The paper develops the new algorithm to exhibit this behavior and proves a theoretical mistake bound for the method compared to the best linear predictor in hindsight. Experiments over three multitask learning benchmark datasets show clearly superior performance over baselines such as assuming task independence, learning only from the oracle and not learning from peer tasks.
