paragraphs: This paper considers several related learning tasks that receive data over time. A learner can ask a human for a label, but doing so for every uncertain example ignores information already available from other tasks. The proposed approach treats those other learners as peers that may supply a sufficiently confident answer.

For each task, the algorithm first checks whether peer knowledge is adequate. It can combine peers using weights based on task similarity, or consult the single most similar task. When confidence is sufficient, it uses the peer-provided label. Otherwise, it asks the human oracle, reserving human input for cases that peers cannot resolve confidently.

The authors prove a mistake bound relative to the best linear predictor chosen in hindsight. Experiments on three multitask benchmark datasets also show better performance than the tested alternatives, including treating tasks independently and relying only on oracle labels. Together, these results support selectively sharing information across tasks as a way to make online learning and human querying work together.
summary.tldr: An online multitask learner consults confident peers before asking a human for labels, with theoretical and experimental support.

title: Active Learning from Peers

abstract: The design of codes for communicating reliably over a statistically well defined channel is an important endeavor involving deep mathematical research and wide- ranging practical applications. In this work, we present the first family of codes obtained via deep learning, which significantly beats state-of-the-art codes designed over several decades of research. The communication channel under consideration is the Gaussian noise channel with feedback, whose study was initiated by Shannon; feedback is known theoretically to improve reliability of communication, but no practical codes that do so have ever been successfully constructed. We break this logjam by integrating information theoretic insights harmoniously with recurrent-neural-network based encoders and decoders to create novel codes that outperform known codes by 3 orders of magnitude in reliability. We also demonstrate several desirable properties in the codes: (a) generalization to larger block lengths; (b) composability with known codes; (c) adaptation to practical constraints. This result also presents broader ramifications to coding theory: even when the channel has a clear mathematical model, deep learning methodologies, when combined with channel specific information-theoretic insights, can potentially beat state-of-the-art codes, constructed over decades of mathematical research.

paragraphs: Communication codes help messages survive noise during transmission. This paper studies a Gaussian noise channel with feedback, where information returned from the receiving side can help improve reliability. Although feedback was theoretically known to offer such benefits, the abstract describes a gap between that promise and successful practical code construction.

Deepcode combines channel-specific information-theoretic insights with recurrent neural network encoders and decoders. The contribution is a family of learned codes that uses this combination to achieve much more reliable communication. The authors report an improvement of three orders of magnitude in reliability over known codes for the channel under consideration.

The learned codes also demonstrate generalization to longer message blocks, compatibility with existing codes, and adaptation to practical constraints. These properties matter because a coding method must fit into communication settings beyond a single training configuration. More broadly, the results suggest that deep learning combined with mathematical knowledge of a channel can improve code design even when that channel already has a precise statistical description.
summary.tldr: Deepcode combines recurrent networks with information-theoretic insights to improve reliability by three orders of magnitude for Gaussian noise communication with feedback.

title: Deepcode: Feedback Codes via Deep Learning

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) with derivatives are useful in many applications, including Bayesian optimization, implicit surface reconstruction, and terrain reconstruction. Fitting a GP to function values and derivatives at $n$ points in $d$ dimensions requires linear solves and log determinants with an ${n(d+1) \times n(d+1)}$ positive definite matrix-- leading to prohibitive $\mathcal{O}(n^3d^3)$ computations for standard direct methods. We propose iterative solvers using fast $\mathcal{O}(nd)$ matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs), together with pivoted Cholesky preconditioning that cuts the iterations to convergence by several orders of magnitude, allowing for fast kernel learning and prediction. Our approaches, together with dimensionality reduction, allows us to scale Bayesian optimization with derivatives to high-dimensional problems and large evaluation budgets.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression can incorporate both function values and derivatives, making it useful for optimization and reconstruction tasks. The computational burden grows rapidly because each point contributes a value and derivative information across dimensions. With n points in d dimensions, standard direct methods require computations scaling as O(n³d³).

The paper replaces those costly direct computations with iterative solvers built around O(nd) matrix-vector multiplications. It also uses pivoted Cholesky preconditioning to reduce the number of iterations needed for convergence. The authors report reductions of several orders of magnitude in iteration counts, supporting faster kernel learning as well as prediction.

The two improvements address complementary parts of the cost: the work performed in an iteration and the number of iterations required. Combined with dimensionality reduction, the approach scales derivative-based Bayesian optimization to high-dimensional problems and large evaluation budgets. The stated result shows how more efficient numerical computation can make derivative information usable at a larger scale in Gaussian process models, where standard matrix operations would otherwise be prohibitive.
summary.tldr: Fast matrix-vector products and preconditioned iterative solvers make Gaussian processes with derivative observations computationally scalable.

title: Scaling Gaussian Process Regression with Derivatives

abstract: Autonomous agents situated in real-world environments must be able to master large repertoires of skills. While a single short skill can be learned quickly, it would be impractical to learn every task independently. Instead, the agent should share knowledge across behaviors such that each task can be learned efficiently, and such that the resulting model can generalize to new tasks, especially ones that are compositions or subsets of tasks seen previously. A policy conditioned on a goal or demonstration has the potential to share knowledge between tasks if it sees enough diversity of inputs. However, these methods may not generalize to a more complex task at test time. We introduce compositional plan vectors (CPVs) to enable a policy to perform compositions of tasks without additional supervision. CPVs represent trajectories as the sum of the subtasks within them. We show that CPVs can be learned within a one-shot imitation learning framework without any additional supervision or information about task hierarchy, and enable a demonstration-conditioned policy to generalize to tasks that sequence twice as many skills as the tasks seen during training. Analogously to embeddings such as word2vec in NLP, CPVs can also support simple arithmetic operations -- for example, we can add the CPVs for two different tasks to command an agent to compose both tasks, without any additional training.

paragraphs: An agent with many skills would benefit from combining what it already knows into longer tasks. Learning every possible combination independently would be impractical. This paper introduces compositional plan vectors, or CPVs, as representations that help a demonstration-conditioned policy reuse learned behavior when facing new compositions of tasks.

A CPV represents a trajectory as the sum of its constituent subtasks. The authors show that these representations can be learned through one-shot imitation learning without extra supervision or information specifying a task hierarchy. This matters because the compositional structure is learned within the imitation framework instead of requiring separately supplied descriptions of how each task breaks down.

The reported policy generalizes to tasks sequencing twice as many skills as those encountered during training. The vectors also support arithmetic: adding the representations of two tasks can command their composition without further training. These findings show that the learned representation can serve both as a description of demonstrated behavior and as a means of specifying new combinations.
summary.tldr: Compositional plan vectors let an imitation-learning policy combine tasks through vector arithmetic and generalize to longer skill sequences.

title: Compositional Plan Vectors

abstract: We investigate active learning by pairwise similarity over the leaves of trees originating from hierarchical clustering procedures. In the realizable setting, we provide a full characterization of the number of queries needed to achieve perfect reconstruction of the tree cut. In the non-realizable setting, we rely on known important-sampling procedures to obtain regret and query complexity bounds. Our algorithms come with theoretical guarantees on the statistical error and, more importantly, lend themselves to {\em linear-time} implementations in the relevant parameters of the problem. We discuss such implementations, prove running time guarantees for them, and present preliminary experiments on real-world datasets showing the compelling practical performance of our algorithms as compared to both passive learning and simple active learning baselines.

Our algorithms come with theoretical guarantees on the statistical error and, more importantly, lend themselves to {\em linear-time} implementations in the relevant parameters of the problem. paragraphs: A hierarchical clustering organizes data in a tree, but using it often requires selecting a flat collection of clusters. This paper studies how to identify such a tree cut by actively asking whether pairs of items at the leaves are similar. The aim is to select informative questions rather than obtain pairwise judgments passively.

The authors distinguish whether the desired clustering can be represented exactly by a cut of the given tree. In this realizable setting, they fully characterize how many queries are needed for perfect reconstruction. When exact representation is unavailable, they use existing importance-sampling procedures to obtain regret and query-complexity bounds.

The algorithms combine statistical guarantees with implementations whose running time is linear in the relevant problem parameters. This matters because reducing the number of requested judgments would be less useful if choosing those judgments were prohibitively expensive. The paper proves implementation-time guarantees and presents preliminary experiments on real datasets, reporting compelling practical performance against passive learning and simple active learning baselines.
summary.tldr: Active pairwise similarity queries can turn a clustering tree into flat clusters with query guarantees and efficient implementations.

title: Flattening a Hierarchical Clustering through Active Learning

abstract: Despite the phenomenal success of deep neural networks in a broad range of learning tasks, there is a lack of theory to understand the way they work. In particular, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are known to perform much better than Fully-Connected Networks (FCNs) on spatially structured data: the architectural structure of CNNs benefits from prior knowledge on the features of the data, for instance their translation invariance. The aim of this work is to understand this fact through the lens of dynamics in the loss landscape. We introduce a method that maps a CNN to its equivalent FCN (denoted as eFCN). Such an embedding enables the comparison of CNN and FCN training dynamics directly in the FCN space. We use this method to test a new training protocol, which consists in training a CNN, embedding it to FCN space at a certain ``relax time'', then resuming the training in FCN space. We observe that for all relax times, the deviation from the CNN subspace is small, and the final performance reached by the eFCN is higher than that reachable by a standard FCN of same architecture. More surprisingly, for some intermediate relax times, the eFCN outperforms the CNN it stemmed, by combining the prior information of the CNN and the expressivity of the FCN in a complementary way. The practical interest of our protocol is limited by the very large size of the highly sparse eFCN. However, it offers interesting insights into the persistence of architectural bias under stochastic gradient dynamics. It shows the existence of some rare basins in the FCN loss landscape associated with very good generalization. These can only be accessed thanks to the CNN prior, which helps navigate the landscape during the early stages of optimization.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks build assumptions about spatial structure into their architecture. This paper investigates how those assumptions influence training by mapping a convolutional network into an equivalent fully connected network. The mapping lets the authors compare both forms of training within the same fully connected parameter space.

Their protocol first trains a convolutional network, converts it at a chosen relaxation time, and then continues training as a fully connected network. Across the relaxation times studied, the converted network remains close to the convolutional subspace and finishes with better performance than a conventionally trained fully connected network of the same architecture. At some intermediate relaxation times, it also outperforms the originating convolutional network.

These observations suggest that early convolutional structure can guide optimization toward regions with strong generalization, while later flexibility can provide additional benefit. The authors interpret the results as evidence that architectural bias persists under stochastic gradient training. They also identify a practical constraint: the equivalent fully connected network is very large and highly sparse, limiting the protocol's usefulness as a routine training method.
summary.tldr: Convolutional training can guide an equivalent fully connected network toward better solutions, with benefits persisting after architectural constraints are relaxed.

title: Finding the Needle in the Haystack with Convolutions: on the benefits of architectural bias

abstract: We develop a new algorithm for online planning in large scale sequential decision problems that improves upon the worst case efficiency of UCT. The idea is to augment Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with maximum entropy policy optimization, evaluating each search node by softmax values back-propagated from simulation. To establish the effectiveness of this approach, we first investigate the single-step decision problem, stochastic softmax bandits, and show that softmax values can be estimated at an optimal convergence rate in terms of mean squared error. We then extend this approach to general sequential decision making by developing a general MCTS algorithm, Maximum Entropy for Tree Search (MENTS). We prove that the probability of MENTS failing to identify the best decision at the root decays exponentially, which fundamentally improves the polynomial convergence rate of UCT. Our experimental results also demonstrate that MENTS is more sample efficient than UCT in both synthetic problems and Atari 2600 games.

To establish the effectiveness of this approach, we first investigate the single-step decision problem, stochastic softmax bandits, and show that softmax values can be estimated at an optimal convergence rate in terms of mean squared error. We then extend this approach to general sequential decision making by developing a general MCTS algorithm, Maximum Entropy for Tree Search (MENTS). We prove that the probability of MENTS failing to identify the best decision at the root decays exponentially, which fundamentally improves the polynomial convergence rate of UCT. Our experimental results also demonstrate that MENTS is more sample efficient than UCT in both synthetic problems and Atari 2600 games.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search plans by simulating possible sequences of decisions and propagating information through a search tree. This paper modifies that process using maximum-entropy policy optimization. Its algorithm, Maximum Entropy for Tree Search, or MENTS, evaluates nodes using softmax values passed backward from simulations.

The analysis first studies stochastic softmax bandits, a single-step decision problem that isolates the value-estimation component. The authors show that softmax values can be estimated at an optimal convergence rate measured by mean squared error. They then extend this approach to sequential decisions, where the search must account for consequences across multiple steps.

For MENTS, the probability of failing to identify the best root decision decreases exponentially, improving on the polynomial convergence rate of UCT in the stated analysis. Experiments on synthetic problems and Atari 2600 games also find greater sample efficiency than UCT. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical improvement in root-decision reliability with empirical evidence that simulations can be used more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Maximum-entropy tree search improves theoretical root-decision convergence and uses simulations more efficiently than UCT in reported experiments.

title: Maximum Entropy Monte-Carlo Planning

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-objective (MO) blackbox optimization using expensive function evaluations, where the goal is to approximate the true Pareto-set of solutions by minimizing the number of function evaluations. For example, in hardware design optimization, we need to find the designs that trade-off performance, energy, and area overhead using expensive simulations. We propose a novel approach referred to as Max-value Entropy Search for Multi-objective Optimization (MESMO) to solve this problem. MESMO employs an output-space entropy based acquisition function to efficiently select the sequence of inputs for evaluation for quickly uncovering high-quality solutions. We also provide theoretical analysis to characterize the efficacy of MESMO. Our experiments on several synthetic and real-world benchmark problems show that MESMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Expensive optimization becomes more difficult when several objectives compete. A hardware design, for example, may trade performance against energy use and area. The goal is to approximate the Pareto set of useful trade-offs while minimizing costly evaluations, rather than identifying a single design that is best on every objective.

The paper introduces Max-value Entropy Search for Multi-objective Optimization, or MESMO. Its acquisition function uses entropy in the output space to select the next input to evaluate. This turns uncertainty about objective outputs into a guide for deciding where to spend the next expensive measurement or simulation, with the aim of quickly uncovering high-quality solutions.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis characterizing the method's efficacy and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world benchmark problems. MESMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in those experiments. The stated findings support output-space entropy as a useful basis for allocating evaluations when the desired outcome is a collection of competing solutions.
summary.tldr: MESMO uses output-space entropy to choose expensive evaluations and efficiently discover trade-off solutions in multi-objective optimization.

title: Max-value Entropy Search for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We present a new algorithm (ASEBO) for optimizing high-dimensional blackbox functions. ASEBO adapts to the geometry of the function and learns optimal sets of sensing directions, which are used to probe it, on-the-fly. It addresses the exploration-exploitation trade-off of blackbox optimization with expensive blackbox queries by continuously learning the bias of the lower-dimensional model used to approximate gradients of smoothings of the function via compressed sensing and contextual bandits methods. To obtain this model, it leverages techniques from the emerging theory of active subspaces in a novel ES blackbox optimization context. As a result, ASEBO learns the dynamically changing intrinsic dimensionality of the gradient space and adapts to the hardness of different stages of the optimization without external supervision. Consequently, it leads to more sample-efficient blackbox optimization than state-of-the-art algorithms. We provide theoretical results and test ASEBO advantages over other methods empirically by evaluating it on the set of reinforcement learning policy optimization tasks as well as functions from the recently open-sourced Nevergrad library.

paragraphs: Optimizing a high-dimensional blackbox function can require many expensive evaluations because the optimizer must learn which directions are worth probing. ASEBO addresses this by adapting its sensing directions to the function’s geometry during optimization. Its central premise is that the gradient space can have an intrinsic dimensionality that changes as optimization progresses.

The algorithm uses active-subspace techniques to build a lower-dimensional model for approximating gradients of smoothed versions of the function. Compressed sensing and contextual bandit methods help it track the model’s bias and manage exploration versus exploitation. This allows the optimizer to keep learning about useful directions while allocating queries according to the current approximation.

The resulting procedure adapts to different stages of optimization without external supervision. The authors provide theoretical results and evaluate it on reinforcement learning policy optimization tasks and functions from the Nevergrad library. They report greater sample efficiency than leading alternatives, supporting the idea that continually adapting the search space can reduce the number of costly function evaluations needed in the tested problems.
summary.tldr: ASEBO adapts its probing directions to changing low-dimensional gradient structure, improving sample efficiency in tested blackbox optimization problems.

title: From Complexity to Simplicity: Adaptive ES-Active Subspaces for Blackbox Optimization

abstract: We present a novel algorithm to estimate the barycenter of arbitrary probability distributions with respect to the Sinkhorn divergence. Based on a Frank-Wolfe optimization strategy, our approach proceeds by populating the support of the barycenter incrementally, without requiring any pre-allocation. We consider discrete as well as continuous distributions, proving convergence rates of the proposed algorithm in both settings. Key elements of our analysis are a new result showing that the Sinkhorn divergence on compact domains has Lipschitz continuous gradient with respect to the Total Variation and a characterization of the sample complexity of Sinkhorn potentials. Experiments validate the effectiveness of our method in practice.

paragraphs: A barycenter provides a representative distribution for a collection of probability distributions. This paper estimates such a representative using Sinkhorn divergence as the comparison criterion. Its main design choice concerns the barycenter's support: the locations where it places probability mass are built during optimization instead of being allocated beforehand.

The proposed algorithm follows a Frank-Wolfe strategy and incrementally populates that support. This makes support construction part of the estimation process itself. The authors consider both discrete and continuous input distributions and prove convergence rates in each setting, giving theoretical backing to the same general approach across the two types of inputs.

The analysis includes a smoothness result for Sinkhorn divergence on compact domains: its gradient is Lipschitz continuous with respect to total variation. It also characterizes the sample complexity of Sinkhorn potentials. These results support the convergence analysis, while experiments validate the method's practical effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines a way to construct barycenters without preallocated support with mathematical tools explaining its behavior.
summary.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe algorithm builds Sinkhorn barycenter support incrementally and comes with convergence rates for discrete and continuous distributions.

title: Sinkhorn Barycenters with Free Support via Frank-Wolfe Algorithm

abstract: We consider the classical stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with a constraint on the total cost incurred by switching between actions. Under the unit switching cost structure, where the constraint limits the total number of switches, we prove matching upper and lower bounds on regret and provide near-optimal algorithms for this problem. Surprisingly, we discover phase transitions and cyclic phenomena of the optimal regret. That is, we show that associated with the multi-armed bandit problem, there are equal-length phases defined by the number of arms and switching costs, where the regret upper and lower bounds in each phase remain the same and drop significantly between phases. The results enable us to fully characterize the trade-off between regret and incurred switching cost in the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem, contributing new insights to this fundamental problem. Under the general switching cost structure, our analysis reveals a surprising connection between the bandit problem and the shortest Hamiltonian path problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic bandit learning when changing actions consumes a limited budget. The learner must discover rewarding actions while controlling the total cost of moving between them. Under unit switching costs, this becomes a direct limit on the number of times the learner may change its chosen action.

For that setting, the authors prove matching upper and lower regret bounds and give near-optimal algorithms. The surprising finding is that the optimal regret tradeoff has phases. Across equal-length ranges determined by the number of actions and switching costs, the regret bounds remain unchanged, then drop substantially when the switching budget enters the next phase.

This pattern means that additional switching allowance does not improve the theoretical regret bounds smoothly at every increment. The results characterize the tradeoff between learning performance and switching expenditure in the unit-cost setting. For more general switching costs, the analysis reveals a connection to the shortest Hamiltonian path problem, linking action-switching structure to a graph optimization problem.
summary.tldr: Bandit regret under switching limits improves in discrete phases, with general switching costs connecting the problem to shortest Hamiltonian paths.

title: Phase Transitions and Cyclic Phenomena in Bandits with Switching Constraints

abstract: Motivated by federated learning, we consider the hub-and-spoke model of distributed optimization in which a central authority coordinates the computation of a solution among many agents while limiting communication. We first study some past procedures for federated optimization, and show that their fixed points need not correspond to stationary points of the original optimization problem, even in simple convex settings with deterministic updates. In order to remedy these issues, we introduce FedSplit, a class of algorithms based on operator splitting procedures for solving distributed convex minimization with additive structure. We prove that these procedures have the correct fixed points, corresponding to optima of the original optimization problem, and we characterize their convergence rates under different settings. Our theory shows that these methods are provably robust to inexact computation of intermediate local quantities. We complement our theory with some experiments that demonstrate the benefits of our methods in practice.

paragraphs: Federated optimization coordinates many agents through a central hub while trying to limit communication. This paper identifies a fundamental issue with some previous procedures: the points at which their updates stop changing need not be stationary points of the intended objective. The problem can occur even with convex objectives and deterministic updates.

The authors introduce FedSplit, a family of methods built from operator splitting for distributed convex minimization with additive structure. Splitting provides a way to organize the components of the optimization across agents. The authors prove that the resulting procedures have the correct fixed points, corresponding to optima of the original problem, and characterize convergence rates in different settings.

The theory also establishes robustness to inexact computation of intermediate local quantities. This matters because the distributed procedure can retain guarantees when agents approximate those quantities. Experiments complement the theoretical results and demonstrate practical benefits. Together, the findings address both where federated updates converge and how reliably they can reach that destination under imperfect local computation.
summary.tldr: FedSplit uses operator splitting to give distributed convex optimization correct fixed points and convergence guarantees robust to inexact local computation.

title: FedSplit: an algorithmic framework for fast federated optimization

abstract: Recent technological advances in systems neuroscience have led to a shift away from using simple tasks, with low-dimensional, well-controlled stimuli, towards trying to understand neural activity during naturalistic behavior. However, with the increase in number and complexity of task-relevant features, standard analyses such as estimating tuning functions become challenging. Here, we use a Poisson generalized additive model (P-GAM) with spline nonlinearities and an exponential link function to map a large number of task variables (input stimuli, behavioral outputs, or activity of other neurons, modeled as discrete events or continuous variables) into spike counts. We develop efficient procedures for parameter learning by optimizing a generalized cross-validation score and infer marginal confidence bounds for the contribution of each feature to neural responses. This allows us to robustly identify a minimal set of task features that each neuron is responsive to, circumventing computationally demanding model comparison. We show that our estimation procedure outperforms traditional regularized GLMs in terms of both fit quality and computing time. When applied to neural recordings from monkeys performing a virtual reality spatial navigation task, P-GAM reveals mixed selectivity and preferential coupling between neurons with similar tuning.

paragraphs: Studying neural activity during naturalistic behavior involves many interacting task variables, making traditional tuning analyses difficult. This paper develops a way to relate spike counts to numerous stimuli, behavioral outputs, and signals from other neurons. The inputs can include both discrete events and continuous variables, accommodating the varied information present in these recordings.

The approach uses a Poisson generalized additive model with spline nonlinearities and an exponential link function. It learns parameters through efficient optimization of a generalized cross-validation score and estimates marginal confidence bounds for each feature's contribution. These bounds help identify a minimal set of features to which a neuron responds, avoiding computationally demanding comparisons among alternative models.

The authors report better fit quality and lower computing time than traditional regularized generalized linear models. Applied to recordings from monkeys navigating a virtual reality environment, the method reveals mixed selectivity and preferential coupling among neurons with similar tuning. The contribution therefore combines an efficient estimation procedure with a way to interpret how multiple task features relate to neural responses.
summary.tldr: An efficient Poisson additive model identifies task variables associated with neural responses and reveals tuning relationships during naturalistic behavior.

title: Efficient estimation of neural tuning during naturalistic behavior

abstract: In many application settings involving networks, such as messages between users of an on-line social network or transactions between traders in financial markets, the observed data consist of timestamped relational events, which form a continuous-time network. We propose the Community Hawkes Independent Pairs (CHIP) generative model for such networks. We show that applying spectral clustering to an aggregated adjacency matrix constructed from the CHIP model provides consistent community detection for a growing number of nodes and time duration. We also develop consistent and computationally efficient estimators for the model parameters. We demonstrate that our proposed CHIP model and estimation procedure scales to large networks with tens of thousands of nodes and provides superior fits than existing continuous-time network models on several real networks.

paragraphs: Some networks are observed as interactions with timestamps rather than as a single fixed collection of connections. Messages between people and transactions between traders are examples. The paper introduces Community Hawkes Independent Pairs, or CHIP, as a generative model for these continuous-time networks, linking the modeling of relational events with the identification of communities.

For community detection, the authors construct an aggregated adjacency matrix from the model and apply spectral clustering. They prove consistency as both the number of nodes and the observation duration grow. They also develop parameter estimators that are consistent and computationally efficient. These results provide theoretical support for recovering structure and estimating the model in the stated growing-data setting.

The empirical results address whether the approach remains useful at substantial network sizes. CHIP and its estimation procedure handle networks containing tens of thousands of nodes. On several real networks, they also provide better fits than existing continuous-time network models. Together, these findings connect statistical estimation guarantees with demonstrated computational scalability and improved descriptions of observed interaction data.
summary.tldr: CHIP models timestamped network interactions with scalable estimation and consistency guarantees for community detection and model parameters.

title: CHIP: A Hawkes Process Model for Continuous-time Networks with Scalable and Consistent Estimation

abstract: Pruning has become a very powerful and effective technique to compress and accelerate modern neural networks. Existing pruning methods can be grouped into two categories: filter pruning (FP) and weight pruning (WP). FP wins at hardware compatibility but loses at the compression ratio compared with WP. To converge the strength of both methods, we propose to prune the filter in the filter. Specifically, we treat a filter F, whose size is C*K*K, as K*K stripes, i.e., 1*1 filters, then by pruning the stripes instead of the whole filter, we can achieves finer granularity than traditional FP while being hardware friendly. We term our method as SWP (Stripe-Wise Pruning). SWP is implemented by introducing a novel learnable matrix called Filter Skeleton, whose values reflect the optimal shape of each filter. As some recent work has shown that the pruned architecture is more crucial than the inherited important weights, we argue that the architecture of a single filter, i.e., the Filter Skeleton, also matters. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that SWP is more effective compared to the previous FP-based methods and achieves the state-of-art pruning ratio on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets without obvious accuracy drop.

paragraphs: Pruning compresses neural networks by removing parts of their computation. Removing whole filters is compatible with hardware, but removing individual weights can provide stronger compression. This paper proposes an intermediate unit of pruning that preserves structure while making finer choices than whole-filter removal.

A convolutional filter with C channels and a K-by-K spatial footprint is viewed as K squared stripes. Each stripe corresponds to one spatial position across the channels. Stripe-Wise Pruning removes these units using a learnable matrix called the Filter Skeleton, whose values describe the filter's shape. This makes the internal spatial architecture of a filter part of what the method learns.

The authors report that the method is more effective than previous filter-pruning approaches and achieves state-of-the-art pruning ratios on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet without an obvious accuracy drop. The evidence supports the idea that selecting structure within filters can improve compression while remaining hardware friendly. It also emphasizes that a filter's learned shape can matter alongside the broader architecture of the pruned network.
summary.tldr: Stripe-Wise Pruning learns which spatial stripes to remove within filters, achieving strong reported compression without an obvious accuracy drop.

title: Pruning Filter in Filter

abstract: We propose a novel unsupervised generative model that learns to disentangle object identity from other low-level aspects in class-imbalanced data. We first investigate the issues surrounding the assumptions about uniformity made by InfoGAN, and demonstrate its ineffectiveness to properly disentangle object identity in imbalanced data. Our key idea is to make the discovery of the discrete latent factor of variation invariant to identity-preserving transformations in real images, and use that as a signal to learn the appropriate latent distribution representing object identity. Experiments on both artificial (MNIST, 3D cars, 3D chairs, ShapeNet) and real-world (YouTube-Faces) imbalanced datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in disentangling object identity as a latent factor of variation.

Experiments on both artificial (MNIST, 3D cars, 3D chairs, ShapeNet) and real-world (YouTube-Faces) imbalanced datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in disentangling object identity as a latent factor of variation.

paragraphs: Elastic-InfoGAN addresses unsupervised learning of object identity when some classes appear more often than others. The desired representation separates identity from lower-level aspects of an image. The authors first examine InfoGAN’s assumptions about uniformity and demonstrate that these assumptions can prevent it from properly separating object identity in imbalanced data.

The proposed generative model uses identity-preserving transformations of real images as a learning signal. Its key idea is that the discovered discrete factor representing identity should remain invariant under those transformations. This consistency signal helps the model learn an appropriate latent distribution for identity, connecting the representation of identity to the class imbalance present in the data.

Experiments span artificial imbalanced datasets involving MNIST, cars, chairs, and ShapeNet, as well as the real-world YouTube-Faces dataset. The reported results support the method’s ability to isolate object identity as a latent factor. The contribution is an unsupervised approach that uses transformation-based consistency to address the mismatch between a uniformity assumption and unevenly represented identities.
summary.tldr: Elastic-InfoGAN uses identity-preserving transformations to learn an identity representation and latent distribution suited to class-imbalanced data.

title: Elastic-InfoGAN: Unsupervised Disentangled Representation Learning in Class-Imbalanced Data

abstract: SGD with momentum (SGDM) has been widely applied in many machine learning tasks, and it is often applied with dynamic stepsizes and momentum weights tuned in a stagewise manner. Despite of its empirical advantage over SGD, the role of momentum is still unclear in general since previous analyses on SGDM either provide worse convergence bounds than those of SGD, or assume Lipschitz or quadratic objectives, which fail to hold in practice. Furthermore, the role of dynamic parameters has not been addressed. In this work, we show that SGDM converges as fast as SGD for smooth objectives under both strongly convex and nonconvex settings. We also prove that multistage strategy is beneficial for SGDM compared to using fixed parameters. Finally, we verify these theoretical claims by numerical experiments.

Furthermore, the role of dynamic parameters has not been addressed. In this work, we show that SGDM converges as fast as SGD for smooth objectives under both strongly convex and nonconvex settings. We also prove that multistage strategy is beneficial for SGDM compared to using fixed parameters. Finally, we verify these theoretical claims by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent with momentum is widely used, but its practical success has been difficult to explain theoretically. Earlier analyses sometimes gave it worse convergence guarantees than ordinary stochastic gradient descent, or relied on objective assumptions that the authors argue fail in practice. They also left the effects of changing optimization parameters insufficiently explained.

The paper establishes that momentum can match the convergence speed of ordinary stochastic gradient descent for smooth objectives. This result covers both strongly convex and nonconvex settings. Matching that rate matters because it closes a theoretical disadvantage in earlier analyses without claiming that momentum must always converge faster.

The authors also study a multistage strategy, where step sizes and momentum weights change between stages instead of remaining fixed throughout training. They prove that this strategy benefits momentum-based optimization relative to fixed parameters. Numerical experiments support the theoretical claims. Together, the results address both the convergence behavior of momentum and the value of the staged parameter schedules used in practice.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis shows that momentum matches SGD’s convergence rates for smooth objectives and benefits from multistage parameter schedules.

title: An Improved Analysis of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum

abstract: Many problems in machine learning (ML) can be cast as learning functions from sets to graphs, or more generally to hypergraphs; in short, Set2Graph functions. Examples include clustering, learning vertex and edge features on graphs, and learning features on triplets in a collection. A natural approach for building Set2Graph models is to characterize all linear equivariant set-to-hypergraph layers and stack them with non-linear activations. This posses two challenges: (i) the expressive power of these networks is not well understood; and (ii) these models would suffer from high, often intractable computational and memory complexity, as their dimension grows exponentially. This paper advocates a family of neural network models for learning Set2Graph functions that is both practical and of maximal expressive power (universal), that is, can approximate arbitrary continuous Set2Graph functions over compact sets. Testing these models on different machine learning tasks, mainly an application to particle physics, we find them favorable to existing baselines.

paragraphs: Many learning tasks start with a collection of items and require predictions about relationships among them. Set2Graph treats these as functions from sets to graphs or hypergraphs, covering examples such as clustering and predicting features for vertices, edges, or triplets. The challenge is to build models that are both expressive and computationally practical.

One natural construction stacks linear equivariant set-to-hypergraph layers with nonlinear activations. The paper identifies two problems with that route: uncertain expressive power and potentially intractable computation and memory as dimensions grow exponentially. It proposes a family of neural networks intended to address both concerns.

The authors establish universality for their models: they can approximate arbitrary continuous Set2Graph functions over compact sets. This is an expressiveness guarantee for that specified function class. Experiments on several machine-learning tasks, chiefly a particle-physics application, find the models favorable to existing baselines. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support a practical architecture family with a clear account of what it can represent.
summary.tldr: Set2Graph introduces practical neural models that can approximate arbitrary continuous set-to-graph functions over compact sets.

title: Set2Graph: Learning Graphs From Sets

abstract: Despite remarkable performance in producing realistic samples, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) often produce low-quality samples near low-density regions of the data manifold, e.g., samples of minor groups. Many techniques have been developed to improve the quality of generated samples, either by post-processing generated samples or by pre-processing the empirical data distribution, but at the cost of reduced diversity. To promote diversity in sample generation without degrading the overall quality, we propose a simple yet effective method to diagnose and emphasize underrepresented samples during training of a GAN. The main idea is to use the statistics of the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution at each data instance. Based on the observation that the underrepresented samples have a high average discrepancy or high variability in discrepancy, we propose a method to emphasize those samples during training of a GAN. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves GAN performance on various datasets, and it is especially effective in improving the quality and diversity of sample generation for minor groups.

The main idea is to use the statistics of the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution at each data instance. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves GAN performance on various datasets, and it is especially effective in improving the quality and diversity of sample generation for minor groups.

paragraphs: A GAN can produce convincing samples overall while representing less common parts of the data poorly. The paper focuses on low-density regions, including minor groups, where generated samples often have lower quality. It seeks to improve their representation without the loss of diversity that can accompany techniques modifying the data distribution or filtering generated outputs.

The proposed method diagnoses underrepresentation during training using statistics of the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution at individual data instances. The authors observe that poorly represented samples can have either a large average discrepancy or a discrepancy that varies substantially. They use these signals to give such samples greater emphasis during GAN training.

Experiments across several datasets show improved GAN performance, with particularly strong benefits for the quality and diversity of samples from minor groups. The approach matters because it uses information about the model's own changing mismatch with the data to guide training attention. Its reported results support addressing uneven representation directly during learning, alongside the broader goal of maintaining overall sample quality.
summary.tldr: A GAN training method identifies underrepresented examples through discrepancy statistics and improves reported sample quality and diversity, especially for minor groups.

title: Self-Diagnosing GAN: Diagnosing Underrepresented Samples in Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Efficient exploration in deep cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) still remains challenging in complex coordination problems. In this paper, we introduce a novel Episodic Multi-agent reinforcement learning with Curiosity-driven exploration, called EMC. We leverage an insight of popular factorized MARL algorithms that the ``induced" individual Q-values, i.e., the individual utility functions used for local execution, are the embeddings of local action-observation histories, and can capture the interaction between agents due to reward backpropagation during centralized training. Therefore, we use prediction errors of individual Q-values as intrinsic rewards for coordinated exploration and utilize episodic memory to exploit explored informative experience to boost policy training. As the dynamics of an agent's individual Q-value function captures the novelty of states and the influence from other agents, our intrinsic reward can induce coordinated exploration to new or promising states. We illustrate the advantages of our method by didactic examples, and demonstrate its significant outperformance over state-of-the-art MARL baselines on challenging tasks in the StarCraft II micromanagement benchmark.

The authors illustrate the approach with explanatory examples and evaluate it on difficult StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. They report significant improvements over state-of-the-art multi-agent baselines on those tasks. The contribution is a curiosity signal tied to learned multi-agent utilities, paired with memory that helps turn explored experience into improved behavior.
summary.tldr: EMC combines prediction errors in individual agent utilities with episodic memory to improve coordinated exploration and performance on StarCraft II tasks.

title: Episodic Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning with Curiosity-driven Exploration

abstract: Graph neural networks are increasingly becoming the go-to approach in various fields such as computer vision, computational biology and chemistry, where data are naturally explained by graphs. However, unlike traditional convolutional neural networks, deep graph networks do not necessarily yield better performance than shallow graph networks. This behavior usually stems from the over-smoothing phenomenon. In this work, we propose a family of architecturesto control this behavior by design. Our networks are motivated by numerical methods for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) on manifolds, and as such, their behavior can be explained by similar analysis. Moreover, as we demonstrate using an extensive set of experiments, our PDE-motivated networks can generalize and be effective for various types of problems from different fields. Our architectures obtain better or on par with the current state-of-the-art results for problems that are typically approached using different architectures.

paragraphs: Adding layers to a graph neural network does not necessarily improve its predictions. A common reason is over-smoothing, in which repeated processing makes node representations too similar. This paper proposes a family of graph network architectures designed to control that behavior, addressing a structural obstacle to effective deeper graph models.

The designs take inspiration from numerical methods for solving partial differential equations on manifolds. This connection supplies both an architectural foundation and a way to analyze how the networks behave. The aim is to make the evolution of graph representations understandable through related mathematical analysis while controlling smoothing through the network’s design.

An extensive experimental evaluation examines problems across different fields. The architectures match or improve on the reported state of the art for tasks usually handled by different specialized architectures. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed family across multiple kinds of graph problems. The contribution is therefore both a design approach to controlling over-smoothing and evidence that the resulting networks can work effectively beyond a single application.
summary.tldr: PDE-GCN uses numerical ideas from partial differential equations to control graph-network over-smoothing and achieve competitive results across multiple domains.

title: PDE-GCN: Novel Architectures for Graph Neural Networks Motivated by Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Tabular data synthesis has received wide attention in the literature. This is because available data is often limited, incomplete, or cannot be obtained easily, and data privacy is becoming increasingly important. In this work, we present a generalized GAN framework for tabular synthesis, which combines the adversarial training of GANs and the negative log-density regularization of invertible neural networks. The proposed framework can be used for two distinctive objectives. First, we can further improve the synthesis quality, by decreasing the negative log-density of real records in the process of adversarial training. On the other hand, by increasing the negative log-density of real records, realistic fake records can be synthesized in a way that they are not too much close to real records and reduce the chance of potential information leakage. We conduct experiments with real-world datasets for classification, regression, and privacy attacks. In general, the proposed method demonstrates the best synthesis quality (in terms of task-oriented evaluation metrics, e.g., F1) when decreasing the negative log-density during the adversarial training. If increasing the negative log-density, our experimental results show that the distance between real and fake records increases, enhancing robustness against privacy attacks.

paragraphs: Synthetic tabular data can be useful when real records are scarce, incomplete, difficult to obtain, or sensitive. This paper introduces a GAN framework that combines adversarial training with a negative log-density regularizer supplied by an invertible neural network. The regularizer allows the training procedure to pursue two distinct objectives.

Decreasing the negative log-density of real records encourages the model to place greater density on those records, supporting synthesis quality. Increasing it instead encourages generated records to stay farther from real ones while adversarial training supports realism. The direction of this term therefore changes the intended behavior, emphasizing either useful synthetic data or reduced closeness to the source records.

Experiments use real-world datasets for classification, regression, and privacy attacks. Decreasing negative log-density generally yields the best synthesis quality on task-oriented measures such as F1. Increasing it enlarges the observed distance between real and synthetic records and improves resistance to the tested privacy attacks. These are empirical privacy improvements, with the stated objective being to reduce the chance of information leakage.
summary.tldr: A tabular GAN uses invertible-network density regularization to favor either synthesis quality or greater separation from real records and stronger empirical privacy resistance.

title: Invertible Tabular GANs: Killing Two Birds with One Stone for Tabular Data Synthesis

abstract: Articulation-centric 2D/3D pose supervision forms the core training objective in most existing 3D human pose estimation techniques. Except for synthetic source environments, acquiring such rich supervision for each real target domain at deployment is highly inconvenient. However, we realize that standard foreground silhouette estimation techniques (on static camera feeds) remain unaffected by domain-shifts. Motivated by this, we propose a novel target adaptation framework that relies only on silhouette supervision to adapt a source-trained model-based regressor. However, in the absence of any auxiliary cue (multi-view, depth, or 2D pose), an isolated silhouette loss fails to provide a reliable pose-specific gradient and requires to be employed in tandem with a topology-centric loss. To this end, we develop a series of convolution-friendly spatial transformations in order to disentangle a topological-skeleton representation from the raw silhouette. Such a design paves the way to devise a Chamfer-inspired spatial topological-alignment loss via distance field computation, while effectively avoiding any gradient hindering spatial-to-pointset mapping. Experimental results demonstrate our superiority against prior-arts in self-adapting a source trained model to diverse unlabeled target domains, such as a) in-the-wild datasets, b) low-resolution image domains, and c) adversarially perturbed image domains (via UAP).

paragraphs: A system trained to recover a person's 3D pose can struggle when deployed on images unlike its training data. Obtaining detailed pose annotations for every new setting is inconvenient. This paper instead adapts an existing pose regressor using foreground silhouettes, motivated by the authors' observation that standard silhouette estimation from static cameras remains reliable across domain shifts.

The central difficulty is that matching an outline alone does not reliably tell the model how to correct the pose. The authors therefore extract a representation of the silhouette's skeletal topology using spatial transformations compatible with convolutional processing. They combine silhouette supervision with a topology alignment loss based on distance fields and inspired by Chamfer matching. Keeping this computation spatial avoids a conversion to point sets that would hinder gradients.

Experiments report better adaptation than prior methods on unlabeled target domains, including images captured in the wild, low-resolution images, and adversarially perturbed images. The contribution is a way to obtain more useful pose guidance from silhouettes without requiring additional depth, multiple views, or 2D pose cues.
summary.tldr: Combining silhouette matching with skeletal topology alignment enables adaptation of a 3D pose model to unlabeled target domains.

title: Aligning Silhouette Topology for Self-Adaptive 3D Human Pose Recovery

abstract: Achieving transferability of targeted attacks is reputed to be remarkably difficult. The current state of the art has resorted to resource-intensive solutions that necessitate training model(s) for each target class with additional data. In our investigation, we find, however, that simple transferable attacks which require neither model training nor additional data can achieve surprisingly strong targeted transferability. This insight has been overlooked until now, mainly because the widespread practice of attacking with only few iterations has largely limited the attack convergence to optimal targeted transferability. In particular, we, for the first time, identify that a very simple logit loss can largely surpass the commonly adopted cross-entropy loss, and yield even better results than the resource-intensive state of the art. Our analysis spans a variety of transfer scenarios, especially including three new, realistic scenarios: an ensemble transfer scenario with little model similarity, a worse-case scenario with low-ranked target classes, and also a real-world attack on the Google Cloud Vision API. Results in these new transfer scenarios demonstrate that the commonly adopted, easy scenarios cannot fully reveal the actual strength of different attacks and may cause misleading comparative results. We also show the usefulness of the simple logit loss for generating targeted universal adversarial perturbations in a data-free manner. Overall, the aim of our analysis is to inspire a more meaningful evaluation on targeted transferability. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengyuZhao/Targeted-Tansfer.

paragraphs: A targeted transferable attack aims to make a model produce a chosen incorrect prediction using an attack developed elsewhere. This paper reexamines the view that strong targeted transfer requires expensive additional training or extra data. The authors find that simple attacks can transfer surprisingly well, and argue that evaluations using too few iterations have obscured their strength.

A central finding concerns the training objective used to construct the perturbation. A simple logit-based loss substantially outperforms the commonly used cross-entropy loss in their investigation, even exceeding resource-intensive approaches. The analysis links this result to allowing attacks sufficient iterations to develop their targeted transferability, rather than assuming short runs reveal their eventual effectiveness.

The evaluation includes dissimilar-model ensemble transfer, low-ranked target classes, and Google Cloud Vision API attacks. Results show that easier scenarios can give misleading comparisons between methods. The paper also demonstrates the usefulness of the logit loss for data-free targeted universal perturbations. Its broader contribution is an empirical argument for more representative evaluation of targeted transferability, alongside a simpler effective objective.
summary.tldr: Simple logit-loss attacks show strong targeted transferability, highlighting how iteration budgets and evaluation scenarios can distort attack comparisons.

title: On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Targeted Attacks

abstract: We study the problem of learning to estimate the 3D object pose from a few labelled examples and a collection of unlabelled data. Our main contribution is a learning framework, neural view synthesis and matching, that can transfer the 3D pose annotation from the labelled to unlabelled images reliably, despite unseen 3D views and nuisance variations such as the object shape, texture, illumination or scene context. In our approach, objects are represented as 3D cuboid meshes composed of feature vectors at each mesh vertex. The model is initialized from a few labelled images and is subsequently used to synthesize feature representations of unseen 3D views. The synthesized views are matched with the feature representations of unlabelled images to generate pseudo-labels of the 3D pose. The pseudo-labelled data is, in turn, used to train the feature extractor such that the features at each mesh vertex are more invariant across varying 3D views of the object. Our model is trained in an EM-type manner alternating between increasing the 3D pose invariance of the feature extractor and annotating unlabelled data through neural view synthesis and matching. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed semi-supervised learning framework for 3D pose estimation on the PASCAL3D+ and KITTI datasets. We find that our approach outperforms all baselines by a wide margin, particularly in an extreme few-shot setting where only 7 annotated images are given. Remarkably, we observe that our model also achieves an exceptional robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios that involve partial occlusion.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate an object's three-dimensional pose using a few labeled images and a larger unlabeled collection. The challenge is transferring pose information across previously unseen views and variations in shape, texture, lighting, and scene context. The proposed framework combines neural view synthesis with feature matching to make that transfer.

Objects are represented by three-dimensional cuboid meshes with feature vectors at their vertices. After initialization from labeled images, the model synthesizes feature representations for unseen viewpoints. Matching those representations against unlabeled images produces estimated pose labels. Those pseudo-labels then help train a feature extractor whose vertex features remain more consistent across different views.

Training alternates between improving the features and assigning poses to unlabeled data, following an EM-type procedure. On PASCAL3D+ and KITTI, the authors report large gains over all evaluated baselines, particularly with only seven annotated images. They also observe strong robustness to partial occlusion in out-of-distribution scenarios. The findings support a learning loop in which synthesized views and improved features help extend scarce pose annotations.
summary.tldr: Synthesizing and matching feature-based object views transfers scarce 3D pose labels to unlabeled images and improves few-shot pose estimation.

title: Neural View Synthesis and Matching for Semi-Supervised Few-Shot Learning of 3D Pose

abstract: We show that diffusion models can achieve image sample quality superior to the current state-of-the-art generative models. We achieve this on unconditional image synthesis by finding a better architecture through a series of ablations. For conditional image synthesis, we further improve sample quality with classifier guidance: a simple, compute-efficient method for trading off diversity for fidelity using gradients from a classifier. We achieve an FID of 2.97 on ImageNet 128$\times$128, 4.59 on ImageNet 256$\times$256, and 7.72 on ImageNet 512$\times$512, and we match BigGAN-deep even with as few as 25 forward passes per sample, all while maintaining better coverage of the distribution. Finally, we find that classifier guidance combines well with upsampling diffusion models, further improving FID to 3.94 on ImageNet 256$\times$256 and 3.85 on ImageNet 512$\times$512.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates that diffusion models can produce images with sample quality exceeding the state-of-the-art generative models considered in the study. For unconditional generation, the authors improve the model architecture through a series of ablations. This establishes architectural design as an important part of the reported gains.

For conditional generation, they introduce classifier guidance, which uses gradients from a classifier to influence image synthesis. The method provides a computationally efficient way to trade diversity for fidelity. That tradeoff matters when interpreting sample quality: stronger guidance can improve fidelity while changing how broadly the generated samples cover possible outputs.

The reported ImageNet FID scores are 2.97 at 128 × 128, 4.59 at 256 × 256, and 7.72 at 512 × 512. The models match BigGAN-deep with as few as 25 forward passes per sample while retaining better distribution coverage. Combining classifier guidance with upsampling diffusion models further improves FID to 3.94 at 256 × 256 and 3.85 at 512 × 512.
summary.tldr: Improved architectures and classifier guidance let diffusion models surpass comparison generators in image quality while offering a diversity–fidelity tradeoff.

title: Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis

abstract: In this paper we consider multi-objective reinforcement learning where the objectives are balanced using preferences. In practice, the preferences are often given in an adversarial manner, e.g., customers can be picky in many applications. We formalize this problem as an episodic learning problem on a Markov decision process, where transitions are unknown and a reward function is the inner product of a preference vector with pre-specified multi-objective reward functions. We consider two settings. In the online setting, the agent receives a (adversarial) preference every episode and proposes policies to interact with the environment. We provide a model-based algorithm that achieves a nearly minimax optimal regret bound $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(\sqrt{\min\{d,S\}\cdot H^2 SAK}\bigr)$, where $d$ is the number of objectives, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, $H$ is the length of the horizon, and $K$ is the number of episodes. Furthermore, we consider preference-free exploration, i.e., the agent first interacts with the environment without specifying any preference and then is able to accommodate arbitrary preference vector up to $\epsilon$ error. Our proposed algorithm is provably efficient with a nearly optimal trajectory complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl({\min\{d,S\}\cdot H^3 SA}/{\epsilon^2}\bigr)$. This result partly resolves an open problem raised by \citet{jin2020reward}.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when different users can value the same outcomes differently. The environment has several predefined reward components, and a preference vector determines how they combine into a single reward. The agent must learn unknown transitions while accommodating preferences that may be chosen adversarially, rather than following a predictable pattern.

In the online setting, a new preference arrives each episode before the agent chooses how to act. The authors give a model-based algorithm with a nearly minimax optimal regret bound. Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning instead of already knowing how to act well. The bound explicitly accounts for the number of objectives, states, actions, and episode length.

The second setting separates exploration from preferences: the agent first collects experience without a specified preference, then supports arbitrary preferences within a chosen error tolerance. Its trajectory requirement is also nearly optimal. Together, these results quantify how much learning is needed to serve changing objectives, with dependence on the smaller of the objective count and state count.
summary.tldr: The paper gives nearly optimal learning guarantees for agents that must accommodate changing or initially unknown preferences over multiple objectives.

title: Accommodating Picky Customers: Regret Bound and Exploration Complexity for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Explicit deep generative models (DGMs), e.g., VAEs and Normalizing Flows, have shown to offer an effective data modelling alternative for lossless compression. However, DGMs themselves normally require large storage space and thus contaminate the advantage brought by accurate data density estimation.To eliminate the requirement of saving separate models for different target datasets, we propose a novel setting that starts from a pretrained deep generative model and compresses the data batches while adapting the model with a dynamical system for only one epoch.We formalise this setting as that of One-Shot Online Adaptation (OSOA) of DGMs for lossless compression and propose a vanilla algorithm under this setting. Experimental results show that vanilla OSOA can save significant time versus training bespoke models and space versus using one model for all targets.With the same adaptation step number or adaptation time, it is shown vanilla OSOA can exhibit better space efficiency, e.g., $47\%$ less space, than fine-tuning the pretrained model and saving the fine-tuned model.Moreover, we showcase the potential of OSOA and motivate more sophisticated OSOA algorithms by showing further space or time efficiency with multiple updates per batch and early stopping.

paragraphs: Deep generative models can support effective lossless compression by accurately modeling data distributions. However, storing a separate large model for each target dataset can consume the space that better compression saves. This paper introduces One-Shot Online Adaptation, or OSOA, to address that model-storage burden.

OSOA starts with a pretrained model and compresses successive data batches while adapting the model through a dynamical system over a single epoch. The authors formalize this setting and introduce a basic algorithm. The key idea is to incorporate adaptation into the compression process, eliminating the requirement to save a separate model for every target dataset.

Experiments show time savings compared with training bespoke models and space savings compared with using one unchanged model for all targets. Under matched adaptation steps or time, the basic method can also outperform fine-tuning followed by storing the adapted model, with an example of 47% less space. Multiple updates per batch and early stopping provide further demonstrated opportunities for space or time savings.
summary.tldr: OSOA adapts a pretrained generative model while compressing data in one epoch, reducing the time and storage costs of dataset-specific compression.

title: OSOA: One-Shot Online Adaptation of Deep Generative Models for Lossless Compression

abstract: Rationales, snippets of extracted text that explain an inference, have emerged as a popular framework for interpretable natural language processing (NLP). Rationale models typically consist of two cooperating modules: a selector and a classifier with the goal of maximizing the mutual information (MMI) between the "selected" text and the document label. Despite their promises, MMI-based methods often pick up on spurious text patterns and result in models with nonsensical behaviors. In this work, we investigate whether counterfactual data augmentation (CDA), without human assistance, can improve the performance of the selector by lowering the mutual information between spurious signals and the document label. Our counterfactuals are produced in an unsupervised fashion using class-dependent generative models. From an information theoretic lens, we derive properties of the unaugmented dataset for which our CDA approach would succeed. The effectiveness of CDA is empirically evaluated by comparing against several baselines including an improved MMI-based rationale schema on two multi-aspect datasets. Our results show that CDA produces rationales that better capture the signal of interest.

Rationale models typically consist of two cooperating modules: a selector and a classifier with the goal of maximizing the mutual information (MMI) between the "selected" text and the document label. Despite their promises, MMI-based methods often pick up on spurious text patterns and result in models with nonsensical behaviors. In this work, we investigate whether counterfactual data augmentation (CDA), without human assistance, can improve the performance of the selector by lowering the mutual information between spurious signals and the document label. Our counterfactuals are produced in an unsupervised fashion using class-dependent generative models. From an information theoretic lens, we derive properties of the unaugmented dataset for which our CDA approach would succeed. The effectiveness of CDA is empirically evaluated by comparing against several baselines including an improved MMI-based rationale schema on two multi-aspect datasets. Our results show that CDA produces rationales that better capture the signal of interest.

paragraphs: Text rationales are selected snippets intended to explain a prediction. A typical rationale model pairs a selector with a classifier and rewards selected text that carries information about the document label. However, informative text can include accidental correlations, so this objective can produce explanations that focus on spurious patterns and yield nonsensical behavior.

The paper investigates automatically generated counterfactual data as a way to weaken those misleading correlations. Class-dependent generative models produce the additional examples without human assistance. The intended effect is to reduce the information that spurious signals provide about the label, encouraging the selector to attend to the signal actually of interest.

The authors analyze the approach through information theory and derive properties of the original dataset under which the augmentation would succeed. They then evaluate it on two multi-aspect datasets against several baselines, including an improved mutual-information-based rationale method. The reported rationales better capture the intended signal. The contribution combines a conditional account of why augmentation can help with empirical evidence that it improves rationale selection.
summary.tldr: Automatically generated counterfactual examples help text-rationale models focus on relevant signals by weakening spurious label correlations.

title: Making a (Counterfactual) Difference One Rationale at a Time

abstract: Complex physical tasks entail a sequence of object interactions, each with its own preconditions -- which can be difficult for robotic agents to learn efficiently solely through their own experience. We introduce an approach to discover activity-context priors from in-the-wild egocentric video captured with human worn cameras. For a given object, an activity-context prior represents the set of other compatible objects that are required for activities to succeed (e.g., a knife and cutting board brought together with a tomato are conducive to cutting). We encode our video-based prior as an auxiliary reward function that encourages an agent to bring compatible objects together before attempting an interaction. In this way, our model translates everyday human experience into embodied agent skills. We demonstrate our idea using egocentric EPIC-Kitchens video of people performing unscripted kitchen activities to benefit virtual household robotic agents performing various complex tasks in AI2-iTHOR, significantly accelerating agent learning.
