For each object, an activity-context prior describes other objects that are compatible with successful activities involving it. A tomato, for example, can be brought together with a knife and cutting board for cutting. The method converts these video-derived relationships into an auxiliary reward that encourages the agent to gather compatible objects before interacting with them.

The authors use unscripted kitchen activities from EPIC-Kitchens to support virtual household agents performing complex tasks in AI2-iTHOR. Their experiments show significantly faster agent learning. The demonstrated transfer is from human video to simulated embodied behavior: observed object relationships become incentives for useful preparation. This gives the agent information about interaction preconditions without requiring it to discover every such relationship solely from its own experience.
summary.tldr: Object relationships learned from first-person human videos provide auxiliary rewards that accelerate virtual household-agent learning.

title: Shaping embodied agent behavior with activity-context priors from egocentric video

abstract: Deep generative modeling has the potential to cause significant harm to society. Recognizing this threat, a magnitude of research into detecting so-called "Deepfakes'' has emerged. This research most often focuses on the image domain, while studies exploring generated audio signals have---so-far---been neglected. In this paper we make three key contributions to narrow this gap. First, we provide researchers with an introduction to common signal processing techniques used for analyzing audio signals. Second, we present a novel data set, for which we collected nine sample sets from five different network architectures, spanning two languages. Finally, we supply practitioners with two baseline models, adopted from the signal processing community, to facilitate further research in this area.

paragraphs: WaveFake addresses the detection of generated audio, an area the authors identify as receiving less attention than image deepfakes. The paper responds to potential harms from generative modeling by providing resources for studying audio detection. Its contribution combines background material, a dataset, and baseline implementations intended to make further research easier.

The dataset contains nine sample sets produced using five different network architectures and spans two languages. This gives researchers generated audio from several model architectures within a common resource. The accompanying introduction to audio signal-processing techniques helps explain the kinds of analysis relevant to working with these signals.

The authors also provide two baseline models adapted from the signal-processing community. These give practitioners concrete starting points for experimentation alongside the data. The paper's stated contribution is the creation of an accessible research foundation for audio deepfake detection: researchers receive examples to study, methods for analyzing audio, and initial detection approaches to build upon. The combination broadens the available infrastructure for investigating generated speech and other audio signals.
summary.tldr: WaveFake supports audio deepfake research with samples from five generative architectures, two languages, signal-processing guidance, and two baseline models.

title: WaveFake: A Data Set to Facilitate Audio Deepfake Detection

abstract: Imitation learning often needs a large demonstration set in order to handle the full range of situations that an agent might find itself in during deployment. However, collecting expert demonstrations can be expensive. Recent work in vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP has shown that auxiliary representation learning objectives can reduce the need for large amounts of expensive, task-specific data. Our Empirical Investigation of Representation Learning for Imitation (EIRLI) investigates whether similar benefits apply to imitation learning. We propose a modular framework for constructing representation learning algorithms, then use our framework to evaluate the utility of representation learning for imitation across several environment suites. In the settings we evaluate, we find that existing algorithms for image-based representation learning provide limited value relative to a well-tuned baseline with image augmentations. To explain this result, we investigate differences between imitation learning and other settings where representation learning has provided significant benefit, such as image classification. Finally, we release a well-documented codebase which both replicates our findings and provides a modular framework for creating new representation learning algorithms out of reusable components.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains agents from expert demonstrations, but obtaining enough demonstrations to cover deployment situations can be expensive. This paper asks whether learning useful internal representations through additional training objectives can reduce that burden. The motivation comes from successes in other areas, including vision and language, where representation learning has helped make better use of task-specific data.

The authors build a modular framework for assembling representation learning algorithms and use it to evaluate imitation learning across several environment suites. Their comparison includes a carefully tuned baseline that uses image augmentations. This makes the question concrete: do the additional representation learning methods offer value beyond that baseline?

In the evaluated settings, existing image-based representation learning algorithms provide limited additional benefit. The authors investigate differences between imitation learning and settings such as image classification to understand this result. Their findings qualify the expectation that benefits transfer automatically between tasks. They also release documented, reusable code for reproducing the study and constructing new algorithms.
summary.tldr: Across the evaluated imitation learning settings, existing representation learning methods add limited value beyond a well-tuned baseline with image augmentations.

title: An Empirical Investigation of Representation Learning for Imitation

abstract: Visual tasks vary a lot in their output formats and concerned contents, therefore it is hard to process them with an identical structure. One main obstacle lies in the high-dimensional outputs in object-level visual tasks. In this paper, we propose an object-centric vision framework, Obj2Seq. Obj2Seq takes objects as basic units, and regards most object-level visual tasks as sequence generation problems of objects. Therefore, these visual tasks can be decoupled into two steps. First recognize objects of given categories, and then generate a sequence for each of these objects. The definition of the output sequences varies for different tasks, and the model is supervised by matching these sequences with ground-truth targets. Obj2Seq is able to flexibly determine input categories to satisfy customized requirements, and be easily extended to different visual tasks. When experimenting on MS COCO, Obj2Seq achieves 45.7% AP on object detection, 89.0% AP on multi-label classification and 65.0% AP on human pose estimation. These results demonstrate its potential to be generally applied to different visual tasks. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/Obj2Seq.

paragraphs: Object detection, image classification, and pose estimation require different kinds of output, making a shared visual architecture difficult to design. Obj2Seq addresses this by treating objects as the basic units of prediction and expressing most object-level visual tasks as sequence generation. The sequence format changes with the task while retaining the same organizing structure.

The framework first recognizes objects belonging to specified categories. It then generates a sequence for each recognized object, with training based on matching the sequences to ground-truth targets. Allowing the input categories to be selected also lets users specify which object categories are relevant to their requirements.

On MS COCO, the authors report average precision of 45.7% for detection, 89.0% for multi-label classification, and 65.0% for human pose estimation. These task-specific results demonstrate that the framework can operate across several different output types. They support its potential as a general object-centric framework, with the common representation providing a practical route for extending the architecture to additional visual tasks.
summary.tldr: Obj2Seq unifies several visual tasks by recognizing requested object categories and generating a task-specific sequence for each object.

title: Obj2Seq: Formatting Objects as Sequences with Class Prompt for Visual Tasks

abstract: In this work we propose a batch Bayesian optimization method for combinatorial problems on permutations, which is well suited for expensive-to-evaluate objectives. We first introduce LAW, an efficient batch acquisition method based on determinantal point processes using the acquisition weighted kernel. Relying on multiple parallel evaluations, LAW enables accelerated search on combinatorial spaces. We then apply the framework to permutation problems, which have so far received little attention in the Bayesian Optimization literature, despite their practical importance. We call this method LAW2ORDER. On the theoretical front, we prove that LAW2ORDER has vanishing simple regret by showing that the batch cumulative regret is sublinear. Empirically, we assess the method on several standard combinatorial problems involving permutations such as quadratic assignment, flowshop scheduling and the traveling salesman, as well as on a structure learning task.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial decisions involve choosing an ordering, and evaluating a candidate ordering can be expensive. This paper develops Bayesian optimization for such permutation problems, with an emphasis on selecting several candidates that can be evaluated in parallel. The goal is to accelerate search when individual evaluations are costly.

The authors first introduce LAW, a batch acquisition method built from determinantal point processes and an acquisition-weighted kernel. This machinery selects a batch through a joint rule rather than treating parallel evaluations as unrelated choices. Applying that framework to permutations yields LAW2ORDER, extending batch Bayesian optimization to an important class of discrete search spaces.

The theoretical analysis establishes sublinear batch cumulative regret and uses it to prove vanishing simple regret. In practical terms, the latter guarantee concerns the quality of the best candidate found as search progresses. The empirical evaluation covers quadratic assignment, flowshop scheduling, the traveling salesman problem, and structure learning. The contribution therefore combines a parallel search mechanism, a permutation-focused application, and a formal convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: LAW2ORDER uses batch Bayesian optimization to search permutation spaces in parallel and has a vanishing-simple-regret guarantee.

title: Batch Bayesian Optimization on Permutations using the Acquisition Weighted Kernel

abstract: This work discusses how to achieve worst-case Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) generalization for a variety of distributions based on a relatively small labeling cost. The problem has broad applications, especially in non-i.i.d. open-world scenarios. Previous studies either rely on a large amount of labeling cost or lack of guarantees about the worst-case generalization. In this work, we show for the first time that active model adaptation could achieve both good performance and robustness based on the invariant risk minimization principle. We propose \textsc{Log}, an interactive model adaptation framework, with two sub-modules: active sample selection and causal invariant learning. Specifically, we formulate the active selection as a mixture distribution separation problem and present an unbiased estimator, which could find the samples that violate the current invariant relationship, with a provable guarantee. The theoretical analysis supports that both sub-modules contribute to generalization. A large number of experimental results confirm the promising performance of the new algorithm.

paragraphs: LOG addresses adaptation to distributions that differ from the training data while keeping labeling costs relatively small. The objective includes worst-case generalization across a variety of distributions, rather than performance on just one favorable target. The paper motivates this problem through open-world settings where observations need not follow a single independent, identically distributed source.

The framework combines active sample selection with causal invariant learning. Its sample-selection component searches for examples that violate the invariant relationship currently used by the model. The authors formulate this selection task as separating a mixture distribution and provide an unbiased estimator with a provable guarantee. Labeling informative violations can then support refinement of the learned invariant relationship.

The theoretical analysis supports contributions from both modules to generalization and shows how active adaptation can combine performance with robustness through invariant risk minimization. Extensive experiments report promising performance for the resulting algorithm. The contribution is an interactive approach in which selecting what to label and learning stable relationships work together toward label-efficient generalization.
summary.tldr: LOG combines targeted labeling of invariant-relationship violations with causal invariant learning to improve label-efficient out-of-distribution adaptation.

title: LOG: Active Model Adaptation for Label-Efficient OOD Generalization

abstract: Surface reconstruction for point clouds is an important task in 3D computer vision. Most of the latest methods resolve this problem by learning signed distance functions (SDF) from point clouds, which are limited to reconstructing shapes or scenes with closed surfaces. Some other methods tried to represent shapes or scenes with open surfaces using unsigned distance functions (UDF) which are learned from large scale ground truth unsigned distances. However, the learned UDF is hard to provide smooth distance fields near the surface due to the noncontinuous character of point clouds. In this paper, we propose a novel method to learn consistency-aware unsigned distance functions directly from raw point clouds. We achieve this by learning to move 3D queries to reach the surface with a field consistency constraint, where we also enable to progressively estimate a more accurate surface. Specifically, we train a neural network to gradually infer the relationship between 3D queries and the approximated surface by searching for the moving target of queries in a dynamic way, which results in a consistent field around the surface. Meanwhile, we introduce a polygonization algorithm to extract surfaces directly from the gradient field of the learned UDF. The experimental results in surface reconstruction for synthetic and real scan data show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art under the widely used benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a surface from a point cloud requires turning scattered samples into coherent geometry. Signed distance approaches are limited to closed surfaces in the methods discussed here. Unsigned distance functions can also represent open surfaces, but learning a smooth field near the surface is difficult when the observations are discrete points.

This paper learns an unsigned distance function directly from raw point clouds. It trains a network to move three-dimensional query points toward an estimated surface while enforcing consistency in the surrounding field. The surface estimate improves progressively, and the method dynamically searches for the targets toward which queries should move. This lets the relationship between queries and the estimated geometry evolve during learning.

The authors also introduce a polygonization algorithm that extracts a surface directly from the learned function’s gradient field. Experiments using synthetic data and real scans report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. Together, the learning and extraction procedures address both constructing a consistent distance representation and converting it into a reconstructed surface.
summary.tldr: Progressive learning with field consistency reconstructs surfaces from raw point clouds through an unsigned distance representation.

title: Learning Consistency-Aware Unsigned Distance Functions Progressively from Raw Point Clouds

abstract: A classical result of Johnson and Lindenstrauss states that a set of $n$ high dimensional data points can be projected down to $O(\log n/\epsilon^2)$ dimensions such that the square of their pairwise distances is preserved up to a small distortion $\epsilon\in(0,1)$. It has been proved that the JL lemma is optimal for the general case, therefore, improvements can only be explored for special cases. This work aims to improve the $\epsilon^{-2}$ dependency based on techniques inspired by the Hutch++ Algorithm, which reduces $\epsilon^{-2}$ to $\epsilon^{-1}$ for the related problem of implicit matrix trace estimation. We first present an algorithm to estimate the Euclidean lengths of the rows of a matrix. We prove for it element-wise probabilistic bounds that are at least as good as standard JL approximations in the worst-case, but are asymptotically better for matrices with decaying spectrum. Moreover, for any matrix, regardless of its spectrum, the algorithm achieves $\epsilon$-accuracy for the total, Frobenius norm-wise relative error using only $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ queries. This is a quadratic improvement over the norm-wise error of standard JL approximations. We also show how these results can be extended to estimate (i) the Euclidean distances between data points and (ii) the statistical leverage scores of tall-and-skinny data matrices, which are ubiquitous for many applications, with analogous theoretical improvements. Proof-of-concept numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss result explains how dimensionality reduction can approximately preserve pairwise distances. Its general guarantee is already optimal, so this paper looks for improvements through special matrix structure and different measures of approximation error. The approach draws inspiration from Hutch++, an algorithm that improves accuracy dependence for matrix trace estimation.

The authors first construct an algorithm for estimating the Euclidean lengths of matrix rows. Its probabilistic guarantees for individual rows are at least as good as standard Johnson–Lindenstrauss approximations in the worst case. A separate guarantee concerns total relative error measured using the Frobenius norm. For this aggregate criterion, the algorithm needs only O(1/epsilon) queries for any matrix, regardless of its spectrum, improving the standard quadratic dependence on inverse accuracy. The results extend to pairwise distances and statistical leverage scores. Proof-of-concept experiments support the analysis, while the distinction between individual and aggregate guarantees explains how the improvements coexist with general optimality.
summary.tldr: A matrix estimation method improves on standard distance approximations for decaying spectra and achieves better aggregate-error query complexity for any matrix.

title: Approximate Euclidean lengths and distances beyond Johnson-Lindenstrauss

abstract: In many web applications, deep learning-based CTR prediction models (deep CTR models for short) are widely adopted. Traditional deep CTR models learn patterns in a static manner, i.e., the network parameters are the same across all the instances. However, such a manner can hardly characterize each of the instances which may have different underlying distributions. It actually limits the representation power of deep CTR models, leading to sub-optimal results. In this paper, we propose an efficient, effective, and universal module, named as Adaptive Parameter Generation network (APG), which can dynamically generate parameters for deep CTR models on-the-fly based on different instances. Extensive experimental evaluation results show that APG can be applied to a variety of deep CTR models and significantly improve their performance. Meanwhile, APG can reduce the time cost by 38.7\% and memory usage by 96.6\% compared to a regular deep CTR model.We have deployed APG in the industrial sponsored search system and achieved 3\% CTR gain and 1\% RPM gain respectively.

paragraphs: Click-through rate prediction estimates whether a user will click an item in a web application. Conventional deep models use the same learned network parameters for every example. The authors argue that this fixed treatment limits how well a model can represent examples arising from different underlying distributions.

The Adaptive Parameter Generation network, or APG, generates model parameters dynamically according to the instance being processed. This makes instance-specific adaptation part of prediction itself. APG is presented as a module that can be incorporated into different deep click-through rate models, and the reported experiments show significant performance improvements across a variety of those models.

The paper also reports efficiency and deployment results. Compared with a regular deep click-through rate model, APG can reduce time cost by 38.7% and memory use by 96.6%. In an industrial sponsored search deployment, it achieved a 3% click-through rate gain and a 1% RPM gain. These results show that the tested form of adaptive parameter generation improved prediction while also offering substantial resource savings in the reported comparison.
summary.tldr: APG generates instance-specific parameters for click prediction, with reported gains in predictive performance, efficiency, and industrial deployment.

title: APG: Adaptive Parameter Generation Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction

abstract: Many practical settings allow a learner to defer predictions to one or more costly experts. For example, the learning to defer paradigm allows a learner to defer to a human expert, at some monetary cost. Similarly, the adaptive inference paradigm allows a base model to defer to one or more large models, at some computational cost. The goal in these settings is to learn classification and deferral mechanisms to optimise a suitable accuracy-cost tradeoff. To achieve this, a central issue studied in prior work is the design of a coherent loss function for both mechanisms. In this work, we demonstrate that existing losses have two subtle limitations: they can encourage underfitting when there is a high cost of deferring, and the deferral function can have a weak dependence on the base model predictions. To resolve these issues, we propose a post-hoc training scheme: we train a deferral function on top of a base model, with the objective of predicting to defer when the base model's error probability exceeds the cost of the expert model. This may be viewed as applying a partial surrogate to the ideal deferral loss, which can lead to a tighter approximation and thus better performance. Empirically, we verify the efficacy of post-hoc training on benchmarks for learning to defer and adaptive inference.

paragraphs: A predictive system can sometimes hand a decision to a human expert or a larger model, but doing so incurs monetary or computational cost. Learning to defer aims to balance that cost against accuracy. This paper examines how training objectives shape both the base predictor and the decision to request expert help.

The authors identify two problems with existing losses: high deferral costs can encourage underfitting, and the deferral rule can depend too weakly on the base model's predictions. Their alternative trains the deferral function after the base model. Its objective is to request help when the base model's error probability exceeds the expert model's cost.

They interpret this procedure as using a partial surrogate for the ideal deferral loss, which can provide a tighter approximation and better performance. Benchmark experiments in learning to defer and adaptive inference support the effectiveness of the post-hoc scheme. The contribution ties the handoff decision more directly to the trained predictor's expected error and the price of obtaining expert assistance.
summary.tldr: Training a deferral rule after the base model helps balance predicted error against expert cost and addresses weaknesses in existing losses.

title: Post-hoc estimators for learning to defer to an expert

abstract: Multiple kernel clustering (MKC) is an important research topic that has been widely studied for decades. However, current methods still face two problems: inefficient when handling out-of-sample data points and lack of theoretical study of the stability and generalization of clustering. In this paper, we propose a novel method that can efficiently compute the embedding of out-of-sample data with a solid generalization guarantee. Specifically, we approximate the eigen functions of the integral operator associated with the linear combination of base kernel functions to construct low-dimensional embeddings of out-of-sample points for efficient multiple kernel clustering. In addition, we, for the first time, theoretically study the stability of clustering algorithms and prove that the single-view version of the proposed method has uniform stability as $\mathcal{O}\left(Kn^{-3/2}\right)$ and establish an upper bound of excess risk as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(Kn^{-3/2}+n^{-1/2}\right)$, where $K$ is the cluster number and $n$ is the number of samples. We then extend the theoretical results to multiple kernel scenarios and find that the stability of MKC depends on kernel weights. As an example, we apply our method to a novel MKC algorithm termed SimpleMKKM and derive the upper bound of its excess clustering risk, which is tighter than the current results. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Multiple-kernel clustering combines different kernel functions to group data, but handling new points efficiently and understanding generalization remain challenges. This paper addresses both by constructing low-dimensional embeddings for out-of-sample points and studying the stability of the resulting clustering method.

Applied to SimpleMKKM, the method yields a tighter upper bound on excess clustering risk than existing results. Experiments support its effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution connects practical handling of unseen points with theoretical control over stability and generalization.
summary.tldr: An eigenfunction-based embedding method makes new-point kernel clustering efficient while providing stability and generalization guarantees.

title: Stability and Generalization of Kernel Clustering: from Single Kernel to Multiple Kernel

abstract: Forecasting complex time series is ubiquitous and vital in a range of applications but challenging. Recent advances endeavor to achieve progress by incorporating various deep learning techniques (e.g., RNN and Transformer) into sequential models. However, clear patterns are still hard to extract since time series are often composed of several intricately entangled components. Motivated by the success of disentangled variational autoencoder in computer vision and classical time series decomposition, we plan to infer a couple of representations that depict seasonal and trend components of time series. To achieve this goal, we propose LaST, which, based on variational inference, aims to disentangle the seasonal-trend representations in the latent space. Furthermore, LaST supervises and disassociates representations from the perspectives of themselves and input reconstruction, and introduces a series of auxiliary objectives. Extensive experiments prove that LaST achieves state-of-the-art performance on time series forecasting task against the most advanced representation learning and end-to-end forecasting models. For reproducibility, our implementation is publicly available on Github.

paragraphs: Forecasting a time series is difficult when several kinds of variation are entangled. Recurring seasonal behavior and broader trends can overlap, making useful patterns hard to extract. LaST approaches this problem by learning separate latent representations intended to describe these two components, drawing on both classical time-series decomposition and disentangled representation learning.

The method uses variational inference to learn the seasonal and trend representations. It introduces auxiliary objectives that supervise the representations and encourage their separation. These objectives consider both the representations themselves and their role in reconstructing the input, connecting the desired separation to the observed time series.

The authors report state-of-the-art forecasting results in extensive experiments against advanced representation-learning methods and end-to-end forecasting models. The findings support the usefulness of explicitly organizing the learned representation around seasonality and trend. The central contribution is therefore a forecasting approach that gives these components separate roles in latent space and trains that separation through several complementary objectives, with empirical results supporting the overall design.
summary.tldr: LaST learns separate latent seasonal and trend representations and reports state-of-the-art time-series forecasting performance.

title: Learning Latent Seasonal-Trend Representations for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Offline imitation from observations aims to solve MDPs where only task-specific expert states and task-agnostic non-expert state-action pairs are available. Offline imitation is useful in real-world scenarios where arbitrary interactions are costly and expert actions are unavailable. The state-of-the-art ‘DIstribution Correction Estimation’ (DICE) methods minimize divergence of state occupancy between expert and learner policies and retrieve a policy with weighted behavior cloning; however, their results are unstable when learning from incomplete trajectories, due to a non-robust optimization in the dual domain. To address the issue, in this paper, we propose Trajectory-Aware Imitation Learning from Observations (TAILO). TAILO uses a discounted sum along the future trajectory as the weight for weighted behavior cloning. The terms for the sum are scaled by the output of a discriminator, which aims to identify expert states. Despite simplicity, TAILO works well if there exist trajectories or segments of expert behavior in the task-agnostic data, a common assumption in prior work. In experiments across multiple testbeds, we find TAILO to be more robust and effective, particularly with incomplete trajectories.

paragraphs: Offline imitation from observations learns behavior from expert states without seeing the expert's actions. It also has access to a separate collection of non-expert state-action pairs. This setting matters when interacting with the environment is costly and expert action records are unavailable. The paper addresses a particular difficulty: existing distribution-matching methods can become unstable when their recorded trajectories are incomplete.

The proposed method, TAILO, trains a discriminator to recognize states that resemble expert behavior. It then uses the discriminator's outputs in a discounted sum over a trajectory's future states. That sum determines how strongly each example contributes to weighted behavior cloning. Training therefore considers where a recorded behavior leads, rather than assigning importance solely from an isolated state.

The approach works well under the stated assumption that the task-agnostic dataset contains trajectories or segments of expert behavior. Across multiple experimental testbeds, the authors find TAILO more robust and effective, especially with incomplete trajectories. The contribution is a relatively simple way to use trajectory information while avoiding the unstable dual-domain optimization identified in earlier methods.
summary.tldr: TAILO uses future expert-like states to weight offline imitation examples, improving robustness when recorded trajectories are incomplete.

title: A Simple Solution for Offline Imitation from Observations and Examples with Possibly Incomplete Trajectories

abstract: Learning controllers with offline data in decision-making systems is an essential area of research due to its potential to reduce the risk of applications in real-world systems. However, in responsibility-sensitive settings such as healthcare, decision accountability is of paramount importance, yet has not been adequately addressed by the literature.This paper introduces the Accountable Offline Controller (AOC) that employs the offline dataset as the Decision Corpus and performs accountable control based on a tailored selection of examples, referred to as the Corpus Subset. AOC operates effectively in low-data scenarios, can be extended to the strictly offline imitation setting, and displays qualities of both conservation and adaptability.We assess AOC's performance in both simulated and real-world healthcare scenarios, emphasizing its capability to manage offline control tasks with high levels of performance while maintaining accountability.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning builds controllers from previously collected data. This can reduce the need to learn through potentially risky interactions with a real system. In settings such as healthcare, however, a controller also needs to make its decisions accountable. This paper addresses how a learned decision can be connected to examples in the data used to support it.

The proposed Accountable Offline Controller treats the offline dataset as a Decision Corpus. For control, it makes a tailored selection of examples called the Corpus Subset. These examples form the basis of its accountable decision process, giving the corpus a direct role in control rather than using it only as material for training.

The authors report that the approach works effectively when data are limited, combines conservative behavior with adaptability, and extends to strictly offline imitation. Evaluations cover simulated and real-world healthcare scenarios. The reported findings support the possibility of maintaining strong offline control performance while grounding decisions in selected examples, which is the paper's central approach to accountability.
summary.tldr: AOC grounds offline control decisions in selected examples from its dataset to combine performance with accountability.

title: Accountability in Offline Reinforcement Learning: Explaining Decisions with a Corpus of Examples

abstract: We consider a weakly supervised learning scenario where the supervision signal is generated by a transition function $\sigma$ of labels associated with multiple input instances. We formulate this problem as *multi-instance Partial Label Learning (multi-instance PLL)*, which is an extension to the standard PLL problem. Our problem is met in different fields, including latent structural learning and neuro-symbolic integration. Despite the existence of many learning techniques, limited theoretical analysis has been dedicated to this problem. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical study of multi-instance PLL with possibly an unknown transition $\sigma$. Our main contributions are as follows: First, we proposed a necessary and sufficient condition for the learnability of the problem. This condition nontrivially generalizes and relaxes the existing *small ambiguity degree* in PLL literature since we allow the transition to be deterministic. Second, we derived Rademacher-style error bounds based on the top-$k$ surrogate loss that is widely used in the neuro-symbolic literature. Furthermore, we conclude with empirical experiments for learning with an unknown transition. The empirical results align with our theoretical findings; however, they also expose the issue of scalability in the weak supervision literature.

paragraphs: Sometimes supervision describes several inputs together rather than revealing each input's label. This paper studies that situation through a transition function that combines the labels of multiple instances into an observed signal. It formulates the problem as multi-instance Partial Label Learning, including cases where the transition function itself may be unknown.

The paper therefore addresses both whether learning is possible and how particular losses can be analyzed. Its empirical results distinguish that theoretical possibility from the practical challenge of making the approach scale, a limitation explicitly identified in the study.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes learnability under multi-instance weak supervision, derives error bounds, and finds empirical support alongside scalability challenges.

title: On Learning Latent Models with Multi-Instance Weak Supervision

abstract: Measuring the nonlinear dependence between random vectors and testing for their statistical independence is a fundamental problem in statistics. One of the most popular dependence measures is the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC), which has attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, most existing works have focused on either fixed or very high-dimensional covariates. In this work, we bridge the gap between these two scenarios and provide statistical insights into the performance of HSIC when the dimensions grow at different rates. We first show that, under the null hypothesis, the rescaled HSIC converges in distribution to a standard normal distribution. Then we provide a general condition for the HSIC based tests to have nontrivial power in high dimensions. By decomposing this condition, we illustrate how the ability of HSIC to measure nonlinear dependence changes with increasing dimensions. Moreover, we demonstrate that, depending on the sample size, the covariate dimensions and the dependence structures within covariates, the HSIC can capture different types of associations between random vectors. We also conduct extensive numerical studies to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: The Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, or HSIC, measures dependence between random vectors and supports tests of statistical independence. Although it can measure nonlinear relationships, its behavior can change when the vectors contain many dimensions. This paper studies dimensions growing at different rates, connecting settings between fixed-dimensional and very-high-dimensional analyses.

The authors establish that, under the independence null hypothesis in their analysis, a rescaled HSIC statistic converges to a standard normal distribution. They also give a general condition under which HSIC-based tests retain nontrivial power, meaning an ability to detect dependence. Decomposing that condition reveals how increasing dimension changes sensitivity to nonlinear relationships.

The resulting picture depends jointly on sample size, vector dimensions, and dependence among coordinates within each vector. Different combinations allow HSIC to capture different kinds of association between the vectors. Numerical studies validate the theoretical findings. The paper thus explains why calling HSIC a nonlinear dependence measure does not, by itself, describe which relationships it will detect effectively in a particular high-dimensional setting.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how dimension, sample size, and internal dependence affect HSIC's ability to detect statistical relationships.

title: Statistical Insights into HSIC in High Dimensions

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in language understanding and generation. However, such impressive capability typically comes with a substantial model size, which presents significant challenges in both the deployment, inference, and training stages. With LLM being a general-purpose task solver, we explore its compression in a task-agnostic manner, which aims to preserve the multi-task solving and language generation ability of the original LLM. One challenge to achieving this is the enormous size of the training corpus of LLM, which makes both data transfer and model post-training over-burdensome. Thus, we tackle the compression of LLMs within the bound of two constraints: being task-agnostic and minimizing the reliance on the original training dataset. Our method, named LLM-pruner, adopts structural pruning that selectively removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information, maximally preserving the majority of the LLM's functionality. To this end, the performance of pruned models can be efficiently recovered through tuning techniques, LoRA, in merely 3 hours, requiring only 50K data. We validate the LLM-Pruner on three LLMs, including LLaMA, Vicuna, and ChatGLM, and demonstrate that the compressed models still exhibit satisfactory capabilities in zero-shot classification and generation. The code will be made public.

paragraphs: Large language models are expensive to deploy, run, and train because of their size. Compressing them is challenging when the goal is to retain broad language and multitask abilities rather than optimize for one narrow application. The paper also seeks to minimize dependence on the enormous datasets used for original model training.

LLM-Pruner removes coupled model structures judged less critical using gradient information. This structural pruning aims to retain as much functionality as possible while reducing the model. These findings support a task-agnostic compression workflow combining selective structural removal with relatively limited recovery training. The stated objective is preservation of general usefulness under reduced data dependence, rather than compression tailored to a particular downstream task.
summary.tldr: LLM-Pruner combines gradient-guided structural pruning with LoRA recovery to compress language models while retaining broad capabilities.

title: LLM-Pruner: On the Structural Pruning of Large Language Models

abstract: Despite substantial advancements, Natural Language Processing (NLP) models often require post-training adjustments to enforce business rules, rectify undesired behavior, and align with user values. These adjustments involve operationalizing "concepts"—dictating desired model responses to certain inputs. However, it's difficult for a single entity to enumerate and define all possible concepts, indicating a need for a multi-user, collaborative model alignment framework. Moreover, the exhaustive delineation of a concept is challenging, and an improper approach can create shortcuts or interfere with original data or other concepts.To address these challenges, we introduce CoAlign, a framework that enables multi-user interaction with the model, thereby mitigating individual limitations. CoAlign aids users in operationalizing their concepts using Large Language Models, and relying on the principle that NLP models exhibit simpler behaviors in local regions. Our main insight is learning a \emph{local} model for each concept, and a \emph{global} model to integrate the original data with all concepts.We then steer a large language model to generate instances within concept boundaries where local and global disagree.Our experiments show CoAlign is effective at helping multiple users operationalize concepts and avoid interference for a variety of scenarios, tasks, and models.

paragraphs: CoAlign addresses the work of adjusting an NLP model after training to reflect business rules, user values, or corrections to unwanted behavior. The authors describe these desired behaviors as concepts that users must turn into concrete model requirements. Because one person cannot readily enumerate every relevant concept, the framework supports contributions from multiple users.

Its central design pairs a local model for each concept with a global model that integrates all concepts and the original data. This uses the principle that model behavior is simpler within local regions. A large language model then generates examples inside a concept's boundaries where its local model and the global model disagree. Those disagreements expose places where the combined model does not yet reflect the concept.

Experiments across different scenarios, tasks, and models show that CoAlign helps users specify concepts while avoiding interference between them. This matters because adding one behavioral requirement can otherwise disturb another or the original task. The contribution is a collaborative process for making requirements concrete and reconciling them within a shared model.
summary.tldr: CoAlign combines local concept models, a global model, and generated disagreement examples to help multiple users align NLP behavior.

title: Collaborative Alignment of NLP Models

abstract: Automated content filtering and moderation is an important tool that allows online platforms to build striving user communities that facilitate cooperation and prevent abuse. Unfortunately, resourceful actors try to bypass automated filters in a bid to post content that violate platform policies and codes of conduct. To reach this goal, these malicious actors may obfuscate policy violating images (e.g., overlay harmful images by carefully selected benign images or visual patterns) to prevent machine learning models from reaching the correct decision. In this paper, we invite researchers to tackle this specific issue and present a new image benchmark. This benchmark, based on ImageNet, simulates the type of obfuscations created by malicious actors. It goes beyond Image-Net-C and ImageNet-C-bar by proposing general, drastic, adversarial modifications that preserve the original content intent. It aims to tackle a more common adversarial threat than the one considered by lp-norm bounded adversaries. We evaluate 33 pretrained models on the benchmark and train models with different augmentations, architectures and training methods on subsets of the obfuscations to measure generalization. Our hope is that this benchmark will encourage researchers to test their models and methods and try to find new approaches that are more robust to these obfuscations.

paragraphs: Image moderation systems can be challenged by deliberate visual changes that hide problematic content from a model while preserving its intended meaning. This paper introduces an ImageNet-based benchmark for studying such obfuscations. Examples motivating the work include overlaying an image with benign pictures or patterns to interfere with automated recognition.

The benchmark considers substantial, adversarial changes to images. Its focus differs from attacks restricted to small changes under a mathematical distance measure: the intended content can remain present even when the picture changes dramatically. The authors also position these transformations beyond the corruption types covered by ImageNet-C and ImageNet-C-bar, aiming to capture a threat relevant to content filtering.

The study evaluates 33 pretrained models and trains additional models using different augmentations, architectures, and training methods on subsets of the obfuscations. This design examines whether exposure to some transformations helps with others. The stated contribution is a benchmark and evaluation programme that can support research into robustness against these deliberate alterations.
summary.tldr: An ImageNet-based benchmark tests whether image models withstand drastic, deliberate obfuscations that preserve the original content's intent.

title: Benchmarking Robustness to Adversarial Image Obfuscations

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have made significant advances in generating and editing high-quality images. As a result, numerous approaches have explored the ability of diffusion model features to understand and process single images for downstream tasks, e.g., classification, semantic segmentation, and stylization. However, significantly less is known about what these features reveal across multiple, different images and objects. In this work, we exploit Stable Diffusion (SD) features for semantic and dense correspondence and discover that with simple post-processing, SD features can perform quantitatively similar to SOTA representations. Interestingly, the qualitative analysis reveals that SD features have very different properties compared to existing representation learning features, such as the recently released DINOv2: while DINOv2 provides sparse but accurate matches, SD features provide high-quality spatial information but sometimes inaccurate semantic matches. We demonstrate that a simple fusion of these two features works surprisingly well, and a zero-shot evaluation using nearest neighbors on these fused features provides a significant performance gain over state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, e.g., SPair-71k, PF-Pascal, and TSS. We also show that these correspondences can enable interesting applications such as instance swapping in two images. Project page: https://sd-complements-dino.github.io/.

paragraphs: Finding corresponding locations across different images requires recognizing both what a region represents and where it sits within an object. This paper investigates whether features from Stable Diffusion, a model developed for image generation, can support that task. With simple post-processing, those features achieve quantitative results comparable to leading representations.

The authors’ qualitative analysis reveals a useful difference between Stable Diffusion and DINOv2. DINOv2 produces accurate but sparse matches, whereas Stable Diffusion provides strong spatial information while sometimes matching the wrong semantic content. Their strengths therefore address different parts of the correspondence problem: reliable identity matching and richer information about spatial arrangement.

Simply combining the two feature types produces significant gains over state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot nearest-neighbor evaluations on SPair-71k, PF-Pascal, and TSS. The results show that useful correspondence information can emerge from combining these existing representations. The authors also demonstrate instance swapping between two images, illustrating how the resulting matches can support image manipulation beyond correspondence evaluation itself.
summary.tldr: Combining Stable Diffusion’s spatial features with DINOv2’s accurate matches improves zero-shot correspondence across images.

title: A Tale of Two Features: Stable Diffusion Complements DINO for Zero-Shot Semantic Correspondence

abstract: Large language models are trained in two stages: (1) unsupervised pretraining from raw text, to learn general-purpose representations, and (2) large scale instruction tuning and reinforcement learning, to better align to end tasks and user preferences. We measure the relative importance of these two stages by training LIMA, a 65B parameter LLaMa language model fine-tuned with the standard supervised loss on only 1,000 carefully curated prompts and responses, without any reinforcement learning or human preference modeling.LIMA demonstrates remarkably strong performance, learning to follow specific response formats from only a handful of examples in the training data, including complex queries that range from planning trip itineraries to speculating about alternate history.Moreover, the model tends to generalize well to unseen tasks that did not appear in the training data.In a controlled human study, responses from LIMA are either equivalent or strictly preferred to GPT-4 in 43\% of cases; this statistic is as high as 58\% when compared to Bard and 65\% versus DaVinci003, which was trained with human feedback.Taken together, these results strongly suggest that almost all knowledge in large language models is learned during pretraining, and only limited instruction tuning data is necessary to teach models to produce high quality output.

paragraphs: LIMA investigates how much a language model's useful behavior comes from pretraining and how much must be supplied through later alignment. The authors fine-tune a 65-billion-parameter LLaMa model using only 1,000 carefully selected prompts and responses. Training uses a standard supervised loss, without reinforcement learning or a model of human preferences.

The resulting model learns particular response formats from a small number of examples and handles complex requests such as itinerary planning and alternate-history questions. It also tends to generalize to tasks absent from its fine-tuning data. These figures combine ties and preferences. The authors interpret the overall evidence as strongly suggesting that pretraining supplies almost all model knowledge and limited instruction tuning can teach high-quality output.
summary.tldr: LIMA shows strong instruction-following after supervised fine-tuning on 1,000 curated examples, suggesting much of its capability comes from pretraining.

title: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment

abstract: Synthetic time series are often used in practical applications to augment the historical time series dataset, amplify the occurrence of rare events and also create counterfactual scenarios.Distributional-similarity (which we refer to as realism) as well as the satisfaction of certain numerical constraints are common requirements for counterfactual time series generation. For instance, the US Federal Reserve publishes synthetic market stress scenarios given by the constrained time series for financial institutions to assess their performance in hypothetical recessions.Existing approaches for generating constrained time series usually penalize training loss to enforce constraints, and reject non-conforming samples. However, these approaches would require re-training if we change constraints, and rejection sampling can be computationally expensive, or impractical for complex constraints.In this paper, we propose a novel set of methods to tackle the constrained time series generation problem and provide efficient sampling while ensuring the realism of generated time series. In particular, we frame the problem using a constrained optimization framework and then we propose a set of generative methods including 'GuidedDiffTime', a guided diffusion model. We empirically evaluate our work on several datasets for financial and energy data, where incorporating constraints is critical. We show that our approaches outperform existing work both qualitatively and quantitatively, and that 'GuidedDiffTime' does not require re-training for new constraints, resulting in a significant carbon footprint reduction, up to 92% w.r.t. existing deep learning methods.

paragraphs: Synthetic time series are useful for expanding datasets, representing rare events, and constructing counterfactual scenarios. Such sequences may need both realistic statistical behavior and compliance with numerical constraints. This paper addresses that combination, which arises in applications such as financial stress scenarios and energy data.

Existing approaches can encode constraints through training penalties and discard samples that violate them. Changing constraints may then require retraining, while rejecting many samples can become costly or impractical. The authors formulate generation as constrained optimization and develop several generative methods, including the guided diffusion model GuidedDiffTime, to support efficient sampling while maintaining realism.

Evaluations on financial and energy datasets show qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing work. GuidedDiffTime also accommodates new constraints without retraining, which the authors associate with a carbon-footprint reduction of up to 92% relative to existing deep learning methods. This is a reported maximum from the evaluated comparisons. The practical contribution is a generation approach that can respond to changing scenario requirements without repeatedly rebuilding the model.
summary.tldr: GuidedDiffTime generates realistic constrained time series and supports new constraints without retraining.

title: On the Constrained Time-Series Generation Problem

abstract: Under Display Camera (UDC) is a novel imaging system that mounts a digital camera lens beneath a display panel with the panel covering the camera. However, the display panel causes severe degradation to captured images, such as low transmittance, blur, noise, and flare. The restoration of UDC-degraded images is challenging because of the unique luminance and diverse patterns of flares. Existing UDC dataset studies focus on unrealistic or synthetic UDC degradation rather than real-world UDC images. In this paper, we propose a real-world UDC dataset called UDC-SIT. To obtain the non-degraded and UDC-degraded images for the same scene, we propose an image-capturing system and an image alignment technique that exploits discrete Fourier transform (DFT) to align a pair of captured images. UDC-SIT also includes comprehensive annotations missing from other UDC datasets, such as light source, day/night, indoor/outdoor, and flare components (e.g., shimmers, streaks, and glares). We compare UDC-SIT with four existing representative UDC datasets and present the problems with existing UDC datasets. To show UDC-SIT's effectiveness, we compare UDC-SIT and a representative synthetic UDC dataset using four representative learnable image restoration models. The result indicates that the models trained with the synthetic UDC dataset are impractical because the synthetic UDC dataset does not reflect the actual characteristics of UDC-degraded images. UDC-SIT can enable further exploration in the UDC image restoration area and provide better insights into the problem. UDC-SIT is available at: https://github.com/mcrl/UDC-SIT.

paragraphs: Placing a camera behind a display introduces image degradation, including reduced light transmission, blur, noise, and flare. Restoration is especially difficult because flares vary in brightness and shape. This paper introduces UDC-SIT to address the gap between real under-display camera images and the unrealistic or synthetic degradation emphasized by existing datasets.

The authors develop a capture system for obtaining degraded and non-degraded views of the same scene. A discrete Fourier transform-based alignment method brings the paired captures into correspondence. The dataset also annotates light sources, day versus night, indoor versus outdoor settings, and flare components such as shimmers, streaks, and glares, providing detail for studying the degradation.

The paper compares UDC-SIT with four existing datasets and evaluates four learnable restoration models using UDC-SIT and a representative synthetic dataset. The results indicate that training on the synthetic dataset is impractical for the real degradation studied because its images miss actual camera characteristics. UDC-SIT supplies paired real-world evidence for developing restoration methods and examining these mismatches.
summary.tldr: UDC-SIT provides aligned real-world image pairs and detailed annotations for studying and restoring under-display camera degradation.

title: UDC-SIT: A Real-World Dataset for Under-Display Cameras

abstract: Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) predictive models hold the promise of improved compliance with given constraints, systematic generalization, and interpretability, as they allow to infer labels that are consistent with some prior knowledge by reasoning over high-level concepts extracted from sub-symbolic inputs. It was recently shown that NeSy predictors are affected by *reasoning shortcuts*: they can attain high accuracy but by leveraging concepts with \textit{unintended semantics}, thus coming short of their promised advantages. Yet, a systematic characterization of reasoning shortcuts and of potential mitigation strategies is missing. This work fills this gap by characterizing them as unintended optima of the learning objective and identifying four key conditions behind their occurrence. Based on this, we derive several natural mitigation strategies, and analyze their efficacy both theoretically and empirically. Our analysis shows reasoning shortcuts are difficult to deal with, casting doubts on the trustworthiness and interpretability of existing NeSy solutions.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic models combine concepts extracted from inputs with reasoning based on prior knowledge. This structure promises predictions that obey constraints and are easier to interpret. However, a model can obtain accurate labels while assigning unintended meanings to its internal concepts. The paper investigates these reasoning shortcuts and why they undermine the intended benefits of the architecture.

The authors characterize shortcuts as unintended optima of the learning objective. In other words, optimizing the training goal can reward concept representations whose meanings differ from what the designer intended. They identify four conditions behind the occurrence of these solutions and use that analysis to derive several mitigation strategies.

The proposed strategies are examined theoretically and empirically. The analysis finds that reasoning shortcuts remain difficult to handle, raising concerns about the trustworthiness and interpretability of existing neuro-symbolic systems. The key implication is that correct predictions and consistency with supplied knowledge do not by themselves establish that learned concepts have their intended semantics. Understanding the learning objective's alternative solutions is therefore central to assessing these models.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how neuro-symbolic models can learn unintended concept meanings and analyzes strategies for mitigating these reasoning shortcuts.

title: Not All Neuro-Symbolic Concepts Are Created Equal: Analysis and Mitigation of Reasoning Shortcuts

abstract: We present a novel alignment-before-generation approach to tackle the challenging task of generating general 3D shapes based on 2D images or texts. Directly learning a conditional generative model from images or texts to 3D shapes is prone to producing inconsistent results with the conditions because 3D shapes have an additional dimension whose distribution significantly differs from that of 2D images and texts. To bridge the domain gap among the three modalities and facilitate multi-modal-conditioned 3D shape generation, we explore representing 3D shapes in a shape-image-text-aligned space. Our framework comprises two models: a Shape-Image-Text-Aligned Variational Auto-Encoder (SITA-VAE) and a conditional Aligned Shape Latent Diffusion Model (ASLDM). The former model encodes the 3D shapes into the shape latent space aligned to the image and text and reconstructs the fine-grained 3D neural fields corresponding to given shape embeddings via the transformer-based decoder. The latter model learns a probabilistic mapping function from the image or text space to the latent shape space. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed approach can generate higher-quality and more diverse 3D shapes that better semantically conform to the visual or textural conditional inputs, validating the effectiveness of the shape-image-text-aligned space for cross-modality 3D shape generation.

paragraphs: Michelangelo generates 3D shapes from images or text by first aligning how those different kinds of information are represented. The motivation is that directly learning an image-to-shape or text-to-shape mapping can produce shapes that do not match the condition. The paper attributes this difficulty to the distributional gap between 3D shapes and the other modalities.

The framework has two components. A Shape-Image-Text-Aligned Variational Auto-Encoder places shapes in a latent space aligned with images and text. Its transformer decoder reconstructs detailed 3D neural fields from those shape embeddings. A conditional Aligned Shape Latent Diffusion Model then learns a probabilistic mapping from image or text representations into the aligned shape space.

This division makes alignment a foundation for generation: the generative model works with shape representations already connected to the conditioning modalities. The reported experiments produce higher-quality, more diverse shapes that better match the meaning of visual or textual inputs. These findings support the usefulness of the shared representation for cross-modal 3D generation, with the benefits demonstrated through the authors’ experimental comparisons.
summary.tldr: Michelangelo aligns shape, image, and text representations before diffusion-based generation to improve the quality and condition matching of 3D shapes.

title: Michelangelo: Conditional 3D Shape Generation based on Shape-Image-Text Aligned Latent Representation

abstract: We study matrix estimation problems arising in reinforcement learning with low-rank structure. In low-rank bandits, the matrix to be recovered specifies the expected arm rewards, and for low-rank Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), it characterizes the transition kernel of the MDP. In both cases, each entry of the matrix carries important information, and we seek estimation methods with low entry-wise prediction error. Importantly, these methods further need to accommodate for inherent correlations in the available data (e.g. for MDPs, the data consists of system trajectories). We investigate the performance of simple spectral-based matrix estimation approaches: we show that they efficiently recover the singular subspaces of the matrix and exhibit nearly-minimal entry-wise prediction error. These new results on low-rank matrix estimation make it possible to devise reinforcement learning algorithms that fully exploit the underlying low-rank structure. We provide two examples of such algorithms: a regret minimization algorithm for low-rank bandit problems, and a best policy identification algorithm for low-rank MDPs. Both algorithms yield state-of-the-art performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning problems contain a low-rank matrix describing expected rewards or transition probabilities. Recovering this matrix accurately can help learning, but every individual entry matters for decisions. The data can also be correlated, especially when collected as trajectories through a system. This paper studies matrix estimation with both requirements in view.

The authors analyze simple spectral methods and show that they efficiently recover the matrix's singular subspaces while achieving nearly minimal entry-wise prediction error. The emphasis on individual entries is consequential: a useful estimate must preserve the specific rewards or transitions represented by those entries. The analysis accommodates correlations inherent in the observations rather than relying solely on an independent-data viewpoint.

These estimation results support two reinforcement learning algorithms that exploit the low-rank structure. One minimizes regret in low-rank bandit problems; the other identifies the best policy in low-rank Markov decision processes. Both receive state-of-the-art performance guarantees. The paper therefore connects a matrix-estimation result to decision-making guarantees, showing how accurate recovery of structured information can support effective learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: Spectral matrix estimation achieves strong entry-wise guarantees with correlated data and enables theoretically strong algorithms for low-rank bandits and MDPs.

title: Spectral Entry-wise Matrix Estimation for Low-Rank Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large language models are commonly trained on a mixture of filtered web data and curated ``high-quality'' corpora, such as social media conversations, books, or technical papers. This curation process is believed to be necessary to produce performant models with broad zero-shot generalization abilities. However, as larger models requiring pretraining on trillions of tokens are considered, it is unclear how scalable is curation, and whether we will run out of unique high-quality data soon. At variance with previous beliefs, we show that properly filtered and deduplicated web data alone can lead to powerful models; even significantly outperforming models trained on The Pile. Despite extensive filtering, the high-quality data we extract from the web is still plentiful, and we are able to obtain five trillion tokens from CommonCrawl. We publicly release an extract of 500 billion tokens from our RefinedWeb dataset, and 1.3/7.5B parameters language models trained on it.

paragraphs: Language-model training commonly mixes filtered web pages with curated sources such as books, conversations, and technical papers. Such curation has been viewed as necessary for strong performance and broad zero-shot generalization. This paper questions that assumption as training requirements grow to trillions of tokens and curated data become harder to scale.

The authors show that web data alone can support powerful models when it is carefully filtered and deduplicated. In their comparisons, models trained this way significantly outperform models trained on The Pile. The claim depends on the quality of the processing: the contribution centers on making a large web collection suitable for training.

Even after extensive filtering, the authors obtain five trillion tokens from CommonCrawl. They release a 500-billion-token portion of RefinedWeb and language models with 1.3 billion and 7.5 billion parameters trained on it. The findings indicate that well-processed web data can provide both substantial scale and strong model performance, challenging the presumed necessity of adding curated corpora.
summary.tldr: RefinedWeb shows that carefully filtered and deduplicated web data alone can train strong language models while remaining available at trillion-token scale.

title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM: Outperforming Curated Corpora with Web Data Only

abstract: Hierarchical clustering has usually been addressed by discrete optimization using heuristics or continuous optimization of relaxed scores for hierarchies. In this work, we propose to optimize expected scores under a probabilistic model over hierarchies. (1) We show theoretically that the global optimal values of the expected Dasgupta cost and Tree-Sampling divergence (TSD), two unsupervised metrics for hierarchical clustering, are equal to the optimal values of their discrete counterparts contrary to some relaxed scores. (2) We propose Expected Probabilistic Hierarchies (EPH), a probabilistic model to learn hierarchies in data by optimizing expected scores. EPH uses differentiable hierarchy sampling enabling end-to-end gradient descent based optimization, and an unbiased subgraph sampling approach to scale to large datasets. (3) We evaluate EPH on synthetic and real-world datasets including vector and graph datasets. EPH outperforms all other approaches quantitatively and provides meaningful hierarchies in qualitative evaluations.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into nested groups, making the quality of an entire hierarchy the object of optimization. This paper proposes learning a probability distribution over hierarchies and optimizing the expected score under that distribution. The approach provides a probabilistic way to search for good hierarchical structures using gradient-based learning.

A key theoretical result concerns two objectives: Dasgupta cost and Tree-Sampling divergence. The authors prove that their expected formulations have the same globally optimal values as the corresponding discrete objectives. This preserves the optimum value for these scores, unlike some relaxed formulations. The result concerns the objectives' global optima; it does not itself establish that a training run reaches them.

The proposed Expected Probabilistic Hierarchies model uses differentiable hierarchy sampling for end-to-end optimization. An unbiased subgraph-sampling method enables scaling to large datasets. Evaluations include synthetic and real-world data in both vector and graph forms. EPH outperforms the compared approaches quantitatively, while qualitative assessments find meaningful hierarchical organization.
summary.tldr: EPH learns distributions over hierarchies using expected objectives that preserve the discrete global optimum values for two clustering scores.

title: Expected Probabilistic Hierarchies

abstract: Brain stimulation has the potential to create desired neural population activity states. However, it is challenging to search the large space of stimulation parameters, for example, selecting which subset of electrodes to be used for stimulation. In this scenario, creating a model that maps the configuration of stimulation parameters to the brain’s response can be beneficial. Training such an expansive model usually requires more stimulation-response samples than can be collected in a given experimental session. Furthermore, changes in the properties of the recorded activity over time can make it challenging to merge stimulation-response samples across sessions. To address these challenges, we propose MiSO (MicroStimulation Optimization), a closed-loop stimulation framework to drive neural population activity toward specified states by optimizing over a large stimulation parameter space. MiSO consists of three key components: 1) a neural activity alignment method to merge stimulation-response samples across sessions, 2) a statistical model trained on the merged samples to predict the brain's response to untested stimulation parameter configurations, and 3) an online optimization algorithm to adaptively update the stimulation parameter configuration based on the model's predictions. In this study, we implemented MiSO with a factor analysis (FA) based alignment method, a convolutional neural network (CNN), and an epsilon greedy optimization algorithm. We tested MiSO in closed-loop experiments using electrical microstimulation in the prefrontal cortex of a non-human primate. Guided by the CNN predictions, MiSO successfully searched amongst thousands of stimulation parameter configurations to drive the neural population activity toward specified states. More broadly, MiSO increases the clinical viability of neuromodulation technologies by enabling the use of many-fold larger stimulation parameter spaces.

paragraphs: Choosing brain-stimulation settings becomes difficult when many electrode combinations and other parameters are available. A predictive model could guide the search, but one experimental session may provide too few examples. Combining sessions introduces another challenge because recorded neural activity changes over time.

MiSO addresses both problems through a closed-loop framework. It first aligns neural activity across sessions so their stimulation-response samples can be combined. A statistical model learns from those samples to predict responses to untested configurations. An online optimizer then uses those predictions to adaptively choose stimulation settings. The implementation uses factor analysis for alignment, a convolutional neural network for prediction, and epsilon-greedy optimization.

The authors test MiSO with electrical microstimulation in the prefrontal cortex of a non-human primate. Guided by model predictions, it successfully searches thousands of parameter configurations and moves neural population activity toward specified states. This demonstrates how combining data across sessions with adaptive search can make larger stimulation spaces usable, supporting the framework's proposed relevance to neuromodulation.
summary.tldr: MiSO combines cross-session neural alignment, response prediction, and adaptive search to steer neural activity through brain stimulation.

title: MiSO: Optimizing brain stimulation to create neural population activity states

abstract: In this paper, we focus on simple bilevel optimization problems, where we minimize a convex smooth objective function over the optimal solution set of another convex smooth constrained optimization problem. We present a novel bilevel optimization method that locally approximates the solution set of the lower-level problem using a cutting plane approach and employs an accelerated gradient-based update to reduce the upper-level objective function over the approximated solution set. We measure the performance of our method in terms of suboptimality and infeasibility errors and provide non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for both error criteria. Specifically, when the feasible set is compact, we show that our method requires at most $\mathcal{O}(\max\\{1/\sqrt{\epsilon_{f}}, 1/\epsilon_g\\})$ iterations to find a solution that is $\epsilon_f$-suboptimal and $\epsilon_g$-infeasible. Moreover, under the additional assumption that the lower-level objective satisfies the $r$-th Hölderian error bound, we show that our method achieves an iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\max\\{\epsilon_{f}^{-\frac{2r-1}{2r}},\epsilon_{g}^{-\frac{2r-1}{2r}}\\})$, which matches the optimal complexity of single-level convex constrained optimization when $r=1$.
