paragraphs: Training large neural networks consumes substantial memory, including memory for intermediate activations. Activation compression reduces that footprint, but compression also affects the gradients used for learning. GACT is a framework intended to make this approach applicable across network architectures without requiring detailed knowledge of their individual operators or architectural structure.

The authors analyze a linearized version of the approximate gradient produced by activation-compressed training and establish a convergence result. To support stable training in practice, GACT estimates at runtime how compressing each tensor affects the gradient. It uses those estimates to select tensor-specific compression ratios, making the compression decision responsive to its training impact.

Implemented as a PyTorch library, GACT is evaluated on convolutional networks, transformers, and graph neural networks. The reported results include activation-memory reductions of up to 8.1 times and batch sizes 4.2 to 24.7 times larger, with negligible accuracy loss. These results show how reducing activation storage can expand feasible training batch sizes across several architecture families.
summary.tldr: GACT adapts activation compression to each tensor's gradient impact, reducing training memory across multiple neural-network architectures.

title: GACT: Activation Compressed Training for Generic Network Architectures

abstract: When training neural networks with simulated quantization, we observe that quantized weights can, rather unexpectedly, oscillate between two grid-points. The importance of this effect and its impact on quantization-aware training (QAT) are not well-understood or investigated in literature. In this paper, we delve deeper into the phenomenon of weight oscillations and show that it can lead to a significant accuracy degradation due to wrongly estimated batch-normalization statistics during inference and increased noise during training. These effects are particularly pronounced in low-bit ($\leq$ 4-bits) quantization of efficient networks with depth-wise separable layers, such as MobileNets and EfficientNets. In our analysis we investigate several previously proposed QAT algorithms and show that most of these are unable to overcome oscillations. Finally, we propose two novel QAT algorithms to overcome oscillations during training: oscillation dampening and iterative weight freezing. We demonstrate that our algorithms achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for low-bit (3 & 4 bits) weight and activation quantization of efficient architectures, such as MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, and EfficentNet-lite on ImageNet. Our source code is available at https://github.com/qualcomm-ai-research/oscillations-qat.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training simulates the restricted numerical precision a network will use. This paper examines a failure mode in which quantized weights repeatedly switch between two available values. The authors show that these oscillations can significantly reduce accuracy, making their behavior an important part of understanding low-precision training.

The analysis identifies two consequences: increased noise during training and incorrectly estimated batch-normalization statistics used at inference. The effects are especially pronounced at four bits or fewer in efficient networks with depth-wise separable layers, including MobileNets and EfficientNets. Examining several existing quantization-aware training algorithms, the authors find that most do not overcome the oscillations.

The proposed remedies are oscillation dampening and iterative weight freezing, two training algorithms designed to address the switching behavior. On ImageNet, they achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for three- and four-bit weight and activation quantization in architectures including MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, and EfficientNet-lite. The work connects a specific training instability to deployment accuracy and shows that directly addressing it improves the reported low-bit results.
summary.tldr: Two methods that address oscillating quantized weights improve low-bit network accuracy by targeting a harmful training instability.

title: Overcoming Oscillations in Quantization-Aware Training

abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning offers an appealing formalism for describing control problems in which the passage of time is not naturally divided into discrete increments. Here we consider the problem of predicting the distribution of returns obtained by an agent interacting in a continuous-time, stochastic environment. Accurate return predictions have proven useful for determining optimal policies for risk-sensitive control, learning state representations, multiagent coordination, and more. We begin by establishing the distributional analogue of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for Ito diffusions and the broader class of Feller-Dynkin processes. We then specialize this equation to the setting in which the return distribution is approximated by N uniformly-weighted particles, a common design choice in distributional algorithms. Our derivation highlights additional terms due to statistical diffusivity which arise from the proper handling of distributions in the continuous-time setting. Based on this, we propose a tractable algorithm for approximately solving the distributional HJB based on a JKO scheme, which can be implemented in an online, control algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of such an algorithm in a synthetic control problem.

paragraphs: Some control problems evolve continuously rather than in naturally separated steps. This paper studies how to predict the distribution of returns an agent obtains in such stochastic environments. Predicting a distribution describes the range of possible returns, which can support applications such as risk-sensitive control, representation learning, and coordination between agents.

They then examine the common approximation that represents a return distribution using N equally weighted particles. The solver can be incorporated into an online control algorithm, connecting the mathematical formulation to a usable learning procedure. A synthetic control problem demonstrates its effectiveness, providing an example of how the distributional continuous-time equations can guide algorithm design.
summary.tldr: The paper derives continuous-time equations for return distributions and uses them to build an approximate online control algorithm.

title: Distributional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations for Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study a new connection between a technical measure called $\mu$-conductance that arises in the study of Markov chains for sampling convex bodies and the network community profile that characterizes size-resolved properties of clusters and communities in social and information networks. The idea of $\mu$-conductance is similar to the traditional graph conductance, but disregards sets with small volume. We derive a sequence of optimization problems including a low-rank semi-definite program from which we can derive a lower bound on the optimal $\mu$-conductance value. These ideas give the first theoretically sound bound on the behavior of the network community profile for a wide range of cluster sizes. The algorithm scales up to graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes and we demonstrate how our framework validates the predicted structures of real-world graphs.

paragraphs: A network community profile describes how the quality of clusters changes with their size. This paper connects that profile to μ-conductance, a measure originating in work on Markov chains for sampling convex bodies. Like ordinary graph conductance, it concerns how well groups are separated, but it excludes sets with small volume.

The authors derive a sequence of optimization problems, including a low-rank semidefinite program, that produces a lower bound on the optimal μ-conductance value. This supplies a mathematical bound on community structure across a range of sizes. It complements searching for good clusters by establishing limits on how good the relevant optimum can be.

The paper presents these as the first theoretically sound bounds on network community profile behavior over a wide range of cluster sizes. Its algorithm scales to graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes. Demonstrations on real-world graphs show how the framework can validate predicted structures. The contribution therefore joins a theoretical connection between two measures with a computational method large enough to examine substantial networks.
summary.tldr: Low-rank semidefinite optimization provides theoretical bounds on community quality across cluster sizes in large networks.

title: Theoretical Bounds on the Network Community Profile from Low-rank Semi-definite Programming

abstract: Long-tailed learning is one of the most challenging problems in visual recognition. There are some studies aiming to solve long-tailed classification from the perspective of feature learning. Recent work proposes to learn the balanced representation by fixing the linear classifier as Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF), since they argue what matters in classification is the structure of the feature, instead of their directions. Holding a different view, in this paper, we show that features with fixed directions may be harmful to the generalization of models, even if it is completely symmetric. To avoid this issue, we propose Representation-Balanced Learning Framework (RBL), which introduces orthogonal matrices to learn directions while maintaining the geometric structure of ETF. Theoretically, our contributions are two-fold: 1). we point out that the feature learning of RBL is insensitive toward training set label distribution, it always learns a balanced representation space. 2). we provide a generalization analysis of proposed RBL through training stability. To analyze the stability of the parameter with orthogonal constraint, we propose a novel training stability analysis paradigm, Two-Parameter Model Stability. Practically, our method is extremely simple in implementation but shows great superiority on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Long-tailed classification involves uneven representation of classes in training data. One proposed response fixes the classifier to an Equiangular Tight Frame, a symmetric geometric arrangement intended to encourage balanced features. This paper argues that symmetry alone does not settle the problem: fixing feature directions may harm generalization even when their arrangement is completely symmetric.

The proposed Representation-Balanced Learning framework introduces orthogonal matrices that let the directions change while preserving the frame's geometry. This separates two design choices that fixed classifiers tie together: the relative structure of the representation and its orientation. The model can therefore learn directions without abandoning the intended balanced arrangement.

The authors theoretically show that RBL's feature learning is insensitive to the training label distribution and learns a balanced representation space. They also analyze generalization through training stability, introducing Two-Parameter Model Stability to handle orthogonally constrained parameters. Experiments report strong performance on several benchmarks with a simple implementation. The central finding is that learning orientation can matter alongside maintaining a balanced geometry.
summary.tldr: RBL learns feature directions while preserving symmetric geometry, addressing potential generalization harm from fixed directions in long-tailed classification.

title: Feature Directions Matter: Long-Tailed Learning via Rotated Balanced Representation

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models for different tasks can be costly and inefficient, and even methods that reduce the number of tuned parameters still require full gradient-based optimization. We propose HyperTuning, a novel approach to model adaptation that uses a hypermodel to generate task-specific parameters for a fixed downstream model. We demonstrate a simple setup for hypertuning with HyperT5, a T5-based hypermodel that produces soft prefixes or LoRA parameters for a frozen T5 model from few-shot examples. We train HyperT5 in two stages: first, hyperpretraining with a modified conditional language modeling objective that trains a hypermodel to generate parameters; second, multi-task fine-tuning (MTF) on a large number of diverse language tasks. We evaluate HyperT5 on P3, MetaICL and Super-NaturalInstructions datasets, and show that it can effectively generate parameters for unseen tasks. Moreover, we show that using hypermodel-generated parameters as initializations for further parameter-efficient fine-tuning improves performance. HyperTuning can thus be a flexible and efficient way to leverage large language models for diverse downstream applications.

We evaluate HyperT5 on P3, MetaICL and Super-NaturalInstructions datasets, and show that it can effectively generate parameters for unseen tasks. HyperTuning can thus be a flexible and efficient way to leverage large language models for diverse downstream applications.

paragraphs: Adapting a large language model can remain costly even when only a small subset of parameters is tuned, because adaptation still requires gradient-based optimization. HyperTuning instead uses a separate hypermodel to generate task-specific parameters for a fixed downstream model. A few examples provide the task information used to produce those parameters.

The paper implements this idea with HyperT5, a T5-based hypermodel that generates soft prefixes or LoRA parameters for a frozen T5 model. HyperT5 itself undergoes two training stages: an objective that teaches it to generate parameters, followed by multi-task fine-tuning across diverse language tasks. The parameter-generation route therefore relies on a previously trained hypermodel.

Evaluations on P3, MetaICL, and Super-NaturalInstructions show that HyperT5 can generate effective parameters for unseen tasks. The generated parameters also improve performance when used to initialize further parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This gives the approach two demonstrated uses: direct task adaptation through generated parameters, and a starting point for additional optimization when further fine-tuning is desired.
summary.tldr: HyperTuning generates task-specific adaptation parameters from few-shot examples and can also improve initialization for further fine-tuning.

title: HyperTuning: Toward Adapting Large Language Models without Back-propagation

abstract: It is quite challenging to ensure the safety of reinforcement learning (RL) agents in an unknown and stochastic environment under hard constraints that require the system state not to reach certain specified unsafe regions. Many popular safe RL methods such as those based on the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) paradigm formulate safety violations in a cost function and try to constrain the expectation of cumulative cost under a threshold. However, it is often difficult to effectively capture and enforce hard reachability-based safety constraints indirectly with such constraints on safety violation cost. In this work, we leverage the notion of barrier function to explicitly encode the hard safety chance constraints, and given that the environment is unknown, relax them to our design of generative-model-based soft barrier functions . Based on such soft barriers, we propose a novel safe RL approach with bi-level optimization that can jointly learn the unknown environment and optimize the control policy, while effectively avoiding the unsafe region with safety probability optimization. Experiments on a set of examples demonstrate that our approach can effectively enforce hard safety chance constraints and significantly outperform CMDP-based baseline methods in system safe rates measured via simulations.

However, it is often difficult to effectively capture and enforce hard reachability-based safety constraints indirectly with such constraints on safety violation cost. In this work, we leverage the notion of barrier function to explicitly encode the hard safety chance constraints, and given that the environment is unknown, relax them to our design of generative-model-based soft barrier functions . Based on such soft barriers, we propose a novel safe RL approach with bi-level optimization that can jointly learn the unknown environment and optimize the control policy, while effectively avoiding the unsafe region with safety probability optimization. Experiments on a set of examples demonstrate that our approach can effectively enforce hard safety chance constraints and significantly outperform CMDP-based baseline methods in system safe rates measured via simulations.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning tasks require keeping the system out of specified unsafe regions. In an unknown, stochastic environment, this is difficult to enforce through a bound on expected cumulative violation costs. That cost-based formulation can be an indirect way of expressing the actual concern: the chance that the system reaches an unsafe state.

The paper uses barrier functions to encode safety chance constraints explicitly. Because the environment is unknown, it relaxes these functions into soft barriers based on a generative model. A bi-level optimization procedure then learns the environment and optimizes the control policy together, using safety probability as part of the optimization.

Experiments on a set of examples show effective enforcement of the safety chance constraints and substantially higher simulated safe rates than the compared constrained Markov decision process methods. These findings concern probabilistic safety in the evaluated stochastic settings. The approach matters because its learning objective is connected more directly to avoiding unsafe regions, rather than relying solely on accumulated violation costs.
summary.tldr: Soft barrier functions support joint environment and policy learning to enforce safety chance constraints, improving simulated safe rates over the evaluated CMDP methods.

title: Enforcing Hard Constraints with Soft Barriers: Safe Reinforcement Learning in Unknown Stochastic Environments

abstract: We propose to minimize a generic differentiable objective with $L_1$ constraint using a simple reparametrization and straightforward stochastic gradient descent. Our proposal is the direct generalization of previous ideas that the $L_1$ penalty may be equivalent to a differentiable reparametrization with weight decay. We prove that the proposed method, spred, is an exact differentiable solver of $L_1$ and that the reparametrization trick is completely “benign" for a generic nonconvex function. Practically, we demonstrate the usefulness of the method in (1) training sparse neural networks to perform gene selection tasks, which involves finding relevant features in a very high dimensional space, and (2) neural network compression task, to which previous attempts at applying the $L_1$-penalty have been unsuccessful. Conceptually, our result bridges the gap between the sparsity in deep learning and conventional statistical learning.

paragraphs: An L1 penalty encourages sparse solutions, making it useful when a model should retain only a small set of features or parameters. This paper presents spred, a way to handle an L1 constraint on a generic differentiable objective using a simple change of parameters and ordinary stochastic gradient descent. It extends earlier connections between L1 penalties and differentiable formulations with weight decay.

The theoretical contribution is an exact differentiable formulation of the L1 problem. The authors also prove that the reparameterization is benign for a generic nonconvex function. These results support using the transformed optimization problem as a principled route to the original sparsity objective, rather than merely as a heuristic that happens to produce small parameters.

Gene selection requires finding relevant features in a very high-dimensional space, while compression seeks a smaller network representation. The reported usefulness in both tasks connects sparsity methods from conventional statistical learning with neural network training through a familiar optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Spred reformulates L1 optimization as a differentiable problem that can be trained with standard stochastic gradient descent.

title: spred: Solving L1 Penalty with SGD

abstract: Neural Network-based active learning (NAL) is a cost-effective data selection technique that utilizes neural networks to select and train on a small subset of samples. While existing work successfully develops various effective or theory-justified NAL algorithms, the understanding of the two commonly used query criteria of NAL: uncertainty-based and diversity-based, remains in its infancy. In this work, we try to move one step forward by offering a unified explanation for the success of both query criteria-based NAL from a feature learning view. Specifically, we consider a feature-noise data model comprising easy-to-learn or hard-to-learn features disrupted by noise, and conduct analysis over 2-layer NN-based NALs in the pool-based scenario. We provably show that both uncertainty-based and diversity-based NAL are inherently amenable to one and the same principle, i.e., striving to prioritize samples that contain yet-to-be-learned features. We further prove that this shared principle is the key to their success-achieve small test error within a small labeled set. Contrastingly, the strategy-free passive learning exhibits a large test error due to the inadequate learning of yet-to-be-learned features, necessitating resort to a significantly larger label complexity for a sufficient test error reduction. Experimental results validate our findings.

paragraphs: Neural active learning chooses which examples to label so that a model can learn from a small labelled subset. Two common strategies prioritize uncertain examples or diverse examples. This paper offers a shared explanation for their success by studying which features the neural network has learned and which remain missing from its representation.

The analysis uses a feature-noise data model containing features that differ in learning difficulty, together with two-layer neural networks selecting examples from a pool. Within this setting, both query strategies tend to prioritize samples containing features that have not yet been learned. This gives a common feature-learning interpretation to selection criteria that initially look different.

The authors prove that this shared behavior enables small test error with a small labelled set. Passive selection, by comparison, inadequately learns the remaining features in the analyzed setting and needs substantially more labels to reduce error sufficiently. Experiments support these findings. The theoretical explanation is grounded in the specified data and network model, rather than claiming that either strategy succeeds under all conditions.
summary.tldr: Under a feature-noise model, uncertainty and diversity sampling both succeed by selecting examples containing features the network has yet to learn.

title: Provably Neural Active Learning Succeeds via Prioritizing Perplexing Samples

abstract: We study constrained comonotone min-max optimization, a structured class of nonconvex-nonconcave min-max optimization problems, and their generalization to comonotone inclusion. In our first contribution, we extend the Extra Anchored Gradient (EAG) algorithm, originally proposed by Yoon and Ryu (2021) for unconstrained min-max optimization, to constrained comonotone min-max optimization and comonotone inclusion, achieving an optimal convergence rate of $O\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$ among all first-order methods. Additionally, we prove that the algorithm’s iterations converge to a point in the solution set. In our second contribution, we extend the Fast Extra Gradient (FEG) algorithm, as developed by Lee and Kim (2021), to constrained comonotone min-max optimization and comonotone inclusion, achieving the same $O\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$ convergence rate. This rate is applicable to the broadest set of comonotone inclusion problems yet studied in the literature. Our analyses are based on simple potential function arguments, which might be useful for analyzing other accelerated algorithms.

paragraphs: Min-max optimization involves competing objectives: one side seeks to minimize a quantity while the other seeks to maximize it. This paper studies problems that also impose constraints and lack the usual convexity and concavity properties. Its guarantees apply to a structured class called comonotone problems, including a more general mathematical formulation called comonotone inclusion.

The first contribution extends Extra Anchored Gradient to this constrained setting. The authors establish a convergence rate of O(1/T), where T is the number of iterations, and show that this rate is optimal among first-order methods for the studied class. They also prove that the iterates themselves converge to a solution, a separate guarantee from a decreasing error measure.

The second contribution extends Fast Extra Gradient and establishes the same rate over what the abstract describes as the broadest comonotone inclusion class studied so far. Both analyses use potential functions to track progress. These arguments may also help analyze other accelerated algorithms, while the stated guarantees remain tied to the comonotone structure.
summary.tldr: The paper extends two accelerated algorithms to constrained comonotone problems, proving optimal O(1/T) convergence rates.

title: Accelerated Algorithms for Constrained Nonconvex-Nonconcave Min-Max Optimization and Comonotone Inclusion

abstract: Generative models, like large language models, are becoming increasingly relevant in our daily lives, yet a theoretical framework to assess their generalization behavior and uncertainty does not exist. Particularly, the problem of uncertainty estimation is commonly solved in an ad-hoc and task-dependent manner. For example, natural language approaches cannot be transferred to image generation. In this paper, we introduce the first bias-variance-covariance decomposition for kernel scores. This decomposition represents a theoretical framework from which we derive a kernel-based variance and entropy for uncertainty estimation. We propose unbiased and consistent estimators for each quantity which only require generated samples but not the underlying model itself. Based on the wide applicability of kernels, we demonstrate our framework via generalization and uncertainty experiments for image, audio, and language generation. Specifically, kernel entropy for uncertainty estimation is more predictive of performance on CoQA and TriviaQA question answering datasets than existing baselines and can also be applied to closed-source models.

paragraphs: Uncertainty measures for generative models are often designed around a particular task or output type. A technique for language generation may therefore offer little help with images. This paper develops a shared mathematical framework based on kernel scores, which assess outputs through a chosen notion of similarity.

The central contribution separates these scores into bias, variance, and covariance components. From this decomposition, the authors derive kernel-based measures of variance and entropy for estimating uncertainty. They also propose unbiased and consistent estimators that use generated samples without requiring access to the model's internal workings.

The authors demonstrate the framework through generalization and uncertainty experiments involving images, audio, and language. On the CoQA and TriviaQA question-answering datasets, kernel entropy predicts performance better than the evaluated baselines. Because the estimators operate on samples, the approach can also be applied to closed-source models. The contribution connects a theoretical account of generative-model behavior with uncertainty measurements that work across several output domains.
summary.tldr: A kernel-score decomposition yields sample-based uncertainty measures that apply across generative domains and can assess closed-source models.

title: A Bias-Variance-Covariance Decomposition of Kernel Scores for Generative Models

abstract: In recent years, there has been a surge in the development of 3D structure-based pre-trained protein models, representing a significant advancement over pre-trained protein language models in various downstream tasks. However, most existing structure-based pre-trained models primarily focus on the residue level, i.e., alpha carbon atoms, while ignoring other atoms like side chain atoms. We argue that modeling proteins at both residue and atom levels is important since the side chain atoms can also be crucial for numerous downstream tasks, for example, molecular docking. Nevertheless, we find that naively combining residue and atom information during pre-training typically fails. We identify a key reason is the information leakage caused by the inclusion of atom structure in the input, which renders residue-level pre-training tasks trivial and results in insufficiently expressive residue representations. To address this issue, we introduce a span mask pre-training strategy on 3D protein chains to learn meaningful representations of both residues and atoms. This leads to a simple yet effective approach to learning protein representation suitable for diverse downstream tasks. Extensive experimental results on binding site prediction and function prediction tasks demonstrate our proposed pre-training approach significantly outperforms other methods. Our code will be made public.

paragraphs: Many protein models based on three-dimensional structure emphasize residues, often represented through alpha carbon atoms. This leaves out other atomic details, including side chains, that can matter for downstream tasks such as molecular docking. The paper investigates how to learn useful representations at both residue and atom levels.

Simply combining these levels can fail during pre-training. The authors identify information leakage as a key reason: atomic structure in the input can reveal enough information to make residue-level training tasks trivial. A model can therefore complete the training task without developing sufficiently expressive residue representations.

The proposed solution masks spans along three-dimensional protein chains during pre-training. This strategy is intended to prevent the shortcut while supporting meaningful learning at both levels of detail. Experiments on binding-site prediction and function prediction show significant improvements over other methods. The findings emphasize that adding structural detail is not sufficient by itself; the training task must make both residue and atom representations informative.
summary.tldr: Span masking addresses information leakage in protein pre-training, enabling useful residue- and atom-level representations with improved prediction results.

title: Pre-Training Protein Bi-level Representation Through Span Mask Strategy On 3D Protein Chains

abstract: Time series analysis is essential for comprehending the complexities inherent in various real-world systems and applications. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently made significant strides, the development of artificial general intelligence (AGI) equipped with time series analysis capabilities remains in its nascent phase. Most existing time series models heavily rely on domain knowledge and extensive model tuning, predominantly focusing on prediction tasks. In this paper, we argue that current LLMs have the potential to revolutionize time series analysis, thereby promoting efficient decision-making and advancing towards a more universal form of time series analytical intelligence. Such advancement could unlock a wide range of possibilities, including time series modality switching and question answering. We encourage researchers and practitioners to recognize the potential of LLMs in advancing time series analysis and emphasize the need for trust in these related efforts. Furthermore, we detail the seamless integration of time series analysis with existing LLM technologies and outline promising avenues for future research.

paragraphs: Time series analysis helps people understand systems through measurements that change over time. The authors argue that much current modeling depends heavily on domain expertise and extensive tuning, with prediction receiving most of the attention. They propose a broader research direction centered on the potential capabilities of large language models.

This position paper presents language models as a possible foundation for more general time series analysis. The envisioned capabilities include question answering and switching between time series and other modalities. Such capabilities could expand the role of a model beyond producing forecasts toward supporting interpretation and decision-making across a wider range of tasks.

The paper discusses integration with existing language-model technologies and identifies promising research directions. Its claims concern potential and an agenda for future work: general time series analytical intelligence remains at an early stage. The authors encourage researchers and practitioners to engage with these efforts and build trust in them. The contribution is a perspective on what the field could pursue, rather than a reported demonstration that this broader intelligence has been achieved.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that language models could broaden time series analysis beyond forecasting toward question answering and more general analytical capabilities.

title: Position: What Can Large Language Models Tell Us about Time Series Analysis

abstract: Common methods for aligning large language models (LLMs) with desired behaviour heavily rely on human-labelled data. However, as models grow increasingly sophisticated, they will surpass human expertise, and the role of human evaluation will evolve into non-experts overseeing experts. In anticipation of this, we ask: can weaker models assess the correctness of stronger models? We investigate this question in an analogous setting, where stronger models (experts) possess the necessary information to answer questions and weaker models (non-experts) lack this information. The method we evaluate is debate, where two LLM experts each argue for a different answer, and a non-expert selects the answer. We find that debate consistently helps both non-expert models and humans answer questions, achieving 76% and 88% accuracy respectively (naive baselines obtain 48% and 60%). Furthermore, optimising expert debaters for persuasiveness in an unsupervised manner improves non-expert ability to identify the truth in debates. Our results provide encouraging empirical evidence for the viability of aligning models with debate in the absence of ground truth.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI system becomes difficult when the system knows more than its evaluator. This paper studies an analogous situation: stronger language models receive information needed to answer a question, while weaker evaluators lack that information. It asks whether a structured exchange between informed models can help the less-informed evaluator identify the correct answer.

The tested protocol is debate. Two expert models argue for different answers, and a non-expert chooses between them. Debate improves accuracy for both model and human evaluators in the experiments. Non-expert models reach 76% accuracy compared with 48% for naive baselines; humans reach 88% compared with 60%. These results show that the arguments can make useful information accessible to the evaluator.

The authors also optimize the expert debaters for persuasiveness without supervised training, finding that this further improves evaluators’ ability to identify the truth. The result is encouraging empirical evidence for debate as an alignment method when ground truth is unavailable. Its force comes from the tested information-asymmetry setting, rather than a universal guarantee about persuasive arguments.
summary.tldr: In an information-asymmetry experiment, debate helps weaker evaluators find correct answers, and training more persuasive debaters improves that ability.

title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers

abstract: Invariant risk minimization (IRM) is an arising approach to generalize invariant features to different environments in machine learning. While most related works focus on new IRM settings or new application scenarios, the mathematical essence of IRM remains to be properly explained. We verify that IRM is essentially a total variation based on $L^2$ norm (TV-$\ell_2$) of the learning risk with respect to the classifier variable. Moreover, we propose a novel IRM framework based on the TV-$\ell_1$ model. It not only expands the classes of functions that can be used as the learning risk and the feature extractor, but also has robust performance in denoising and invariant feature preservation based on the coarea formula. We also illustrate some requirements for IRM-TV-$\ell_1$ to achieve out-of-distribution generalization. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance in several benchmark machine learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn features that remain useful across environments. This paper examines the mathematical structure behind that goal. The authors show that IRM can be understood through an L2-based total variation formulation of how learning risk changes with the classifier variable.

That interpretation motivates a new framework based on L1 total variation. The change expands the function classes available for both the learning risk and the feature extractor. Using the coarea formula, the authors also connect the framework to robust denoising and preservation of invariant features, giving the proposed formulation a mathematical rationale.

The paper discusses requirements for this L1-based version to generalize outside the training distribution. Its formulation alone therefore does not imply unrestricted out-of-distribution success. Experiments show competitive results on several benchmark learning scenarios. The contribution combines an explanation of existing IRM with an alternative formulation that broadens modeling choices and connects invariant learning to tools for controlling variation.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets IRM through total variation and develops an L1-based alternative with broader function classes and competitive benchmark performance.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Is A Total Variation Model

abstract: Deep learning has contributed remarkably to the advancement of time series analysis. Still, deep models can encounter performance bottlenecks in real-world data-scarce scenarios, which can be concealed due to the performance saturation with small models on current benchmarks. Meanwhile, large models have demonstrated great powers in these scenarios through large-scale pre-training. Continuous progress has been achieved with the emergence of large language models, exhibiting unprecedented abilities such as few-shot generalization, scalability, and task generality, which are however absent in small deep models. To change the status quo of training scenario-specific small models from scratch, this paper aims at the early development of large time series models (LTSM). During pre-training, we curate large-scale datasets with up to 1 billion time points, unify heterogeneous time series into single-series sequence (S3) format, and develop the GPT-style architecture toward LTSMs. To meet diverse application needs, we convert forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection of time series into a unified generative task. The outcome of this study is a Time Series Transformer (Timer), which is generative pre-trained by next token prediction and adapted to various downstream tasks with promising capabilities as an LTSM. Code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/thuml/Large-Time-Series-Model.

paragraphs: Timer explores large pretrained models for time-series analysis, motivated by difficulties that smaller models encounter when task-specific data is scarce. The authors argue that saturated benchmarks can hide these difficulties. Their aim is to move beyond training a separate small model from scratch for each scenario toward a model that can be adapted across tasks.

The study curates pretraining datasets containing up to one billion time points and converts heterogeneous series into a common single-series sequence format. It then develops a GPT-style transformer trained through next-token prediction. Forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection are reformulated as generative tasks so that the same modeling approach can address these different application needs.

The resulting Time Series Transformer, Timer, is adapted to downstream tasks and shows promising capabilities as a large time-series model. The contribution is presented as an early development of this direction. It brings together data preparation, a shared sequence format, generative pretraining, and task reformulation to explore how one pretrained architecture can support several kinds of time-series analysis.
summary.tldr: Timer uses large-scale generative pretraining and a unified sequence format to support forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection.

title: Timer: Generative Pre-trained Transformers Are Large Time Series Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become pivotal in advancing the field of artificial intelligence, yet their immense sizes pose significant challenges for both fine-tuning and deployment. Current post-training pruning methods, while reducing the sizes of LLMs, often fail to maintain their original performance. To address these challenges, this paper introduces SPP, a Sparsity-Preserved Parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. Different from existing post-training pruning approaches that struggle with performance retention, SPP proposes to employ lightweight learnable column and row matrices to optimize sparse LLM weights, keeping the structure and sparsity of pruned pre-trained models intact. By element-wise multiplication and residual addition, SPP ensures the consistency of model sparsity pattern and ratio during both training and weight-merging processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPP by applying it to the LLaMA and LLaMA-2 model families with recent post-training pruning methods. Our results show that SPP significantly enhances the performance of models with different sparsity patterns (i.e. unstructured and N:M sparsity), especially for those with high sparsity ratios (e.g. 75%), making it a promising solution for the efficient fine-tuning of sparse LLMs. Code will be made available at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/SPP.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the size of a language model by removing weights, but the resulting sparse model can lose performance. SPP addresses how to fine-tune such models efficiently while retaining the sparsity already created. The goal is to improve a pruned model without disrupting the structure that makes the model sparse.

The method introduces lightweight trainable row and column matrices that modify sparse weights through element-wise multiplication and residual addition. Its construction preserves both the locations of sparse weights and the overall sparsity ratio during training and when the learned changes are merged into the model. Preservation during merging matters because the final model must retain the intended sparse structure too.

Evaluations apply SPP to LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models combined with recent post-training pruning methods. The authors report significant performance gains for both unstructured and N:M sparsity, with particularly strong benefits at high sparsity levels such as 75%. These findings support parameter-efficient adaptation as a way to improve sparse models while keeping their pruning pattern intact.
summary.tldr: SPP improves pruned language models through lightweight fine-tuning that preserves their sparsity pattern and ratio during training and merging.

title: SPP: Sparsity-Preserved Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models

abstract: We present Clifford-Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks (CS-CNNs), a novel class of ${\operatorname{E}}(p, q)$-equivariant CNNs. CS-CNNs process multivector fields on pseudo-Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^{p,q}$. They specialize, for instance, to ${\operatorname{E}}(3)$-equivariance on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and Poincaré-equivariance on Minkowski spacetime $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$. Our approach is based on an implicit parametrization of ${\operatorname{O}}(p,q)$-steerable kernels via Clifford group equivariant neural networks. We significantly and consistently outperform baseline methods on fluid dynamics as well as relativistic electrodynamics forecasting tasks.

paragraphs: Clifford-Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks build geometric symmetries into the way a convolutional model processes information. Their defining property is equivariance: transforming the input according to the relevant symmetry produces a corresponding transformation of the output. The paper develops this idea for multivector fields in pseudo-Euclidean spaces, giving one architectural framework for several different geometric settings.

The framework includes ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean symmetry and the Poincaré symmetry of Minkowski spacetime as particular cases. These examples connect the construction to both spatial and relativistic problems. To construct the required convolution kernels, the authors use an implicit parameterization based on Clifford-group-equivariant neural networks. The kernel construction therefore carries the symmetry requirements into the convolution operation.

The researchers evaluate these networks on forecasting tasks in fluid dynamics and relativistic electrodynamics. They report significant, consistent improvements over baseline methods in both areas. The findings provide empirical support for this shared geometric construction across the two tested physical settings, alongside the paper's broader architectural contribution.
summary.tldr: Clifford-Steerable CNNs encode Euclidean and spacetime symmetries in a unified architecture and outperform baselines on two physical forecasting domains.

title: Clifford-Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: SoftMax is a ubiquitous ingredient of modern machine learning algorithms. It maps an input vector onto a probability simplex and reweights the input by concentrating the probability mass at large entries. Yet, as a smooth approximation to the Argmax function, a significant amount of probability mass is distributed to other, residual entries, leading to poor interpretability and noise. Although sparsity can be achieved by a family of SoftMax variants, they often require an alternative loss function and do not preserve multimodality. We show that this trade-off between multi-modality and sparsity limits the expressivity of SoftMax as well as its variants. We provide a solution to this tension between objectives by proposing a piece-wise differentiable function, termed MultiMax, which adaptively modulates the output distribution according to input entry range. Through comprehensive analysis and evaluation, we show that MultiMax successfully produces a distribution that supresses irrelevant entries while preserving multi-modality, with benefits in image classification, language modeling and machine translation.

paragraphs: MultiMax addresses a tension in turning scores into attention weights. SoftMax emphasizes large scores but also assigns probability mass to less relevant entries, which can introduce noise and reduce interpretability. Alternatives that encourage sparsity can struggle to preserve multiple meaningful peaks in the distribution.

The authors argue that retaining several strong entries while suppressing irrelevant ones matters for expressive attention. Here, multimodality means multiple peaks in the output distribution. They propose MultiMax, a piecewise differentiable function that adapts how it transforms scores according to the range of the input entries. This gives the transformation flexibility beyond applying one uniform pattern of concentration.

Their analysis and evaluations show distributions that suppress irrelevant entries while retaining multiple modes. They report benefits in image classification, language modeling, and machine translation. The contribution is a new score-to-distribution function designed around these two objectives together. The stated findings support the idea that sparse attention can remain expressive when several entries deserve substantial weight, rather than concentrating useful information into only one dominant peak.
summary.tldr: MultiMax suppresses irrelevant attention entries while preserving multiple meaningful peaks in the output distribution.

title: MultiMax: Sparse and Multi-Modal Attention Learning

abstract: As AI research surges in both impact and volume, conferences have imposed submission limits to maintain paper quality and alleviate organizational pressure. In this work, we examine the fairness of desk-rejection systems under submission limits and reveal that existing practices can result in substantial inequities. Specifically, we formally define the paper submission limit problem and identify a critical dilemma: when the number of authors exceeds three, it becomes impossible to reject papers solely based on excessive submissions without negatively impacting innocent authors. Thus, this issue may unfairly affect early-career researchers, as their submissions may be penalized due to co-authors with significantly higher submission counts, while senior researchers with numerous papers face minimal consequences. To address this, we propose an optimization-based fairness-aware desk-rejection mechanism and formally define two fairness metrics: worst-case fairness and average fairness. We prove that optimizing worst-case fairness is NP-hard, whereas average fairness can be efficiently optimized via linear programming. Through case studies, we demonstrate that our proposed system ensures greater equity than existing methods, including those used in CVPR 2025, offering a more socially just approach to managing excessive submissions in AI conferences.

paragraphs: Conference submission limits can affect authors who have not themselves exceeded the limit because papers are shared across coauthors. This paper formalizes that fairness problem for desk rejection. Within its formulation, it identifies an impossibility when the number of authors exceeds three: rejecting papers solely for excessive submissions cannot avoid harming innocent authors.

The authors explain how this can disadvantage early-career researchers whose coauthors have much larger submission counts. They propose choosing desk rejections through a fairness-aware optimization mechanism. Two objectives make fairness explicit: worst-case fairness and average fairness. These provide different ways to assess how the consequences of rejection are distributed across affected authors.

The computational results distinguish those objectives sharply. Optimizing worst-case fairness is NP-hard, while average fairness can be optimized efficiently with linear programming. Case studies show greater equity than existing practices, including those used at CVPR 2025. The framework makes both the collateral effects of submission limits and the computational tradeoffs of fairer rejection policies available for formal analysis.
summary.tldr: A formal analysis exposes fairness problems in submission-limit desk rejections and proposes an efficiently optimizable average-fairness alternative.

title: Dissecting Submission Limit in Desk-Rejections: A Mathematical Analysis of Fairness in AI Conference Policies

abstract: Recent advances in vision backbones have yielded powerful and diverse visual and video encoders. Yet, current Video Large Language Models encode visual inputs using an encoder from a single backbone family, limiting the amount and type of visual information they can process. We propose MERV, a Multi-Encoder Video Representation, which utilizes multiple encoders for a comprehensive video representation. To optimize heterogeneous features from a broad spectrum of encoders and ensure efficient and coherent feature integration, MERV first aligns encoder features spatio-temporally, then projects them into a unified structure, and finally fuses them through cross-attention. Under fair comparison, MERV achieves up to 4.62% higher accuracy than its base model, while introducing minimal extra parameters and training faster than equivalent single-encoder methods after parallelizing visual processing. Qualitative analysis shows MERV successfully captures and integrates domain knowledge from each encoder, opening new possibilities for scaling enhanced video understanding.

paragraphs: Video language models commonly rely on visual encoders from a single backbone family, which limits the range of visual information they can process. MERV, the Multi-Encoder Video Representation, brings several encoders together so their different capabilities can contribute to a more comprehensive representation. The challenge is combining heterogeneous features efficiently and coherently.

MERV first aligns encoder outputs across space and time. It then projects them into a shared structure and combines them using cross-attention. This sequence makes features from different encoders compatible before fusion, allowing the model to draw on multiple sources of visual information within one video representation.

Under fair comparison, the authors report accuracy up to 4.62% higher than the base model with few extra parameters. After visual processing is parallelized, training is also faster than equivalent single-encoder methods. Qualitative analysis indicates that MERV captures and combines domain knowledge from its individual encoders. These findings support integrating specialized visual representations as a route toward stronger video understanding.
summary.tldr: MERV aligns and fuses multiple visual encoders, improving reported video-model accuracy with few additional parameters and faster training after parallelization.

title: Unifying Specialized Visual Encoders for Video Language Models

abstract: Accurate estimation of mutational effects on protein-protein binding energies is an open problem with applications in structural biology and therapeutic design. Several deep learning predictors for this task have been proposed, but, presumably due to the scarcity of binding data, these methods underperform computationally expensive estimates based on empirical force fields. In response, we propose a transfer-learning approach that leverages advances in protein sequence modeling and folding stability prediction for this task. The key idea is to parameterize the binding energy as the difference between the folding energy of the protein complex and the sum of the folding energies of its binding partners. We show that using a pre-trained inverse-folding model as a proxy for folding energy provides strong zero-shot performance, and can be fine-tuned with (1) copious folding energy measurements and (2) more limited binding energy measurements. The resulting predictor, StaB-ddG, is the first deep learning predictor to match the accuracy of the state-of-the-art empirical force-field method FoldX, while offering an over 1,000x speed-up.

paragraphs: Predicting how a mutation changes protein binding is useful for structural biology and therapeutic design. The paper notes that deep-learning predictors have lagged behind expensive empirical force-field estimates, possibly because binding measurements are scarce. Its response is to transfer information from protein sequence modeling and folding-stability prediction.

The key formulation expresses binding energy as the folding energy of the protein complex minus the combined folding energies of its separate partners. This connects the target prediction to folding-energy estimates. A pretrained inverse-folding model serves as a proxy for those energies, producing strong zero-shot performance before task-specific fine-tuning.

The model can then be fine-tuned using abundant folding-energy measurements alongside the smaller supply of binding-energy measurements. The resulting predictor, StaB-ddG, matches the accuracy of FoldX while offering a speedup greater than 1,000 times in the reported comparison. The authors describe it as the first deep-learning predictor to reach that accuracy level, showing how related measurements can help address limited binding data.
summary.tldr: StaB-ddG transfers folding-energy knowledge to mutation-induced binding predictions, matching FoldX accuracy with a reported speedup exceeding 1,000 times.

title: Predicting mutational effects on protein binding from folding energy

abstract: Graph neural networks have been a powerful tool for mesh-based physical simulation. To efficiently model large-scale systems, existing methods mainly employ hierarchical graph structures to capture multi-scale node relations. However, these graph hierarchies are typically manually designed and fixed, limiting their ability to adapt to the evolving dynamics of complex physical systems. We propose EvoMesh, a fully differentiable framework that jointly learns graph hierarchies and physical dynamics, adaptively guided by physical inputs. EvoMesh introduces anisotropic message passing, which enables direction-specific aggregation of dynamic features between nodes within each hierarchy, while simultaneously learning node selection probabilities for the next hierarchical level based on physical context. This design creates more flexible message shortcuts and enhances the model’s capacity to capture long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments on five benchmark physical simulation datasets show that EvoMesh outperforms recent fixed-hierarchy message passing networks by large margins. The project page is available at https://hbell99.github.io/evo-mesh/.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks simulate physical systems by exchanging information among nodes of a mesh. Hierarchical graphs help them represent relationships at multiple scales, but these hierarchies are often manually designed and fixed. EvoMesh makes the hierarchy itself learnable so that information exchange can adapt to the physical system’s evolving dynamics.

The framework jointly learns physical dynamics and graph hierarchies through a fully differentiable process. Within each hierarchy, anisotropic message passing aggregates features differently according to direction. At the same time, the model learns probabilities for selecting nodes at the next hierarchical level, using the physical context to guide those choices.

This design creates more flexible shortcuts for messages and strengthens the model’s ability to capture long-range dependencies. Experiments on five physical-simulation benchmark datasets show large improvements over recent message-passing networks with fixed hierarchies. The stated results support adapting the structure used for computation alongside the simulated dynamics, rather than treating the hierarchy as a permanently chosen part of the model.
summary.tldr: EvoMesh jointly learns physical dynamics and adaptive graph hierarchies, outperforming fixed-hierarchy networks on five simulation benchmarks.

title: EvoMesh: Adaptive Physical Simulation with Hierarchical Graph Evolutions

abstract: Multi-preference optimization enriches language-model alignment beyond pairwise preferences by contrasting entire sets of helpful and undesired responses, enabling richer training signals for large language models. During self-play alignment, these models often produce numerous candidate answers per query, making it computationally infeasible to include all of them in the training objective. We propose Active Multi-Preference Optimization (AMPO), which combines on-policy generation, a multi-preference group-contrastive loss, and active subset selection. Specifically, we score and embed large candidate pools of responses, then pick a small but informative subset—covering reward extremes and distinct semantic clusters—for preference optimization.The resulting contrastive-training scheme identifies not only the best and worst answers but also subtle, underexplored modes crucial for robust alignment. Theoretically, we provide guarantees of expected reward maximization using our active selection method. Empirically, AMPO achieves state-of-the-art results on AlpacaEval with Llama 8B and Mistral 7B. We release our datasets here.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment can compare groups of helpful and undesirable responses, providing a richer signal than a single preferred–rejected pair. During self-play, however, a model can generate more candidate answers than it is practical to include in training. AMPO addresses the resulting selection problem: which small group should represent that larger pool?

The method combines responses generated by the current policy, a group-based contrastive objective, and active subset selection. It scores responses and represents their meaning with embeddings, then selects candidates covering both reward extremes and distinct semantic clusters. This allows training to include strong and weak answers alongside less explored kinds of responses that might otherwise be overlooked.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning expected reward maximization with its selection method. Experiments report state-of-the-art AlpacaEval results using Llama 8B and Mistral 7B. The contribution is therefore both a training approach and a way to allocate limited preference-training capacity across a large candidate pool, using quality and semantic variety to identify informative examples.
summary.tldr: AMPO selects informative, semantically varied response groups from self-play candidates to improve language-model preference optimization.

title: AMPO: Active Multi Preference Optimization for Self-play Preference Selection

abstract: Increasing model size has unlocked a dazzling array of capabilities in language models. At the same time, even frontier models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and prompt injections, despite concerted efforts to make them robust. As both attackers and defenders gain access to more compute, and as models become larger, what will be the effect on robustness? We argue that to answer this question requires a scaling lens, which we adopt in an extensive study of language model robustness across several classification tasks, model families, and adversarial attacks. We find that in the absence of explicit safety training, larger models are not consistently more robust; however, scale improves sample efficiency in adversarial training, though it worsens compute efficiency. Further, we find that increasing attack compute smoothly improves attack success rate against both undefended and adversarially trained models. Finally, after exploring robustness transfer across attacks and threat models, we combine attack and defense scaling rates to study the offense-defense balance. We find that while attack scaling outpaces adversarial training across all models studied, larger adversarially trained models might give defense the advantage in the long run. These results underscore the utility of the scaling lens, and provide a paradigm for evaluating future attacks and defenses on frontier models. Code for this project is available at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/scaling-llm-robustness-paper.

paragraphs: This paper studies language model robustness as a scaling problem: what happens when models, attackers, and defenders receive more computational resources? Across classification tasks, model families, and adversarial attacks, larger models without explicit safety training are not consistently more robust. Size alone therefore does not establish a reliable defensive advantage in the evaluated settings.

For adversarial training, larger models improve sample efficiency but worsen compute efficiency. They can learn more effectively from training examples while requiring more computation for that benefit. Meanwhile, giving attackers more compute steadily increases attack success against both undefended models and models that have undergone adversarial training.

The authors also examine how robustness transfers across attacks and threat models, then combine attack and defense scaling rates. Attack scaling outpaces adversarial training across all models studied, although the analysis suggests larger adversarially trained models might eventually favor defense. That longer-term possibility remains qualified. The contribution is a way to compare changing resource budgets, rather than treating robustness measured at one scale as a fixed property.
summary.tldr: Robustness scaling depends on attack and defense resources, with larger models improving adversarial-training sample efficiency but not compute efficiency.

title: Scaling Trends in Language Model Robustness

abstract: Motion synthesis for diverse object categories holds great potential for 3D content creation but remains underexplored due to two key challenges: (1) the lack of comprehensive motion datasets that include a wide range of high-quality motions and annotations, and (2) the absence of methods capable of handling heterogeneous skeletal templates from diverse objects. To address these challenges, we contribute the following: First, we augment the Truebones Zoo dataset—a high-quality animal motion dataset covering over 70 species—by annotating it with detailed text descriptions, making it suitable for text-based motion synthesis. Second, we introduce rig augmentation techniques that generate diverse motion data while preserving consistent dynamics, enabling models to adapt to various skeletal configurations. Finally, we redesign existing motion diffusion models to dynamically adapt to arbitrary skeletal templates, enabling motion synthesis for a diverse range of objects with varying structures. Experiments show that our method learns to generate high-fidelity motions from textual descriptions for diverse and even unseen objects, setting a strong foundation for motion synthesis across diverse object categories and skeletal templates. Qualitative results are available on this link.

paragraphs: Generating motion from text becomes difficult when objects have very different skeletal structures. A model must connect language to movement while accommodating different arrangements of joints. This paper addresses both the shortage of richly annotated motion data across object categories and the challenge of using heterogeneous skeletal templates.

The authors add detailed text descriptions to Truebones Zoo, an animal-motion dataset covering more than 70 species. They also introduce rig augmentation, which creates diverse motion data while preserving consistent dynamics. These contributions expand the language supervision and skeletal variation available for learning text-controlled movement.

The modeling contribution redesigns existing motion diffusion models so they dynamically adapt to arbitrary skeletal templates. Experiments show high-fidelity motion generation from text for diverse objects, including unseen objects. Together, the data annotations, rig augmentation, and model changes address different parts of the same problem: learning how a requested movement can be expressed by objects with different structures. The findings provide evidence for extending text-to-motion synthesis across a broader range of object categories.
summary.tldr: Text annotations, rig augmentation, and adaptable diffusion models enable motion generation for diverse skeletal structures, including unseen objects.

title: How to Move Your Dragon: Text-to-Motion Synthesis for Large-Vocabulary Objects

abstract: Optimizing data mixtures for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of large language models (LLMs) is critical for developing general-purpose models, yet this area remains underexplored. In this paper, we frame data mixing as an optimization problem and introduce a novel method designed to minimize validation loss. Our approach parametrizes the loss by modeling effective data transferred and leveraging scaling laws for fine-tuning. By experimenting with various small-scale data mixtures, we fit these parameters and derive the optimal weights. We provide both mathematical proofs and empirical results demonstrating that our algorithm achieves excellent overall and individual performance across all domains. Through controlled experiments, we show that models trained with our optimized weights perform on par with those using optimal weights determined via grid search, with per-domain loss only 0.66% higher than the best domain loss from grid search on average. Additionally, we show that reweighting popular SFT datasets using our method improves both validation loss and downstream performance. Finally, we discuss how our method can generalize to guide data selection for domain-specific models and provide insights into SFT.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning often combines data from several domains, making the proportions of those domains an important training decision. This paper treats that decision as an optimization problem whose objective is validation loss. It seeks mixture weights that support both overall performance and performance within individual domains, rather than leaving the proportions to manual selection.

The method models how much effective training data transfers between domains and uses fine-tuning scaling laws to describe loss. Small-scale experiments with different mixtures provide the observations needed to fit this model. The fitted parameters then determine optimized mixture weights. Mathematical analysis and empirical results support the approach’s ability to balance performance across the evaluated domains.

In controlled experiments, the optimized mixtures perform comparably to weights found through grid search. Their per-domain losses average just 0.66% above each domain’s best grid-search loss. Reweighting popular fine-tuning datasets also improves validation loss and downstream performance. The authors additionally discuss extending the approach to data selection for domain-specific models.
summary.tldr: Small-scale mixture experiments and a fitted loss model yield fine-tuning data weights that perform comparably to grid-search choices.

title: Data Mixing Optimization for Supervised Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models

abstract: We revisit the Bayesian Black–Litterman (BL) portfolio model and remove its reliance on subjective investor views. Classical BL requires an investor “view”: a forecast vector $q$ and its uncertainty matrix $\Omega$ that describe how much a chosen portfolio should outperform the market. Our key idea is to treat $(q,\Omega)$ as latent variables and learn them from market data within a single Bayesian network. Consequently, the resulting posterior estimation admits closed-form expression, enabling fast inference and stable portfolio weights. Building on these, we propose two mechanisms to capture how features interact with returns: shared-latent parametrization and feature-influenced views; both recover classical BL and Markowitz portfolios as special cases. Empirically, on 30-year Dow-Jones and 20-year sector-ETF data, we improve Sharpe ratios by 50% and cut turnover by 55% relative to Markowitz and the index baselines. This work turns BL into a fully data-driven, view-free, and coherent Bayesian framework for portfolio optimization.

paragraphs: The classical Black–Litterman portfolio model requires investor views: forecasts about performance relative to the market and an uncertainty matrix expressing confidence in those forecasts. This paper replaces those subjective inputs with quantities learned from market data. It treats both the forecast vector and its uncertainty matrix as latent variables within one Bayesian network.

The resulting posterior estimation has a closed-form expression, which the authors connect to fast inference and stable portfolio weights. They also propose two ways to represent interactions between features and returns: shared-latent parametrization and feature-influenced views. Both formulations include classical Black–Litterman and Markowitz portfolios as special cases, connecting the proposed approach to those established models.

Experiments use 30 years of Dow-Jones data and 20 years of sector-ETF data. The authors report a 50% improvement in Sharpe ratios and a 55% reduction in turnover relative to Markowitz and index baselines. These historical results support the proposed data-driven estimation of views and uncertainty within a coherent portfolio model.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian portfolio model learns investor views and their uncertainty from market data, with improved historical risk-adjusted returns and turnover.

title: Latent Variable Estimation in Bayesian Black-Litterman Models

abstract: Text-to-song generation, the task of creating vocals and accompaniment from textual inputs, poses significant challenges due to domain complexity and data scarcity. Existing approaches often employ multi-stage generation procedures, leading to cumbersome training and inference pipelines, as well as suboptimal overall generation quality due to error accumulation across stages. In this paper, we propose SongGen, a fully open-source, single-stage auto-regressive transformer designed for controllable song generation. The proposed model facilitates fine-grained control over diverse musical attributes, including lyrics and textual descriptions of instrumentation, genre, mood, and timbre, while also offering an optional three-second reference clip for voice cloning. Within a unified auto-regressive framework, SongGen supports two output modes: mixed mode, which generates a mixture of vocals and accompaniment directly, and dual-track mode, which synthesizes them separately for greater flexibility in downstream applications. We explore diverse token pattern strategies for each mode, leading to notable improvements and valuable insights. Furthermore, we design an automated data preprocessing pipeline with effective quality control. To foster community engagement and future research, we will release our model weights, training code, annotated data, and preprocessing pipeline. The code is available at https://github.com/LiuZH-19/SongGen.

paragraphs: Generating a song from text requires coordinating vocals and accompaniment while respecting musical instructions. Existing multistage approaches can create complicated training and inference pipelines, with errors accumulating between stages. SongGen uses a single autoregressive Transformer framework to support controllable song generation within one stage.

Users can specify lyrics and descriptions of instrumentation, genre, mood, and timbre. An optional three-second reference clip supports voice cloning. The framework offers two output modes: one directly produces vocals mixed with accompaniment, while the other generates separate vocal and accompaniment tracks. Separate tracks provide additional flexibility for downstream uses.

The authors investigate different token patterns for both modes and report notable improvements from those choices. They also develop an automated preprocessing pipeline with quality control to support the data preparation needed for training. The abstract describes SongGen as open source, provides available code, and states plans to release weights, training code, annotated data, and the preprocessing pipeline. The contribution combines generation control, alternative output formats, and a unified training approach.
summary.tldr: SongGen uses one autoregressive Transformer to generate controllable songs as mixed audio or separate vocal and accompaniment tracks.

title: SongGen: A Single Stage Auto-regressive Transformer for Text-to-Song Generation

abstract: High-dimensional inference addresses scenarios where the dimension of the data approaches, or even surpasses, the sample size. In these settings, the regularized $M$-estimator is a common technique for inferring parameters. (Negahban et al., 2009) establish a unified framework for establishing convergence rates in the context of high-dimensional scaling, demonstrating that estimation errors are confined within a restricted set, and revealing fast convergence rates. The key assumption underlying their work is the convexity of the loss function. However, many loss functions in high-dimensional contexts are nonconvex. This leads to the question: if the loss function is nonconvex, do estimation errors still fall within a restricted set? If yes, can we recover convergence rates of the estimation error under nonconvex situations? This paper provides affirmative answers to these critical questions.
