The task becomes harder when treatment assignment and the process generating outcomes change over time. Offline balancing methods need full-data access, while parametric online models can become unreliable when their assumed form no longer fits.

The proposed method compresses the stream into feature coresets using discrepancy theory. The contribution connects compact streaming storage with flexible balancing, making it possible to maintain the information needed for treatment-effect estimation while addressing shifts in both assignment and outcomes.
summary.tldr: Discrepancy-based feature coresets enable bounded-memory treatment-effect estimation with direct covariate balancing under distribution shifts.

title: Streaming Covariate Balancing via Discrepancy-Based Feature Coresets

abstract: Long-horizon agentic reasoning necessitates effectively compressing growing interaction histories into a limited context window. Most existing memory systems serialize history as text, where token-level cost is uniform and scales linearly with length, often spending scarce budget on low-value details. To this end, we introduce MemOCR, a multimodal memory agent that improves long-horizon reasoning under tight context budgets by allocating memory space with adaptive information density through visual layout. Concretely, MemOCR maintains a structured rich-text memory (e.g., headings, highlights) and renders it into an image that the agent consults for memory access, visually prioritizing crucial evidence while aggressively compressing auxiliary details. To ensure robustness across varying memory budgets, we train MemOCR with reinforcement learning under budget-aware objectives that expose the agent to diverse compression levels. Across long-context multi-hop and single-hop question-answering benchmarks, MemOCR outperforms strong text-based baselines and achieves more effective context utilization under extreme budgets.

paragraphs: Agents working through long interactions must retain useful evidence within a limited context window. Conventional text memories spend tokens sequentially, and low-value details can consume space needed for crucial information. MemOCR explores a different allocation mechanism: it uses visual layout to give different parts of memory different information densities.

The agent maintains structured rich text, including elements such as headings and highlights, and renders that memory as an image. When consulting its history, it accesses this visual representation. Important evidence receives visual priority, while auxiliary details are compressed more aggressively. Layout therefore becomes part of deciding how the memory budget is distributed across the accumulated information.

MemOCR is trained with reinforcement learning objectives that account for memory budgets and expose it to multiple compression levels. On long-context question-answering benchmarks involving both single-hop and multi-hop questions, it outperforms strong text-memory baselines. The reported gains under extreme budgets indicate that visual organization can improve effective context use for the evaluated long-horizon reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: MemOCR renders structured memory as images, using visual layout to preserve crucial evidence under tight context budgets.

title: MemOCR: Layout-Aware Visual Memory for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning

abstract: Recent video generation models have revealed the emergence of Chain-of-Frame (CoF) reasoning, enabling frame-by-frame visual inference. With this capability, video models have been successfully applied to various visual tasks (e.g., maze solving, visual puzzles). However, their potential to enhance text-to-image (T2I) generation remains largely unexplored due to the absence of a clearly defined visual reasoning starting point and interpretable intermediate states in the T2I generation process. To bridge this gap, we propose CoF-T2I, a model that integrates CoF reasoning into T2I generation via progressive visual refinement, where intermediate frames act as explicit reasoning steps and the final frame is taken as output. To establish such explicit generation process, we curate CoF-Evol-Instruct, a dataset of CoF trajectories that model the generation process from semantics to aesthetics. To further improve quality and avoid motion artifacts, we enable an independent encoding operation for each frame. Experiments show that CoF-T2I significantly outperforms the base video model and achieves competitive performance, reaching 0.86 on GenEval and 7.468 on Imagine-Bench. These results indicate the substantial promise of video models for advancing high-quality text-to-image generation.

Applying this to text-to-image generation raises a practical question: what should the intermediate frames represent? CoF-T2I supplies an explicit progression in which a model refines an image visually and uses the final frame as its output.

title: CoF-T2I: Video Models as Pure Visual Reasoners for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Multimodal-Attributed Graph (MAG) learning has achieved remarkable success in modeling complex real-world systems by integrating graph topology with rich attributes from multiple modalities. With the rapid proliferation of novel MAG models capable of handling intricate cross-modal semantics and structural dependencies, establishing a rigorous and unified evaluation standard has become imperative. Although existing benchmarks have facilitated initial progress, they exhibit critical limitations in domain coverage, encoder flexibility, model diversity, and task scope, presenting significant challenges to fair evaluation. To bridge this gap, we present OpenMAG, a comprehensive benchmark that integrates 19 datasets across 6 domains and incorporates 16 encoders to support both static and trainable feature encoding. OpenMAG further implements a standardized library of 24 state-of-the-art models and supports 8 downstream tasks, enabling fair comparisons within a unified framework. Through systematic assessment of necessity, data quality, effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency, we derive 14 fundamental insights into MAG learning to guide future advancements. Our code is available at https://github.com/YUKI-N810/OpenMAG.

paragraphs: Multimodal-attributed graphs combine relationships between entities with attributes from different modalities. Evaluating models for these graphs requires accounting for both structural dependencies and cross-modal information. OpenMAG addresses gaps in existing benchmarks involving domain coverage, feature encoders, model variety, and the range of downstream tasks, all of which can complicate fair comparisons.

The benchmark brings together 19 datasets spanning six domains, 16 encoders, a standardized implementation library of 24 models, and eight downstream tasks. It supports both fixed feature representations and encoders that can be trained. This shared framework makes it possible to compare a broader set of modeling and encoding choices within a consistent evaluation environment.

The study examines necessity, data quality, effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency, and reports 14 insights into multimodal graph learning. Its contribution is the evaluation infrastructure and systematic assessment, rather than a single new model claimed to outperform the rest. The breadth of the benchmark supports investigation of how data, representations, and model choices interact across different graph-learning settings.
summary.tldr: OpenMAG standardizes multimodal graph evaluation across 19 datasets, 16 encoders, 24 models, and eight tasks.

title: OpenMAG: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal-Attributed Graph

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on factoid question answering, they are still prone to hallucination and untruthful responses, particularly when tasks demand information outside their parametric knowledge. Indeed, truthfulness requires more than accuracy—models must also recognize uncertainty and abstain when unsure to avoid hallucinations. This presents a fundamental challenge for existing methods: approaches that optimize for accuracy often amplify hallucinations, while those that encourage abstention can become overly conservative, sacrificing correct answers. Both extremes ultimately compromise truthfulness. In this work, we present TruthRL, a general reinforcement learning (RL) framework that directly optimizes the truthfulness of LLMs. Specifically, we implement TruthRL using GRPO with a simple yet effective ternary reward that distinguishes correct answers, hallucinations, and abstentions. It incentivizes models to reduce hallucinations not only by providing correct responses, but also by enabling abstention when uncertain, thereby improving truthfulness. Extensive experiments across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks show that TruthRL significantly reduces hallucinations (e.g., 43.5% $\rightarrow$ 19.4%) and improves truthfulness (e.g., 5.3% $\rightarrow$ 37.2%), with consistent gains across various backbone models. Analysis shows that the improvement of TruthRL arises from enhanced capability of LLMs to recognize their knowledge boundary, hence avoiding being overly conservative as the baselines are.

paragraphs: A truthful question-answering model needs to answer correctly when it knows and abstain when it does not. Optimizing accuracy alone can encourage hallucinations, while rewarding refusal too strongly can suppress answers the model could provide correctly. TruthRL treats this balance as a reinforcement learning objective, aiming to improve recognition of the model’s own knowledge boundary.

The framework is implemented with GRPO and a three-way reward that distinguishes correct answers, hallucinations, and abstentions. This gives training a signal about both successful answering and appropriate uncertainty. Reducing hallucination can therefore involve either producing the correct response or declining to answer when the required information is outside the model’s knowledge.

Across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks and multiple backbone models, the authors report consistent gains. Illustrative results reduce hallucinations from 43.5% to 19.4% and raise the reported truthfulness measure from 5.3% to 37.2%. Their analysis attributes improvement to better recognition of knowledge boundaries, avoiding the excessive conservatism observed in baselines. The finding supports treating abstention as a distinct, useful outcome within answer training.
summary.tldr: TruthRL rewards correct answers, hallucinations, and abstentions differently to improve truthfulness without encouraging excessive refusal.

title: TruthRL: Incentivizing Truthful LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study zero-shot inverse problems, where a clean signal is recovered from a single degraded observation without external training data. Contrary to the common belief that such problems require highly complex models, we show that a lightweight neural network, when combined with entropy and complexity regularization in a compression-based formulation, is sufficient for high-quality restoration. We propose Lottery Prior, a compression-based inverse solver that leverages architectural priors from random networks and induces a family of implicit priors through randomness, enabling ensemble-based refinement. We further derive non-asymptotic error bounds for compression-based maximum-likelihood inverse solvers, revealing how rate–distortion constraints act as implicit regularizers. Experiments on denoising, noisy super-resolution, and inpainting demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art with significantly fewer effective parameters. Project page: https://eedavidwu.github.io/LotteryPrior/

paragraphs: Lottery Prior studies recovering a clean signal from one degraded observation without external training data. The paper shows that a lightweight neural network can be sufficient for high-quality restoration when paired with entropy and complexity regularization in a compression-based objective. The emphasis is on constraining the representation, rather than requiring a highly complex model.

The solver uses structural preferences supplied by random network architectures. Randomness induces a family of implicit priors, and an ensemble combines them to refine the reconstruction. Compression provides another source of structure: limits on representation rate and distortion regularize which reconstructions the method favors. These mechanisms work together to guide recovery from the available observation.

The authors derive finite-sample error bounds for compression-based maximum-likelihood inverse solvers, clarifying the regularizing role of rate–distortion constraints. Experiments on denoising, noisy super-resolution, and inpainting report state-of-the-art performance with substantially fewer effective parameters. The results establish the sufficiency of the proposed lightweight formulation in these evaluations, supporting compression and randomized architectural structure as useful tools for restoration.
summary.tldr: Lottery Prior combines lightweight random networks, compression regularization, and ensembles to restore signals without external training data.

title: Lottery Prior: Randomized Neural Compression for Zero-Shot Inverse Problems

abstract: As LLMs proliferate with diverse capabilities and costs, LLM routing has emerged by learning to predict each LLM’s quality and cost for a given query, then selecting the one with high quality and low cost. However, existing routers implicitly assume a single fixed quality and cost per LLM for each query, ignoring that the same LLM’s quality varies with its output length. This causes routers to exclude powerful LLMs when their estimated cost exceeds the budget, missing the opportunity that these LLMs could still deliver high quality at reduced cost with shorter outputs. To address this, we introduce R2-Router, which treats output length budget as a controllable variable and jointly selects the best LLM and length budget, enforcing the budget via length-constrained instructions. This enables R2-Router to discover that a powerful LLM with constrained output can outperform a weaker LLM at comparable cost—efficient configurations invisible to prior methods. Together with the router framework, we construct R2-Bench, the first routing dataset capturing LLM behavior across diverse output length budgets. Experiments show that R2-Router achieves state-of-the-art performance at $4-5\times$ lower cost compared with existing routers. This work opens a new direction: routing as reasoning, where routers evolve from reactive selectors to deliberate reasoners that explore which LLM to use and at what cost budget. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/UCF-ML-Research/R2-Router.

paragraphs: LLM routers choose a model for each query by balancing predicted answer quality against cost. R2-Router questions the assumption that each model has one fixed quality and cost for a query. Output length changes both, so an expensive model might still be a useful choice if it is asked to produce a shorter answer.

The router jointly chooses the model and its output-length budget, using length-constrained instructions to enforce that choice. This expands the configurations available to the routing decision. In particular, it can identify cases where a stronger model with a shorter response outperforms a weaker model at comparable cost. The authors also introduce R2-Bench, a dataset recording model behavior across different output-length budgets.

Experiments report state-of-the-art routing performance at four to five times lower cost than existing routers. The finding supports treating response length as a decision variable alongside model identity. It shows that comparing models under adjustable output budgets can reveal useful quality-cost combinations that fixed-cost routing overlooks.
summary.tldr: R2-Router jointly selects an LLM and response-length budget, finding stronger quality-cost combinations than routing with fixed per-model estimates.

title: R2-Router: A New Paradigm for LLM Routing with Reasoning

abstract: Most existing CLIP-style medical vision–language pretraining methods rely on global or local alignment with substantial paired data. However, global alignment is easily dominated by non-diagnostic information, while local alignment fails to integrate key diagnostic evidence. As a result, learning reliable diagnostic representations becomes difficult, which limits their applicability in medical scenarios with limited paired data. To address this issue, we propose an LLM-Guided Diagnostic Evidence Alignment method (LGDEA), which shifts the pretraining objective toward evidence-level alignment that is more consistent with the medical diagnostic process. Specifically, we leverage LLMs to extract key diagnostic evidence from radiology reports and construct a shared diagnostic evidence space, enabling evidence-aware cross-modal alignment and allowing LGDEA to effectively exploit abundant unpaired medical images and reports, thereby substantially alleviating the reliance on paired data. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves consistent and significant improvements on phrase grounding, image–text retrieval, and zero-shot classification, and even rivals pretraining methods that rely on substantial paired data.

Matching whole images and reports can emphasize irrelevant content, while matching local elements can fail to bring key evidence together. These problems become especially difficult when only a limited amount of paired image–report data is available.

LGDEA changes the alignment target to diagnostic evidence. It uses language models to extract key evidence from radiology reports and constructs a shared evidence space for the visual and textual modalities. Aligning through this space lets the method draw on abundant unpaired images and reports, substantially reducing its dependence on examples where an image is explicitly matched to a report.

The authors report consistent and significant improvements in phrase grounding, image–text retrieval, and zero-shot classification. They also report performance that rivals pretraining methods using substantial paired data. Together, these findings support selecting diagnostically relevant information as the basis for cross-modal learning. The approach connects the meaning needed for downstream medical tasks with a way to use data that lack direct image–report pairings.
summary.tldr: LGDEA aligns medical images and reports through extracted diagnostic evidence, improving several tasks while reducing reliance on paired training data.

title: LLM-Guided Diagnostic Evidence Alignment for Medical Vision–Language Pretraining under Limited Pairing

abstract: Neural operators have emerged as data-driven surrogates for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), and their success hinges on efficiently modeling the long-range, global coupling among spatial points induced by the underlying physics. In many PDE regimes, the induced global interaction kernels are empirically compressible, exhibiting rapid spectral decay that admits low-rank approximations. We leverage this observation to unify representative global mixing modules in neural operators under a shared low-rank template: compressing high-dimensional pointwise features into a compact latent space, processing global interactions within it, and reconstructing the global context back to spatial points. Guided by this view, we introduce Low-Rank Spatial Attention (LRSA) as a clean and direct instantiation of this template. Crucially, unlike prior approaches that often rely on non-standard aggregation or normalization modules, LRSA is built purely from standard Transformer primitives, i.e., attention, normalization, and feed-forward networks, yielding a concise block that is straightforward to implement and directly compatible with hardware-optimized kernels. In our experiments, such a simple construction is sufficient to achieve high accuracy, yielding an average error reduction of over 17% relative to second-best methods, while remaining stable and efficient in mixed-precision training.

summary.tldr: LRSA uses standard Transformer components for low-rank spatial interaction, reporting over 17% lower average error than second-best methods in its experiments.

title: Simple yet Effective: Low-Rank Spatial Attention for Neural Operators

abstract: Time series forecasting is critical in domains such as finance, energy, and healthcare, yet real-world datasets often exhibit non-stationarity, noise, missing values, and distribution shifts, posing severe challenges for generalization. In practice, industry solutions typically rely on customized forecasting frameworks that combine imputation, decomposition, and specialized models. However, such frameworks are costly to engineer and maintain. Moreover, we observe that many frameworks suffer from the impacts of distribution shifts, which degrade their respective performance. It motivates a paradigm that transfers reliably across heterogeneous datasets while accumulating reusable strategy knowledge for large-scale, dynamic environments. Although large language model-based agents have recently shown strong reasoning and tool-use capabilities, existing approaches do not consistently adapt forecasting workflows across diverse time series. We identify two primary factors, including limited strategy-level supervision and the inherent complexity of mapping dataset-specific meta-features to effective forecasting strategies. To address these challenges, we propose BECRA, a novel agent training paradigm that learns forecasting intelligence through contrast-aware exploration and agent-level causal lesson extraction, without human-annotated supervision. BECRA distills symbolic strategy lessons that support in-context planning on unseen datasets, enabling zero-shot training adaptation.

However, such frameworks are costly to engineer and maintain. Moreover, we observe that many frameworks suffer from the impacts of distribution shifts, which degrade their respective performance. It motivates a paradigm that transfers reliably across heterogeneous datasets while accumulating reusable strategy knowledge for large-scale, dynamic environments. Although large language model-based agents have recently shown strong reasoning and tool-use capabilities, existing approaches do not consistently adapt forecasting workflows across diverse time series. We identify two primary factors, including limited strategy-level supervision and the inherent complexity of mapping dataset-specific meta-features to effective forecasting strategies. To address these challenges, we propose BECRA, a novel agent training paradigm that learns forecasting intelligence through contrast-aware exploration and agent-level causal lesson extraction, without human-annotated supervision. BECRA distills symbolic strategy lessons that support in-context planning on unseen datasets, enabling zero-shot training adaptation.

paragraphs: Forecasting workflows often combine several choices: how to fill missing values, separate patterns, and select specialized models. These choices become difficult to maintain when datasets are noisy or their behavior changes. BECRA addresses the problem of teaching an agent to choose forecasting strategies across heterogeneous datasets, rather than requiring a separately engineered workflow for each setting.

The authors identify two obstacles: limited supervision about which strategies work, and the difficulty of connecting dataset characteristics to useful decisions. Their training approach combines contrast-aware exploration with the extraction of causal lessons at the agent level. It learns without human-annotated supervision and distills the resulting experience into symbolic strategy lessons.

Those lessons provide reusable knowledge for planning on unseen datasets through the agent's context. The proposed benefit is adaptation based on accumulated strategy knowledge, including the zero-shot adaptation described in the abstract. The contribution therefore concerns how forecasting decisions are learned and reused: experience becomes explicit guidance for selecting a workflow when the next dataset has different properties.
summary.tldr: BECRA trains forecasting agents to extract reusable strategy lessons from exploration and apply them to unseen datasets without human annotations.

title: Bootstrapped Exploration with Causal Reasoning: A Training Paradigm for Adaptive Forecasting Agent

abstract: LoRA has become a widely adopted method for PEFT, and its initialization methods have attracted increasing attention. However, existing methods have notable limitations: many methods do not incorporate target-domain data, while gradient-based methods exploit data only at a shallow level by relying on one-step gradient decomposition. In this paper, we establish a theoretical framework for data-aware LoRA initialization. Starting from minimizing the expectation of the parameter discrepancy between the fine-tuned and target models, we derive an optimization problem with two components: a bias term, which is related to the parameter distance between the fine-tuned and target models, and is approximated using a Fisher–gradient formulation to preserve anisotropy; and a variance term, which accounts for the uncertainty introduced by sampling stochasticity through the Fisher information. Solving this problem yields an optimal initialization strategy for LoRA, based on which we develop an efficient algorithm, LoRA-DA. Empirical results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that LoRA-DA consistently improves final accuracy over existing initialization methods. Additional studies show faster, more stable convergence, robustness across ranks, and only a small initialization overhead for LoRA-DA. The source code is available at https://github.com/zqy0126/LoRA-DA.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, provides a parameter-efficient way to fine-tune models, but its starting parameters affect the learning process. LoRA-DA develops a theoretical basis for using target data more deeply when choosing the initialization.

The bias component uses a Fisher–gradient approximation that preserves directional differences in the parameter geometry. Further studies report faster and more stable convergence, robustness across ranks, and small initialization overhead. These findings connect a data-aware starting point to both the trajectory and outcome of fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: LoRA-DA uses a data-aware bias–variance objective to initialize low-rank adaptation, improving accuracy and training stability with small overhead.

title: LoRA-DA: Data-Aware Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation via Asymptotic Analysis

abstract: Self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents continually improve by accumulating and reusing past experience, yet it remains unclear whether they faithfully rely on that experience to guide their behavior. We present the first systematic investigation of experience faithfulness—the causal dependence of an agent’s decisions on the experience it is given—in self-evolving LLM agents. Using controlled causal interventions on both raw and condensed forms of experience, we comprehensively evaluate four representative frameworks across 13 LLM backbones and 9 environments. Our analysis uncovers a striking asymmetry: while agents consistently depend on raw experience, they often disregard or misinterpret condensed experience, even when it is the only experience provided. This gap persists across single- and multi-agent configurations and across backbone scales. We trace its underlying causes to three factors: the semantic limitations of condensed content, internal processing biases that suppress experience, and task regimes where pretrained priors already suffice. These findings challenge prevailing assumptions about self-evolving methods and underscore the need for more faithful and reliable approaches to experience integration.

paragraphs: Self-evolving agents collect past experience with the aim of improving future behavior. But storing or presenting that experience does not establish that it actually influences decisions. This paper studies experience faithfulness: whether an agent's behavior causally depends on the experience supplied to it.

The authors intervene on both raw experience and condensed versions of it, examining four agent frameworks across 13 language-model backbones and nine environments. They find a consistent asymmetry. Agents depend on raw experience, but often ignore or misinterpret condensed experience, including when the condensed form is the only experience available. The gap appears in both single-agent and multi-agent configurations and across model scales.

The analysis attributes this behavior to limitations in the meaning preserved by condensed content, internal processing biases that suppress experience, and tasks where pretrained knowledge already suffices. These findings question whether accumulated summaries reliably drive improvement. They also distinguish having a memory mechanism from using its contents faithfully, making causal tests of experience use central to assessing self-evolving agents.
summary.tldr: Controlled interventions show that self-evolving agents often use raw experience but disregard or misinterpret condensed experience.

title: Large Language Model Agents Are Not Always Faithful Self-Evolvers

abstract: Vibe coding is a new software development paradigm in which human engineers prompt a large language model (LLM) agent to complete complex coding tasks with little supervision. Although vibe coding is increasingly adopted, is the generated code really safe to deploy in production? To investigate this question, we propose SUSVIBES, a benchmark consisting of 186 feature-request software engineering tasks from real-world open-source projects, for which human programmers committed vulnerable implementations. We evaluate 12 widely used coding agentic settings with frontier models on the benchmark. Disturbingly, all agents perform poorly in terms of software security. Although 57% of the solutions from SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet are functionally correct, only 11.8% are secure. Further experiments demonstrate that preliminary security strategies, such as augmenting the feature request with vulnerability hints, cannot mitigate these security issues. Our findings raise serious concerns about the widespread adoption of vibe coding, particularly in security-sensitive applications. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/LeiLiLab/susvibes. The leaderboard is at https://leililab.github.io/ susvibes-leaderboard.

paragraphs: Coding agents can implement feature requests with little human supervision, but functional success does not establish that the resulting software is secure. This paper examines that gap using SUSVIBES, a benchmark built from real open-source development tasks where human programmers previously committed vulnerable implementations.

The benchmark contains 186 feature-request tasks, and the evaluation covers 12 coding-agent settings using frontier models. All evaluated agents perform poorly on software security. One reported example makes the gap concrete: SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet produces functionally correct solutions for 57% of tasks, while only 11.8% of its solutions are secure.

The authors also test preliminary security strategies, including adding vulnerability hints to feature requests, and find that these do not mitigate the observed problems. Because the benchmark centers on tasks associated with vulnerable human implementations, its results specifically expose security difficulties in that setting. The findings raise concerns about deploying lightly supervised agent-generated code, especially for security-sensitive applications, and show why functional correctness alone is an insufficient evaluation target.
summary.tldr: SUSVIBES finds a substantial gap between functional correctness and security in coding-agent solutions to real-world feature requests.

title: Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks

abstract: This position paper argues that contemporary AI paradigms are insufficient for supporting complex global goals and introduces Planet-Centered AI (PCAI) as a design philosophy and research agenda that reorients AI toward planetary-scale socio-ecological systems and their long-term trajectories. A planet-centered approach is grounded in systems thinking, treating Earth as an interconnected whole of which humans are part. We diagnose recurring limitations across AI frameworks—many of which remain human-centered—and show why these become especially consequential under current planetary conditions characterized by systemic risk, non-stationarity, and deep uncertainty. We then articulate how PCAI reshapes the AI lifecycle, from problem formulation and model design to evaluation and deployment, by emphasizing alignment with global agendas, developing system-aware AI foundations, trajectory-oriented evaluation, and monitorability. Finally, we advance a falsifiable claim: AI systems optimized without explicit consideration of systemic consequences are more likely to exacerbate systemic instability than to mitigate it.

paragraphs: This paper proposes Planet-Centered AI as a design philosophy for systems that affect interconnected social and ecological processes. It treats humans as part of Earth’s wider systems and asks how AI influences their long-term development. The authors argue that existing approaches, many organized around human-centered objectives, are insufficient for complex global goals.

The paper connects this concern to systemic risks, changing conditions, and deep uncertainty. Under those circumstances, evaluating an isolated task or immediate outcome can leave broader consequences outside the design process. The proposed agenda extends across problem definition, model development, evaluation, and deployment. It emphasizes connections to global agendas, foundations that account for system interactions, evaluation of trajectories over time, and the ability to monitor deployed systems.

The authors also formulate a claim intended to be testable: systems optimized without explicitly considering systemic consequences are more likely to worsen systemic instability than reduce it. This is presented as a falsifiable proposition, rather than an established universal outcome. Its role is to make the research agenda accountable to evidence about how AI affects the larger systems in which it operates.
summary.tldr: Planet-Centered AI would make long-term social and ecological consequences explicit throughout AI design, evaluation, and deployment.

title: Position: AI Must Become Planet-Centered, Not Just Human-Centered

abstract: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is not adequately addressed in AI/ML literature regarding AI-generated media, commonly referred to as "deepfakes". While research on deepfakes currently focuses on its epistemic harms—or harms relating to truth and authenticity—this is misaligned with the dominant reality of generative AI abuse involving sexualized imagery. We conduct a landscape analysis of highly-cited works to demonstrate that technical interventions addressing deepfakes almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII, limiting the research ecosystem to authenticity detection tools. In this position paper, we argue that existing interventions address viewer-centric epistemic harms, such as fraud or scams, but ignore subject-centric dignity harms, such as AIG-NCII. We illustrate that knowing an image is synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may, in some cases, even exacerbate them. We conclude by offering recommendations to realign the field, including updating threat models to consider subject-centered harms and addressing AIG-NCII in AI safety research. Finally, we caution that researchers should only engage in this high-risk domain if they implement safety guardrails for both subjects and researchers and establish partnerships with domain experts in sexual violence prevention.

paragraphs: Deepfake research often asks whether viewers can distinguish authentic media from fabricated media. This position paper argues that this focus misses a major harm of AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery: the violation experienced by the depicted person. Knowing an image is synthetic does not necessarily reduce that harm.

A landscape analysis of highly cited work finds that technical interventions largely center on authenticity detection and give little attention to non-consensual intimate imagery. The authors distinguish viewer-oriented harms involving truth and deception from subject-oriented harms involving dignity. That distinction explains why a detector can succeed technically while leaving the underlying abuse unaddressed.

The paper recommends subject-centered threat models and stronger attention to this abuse in AI-safety research. It also calls for protective practices and partnerships with sexual-violence-prevention experts when studying the domain. The contribution is a critique and research agenda, rather than an evaluation of a new detection model or a claim that authenticity tools have no value.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that deepfake research must address harms to depicted people, which authenticity detection alone cannot resolve.

abstract: We apply classic online learning techniques similar to the perceptron algorithm to the problem of learning a function defined on a graph. The benefit of our approach includes simple algorithms and performance guarantees that we naturally interpret in terms of structural properties of the graph, such as the algebraic connectivity or the diameter of the graph. We also discuss how these methods can be modified to allow active learning on a graph. We present preliminary experiments with encouraging results.

The benefit of our approach includes simple algorithms and performance guarantees that we naturally interpret in terms of structural properties of the graph, such as the algebraic connectivity or the diameter of the graph. We also discuss how these methods can be modified to allow active learning on a graph. We present preliminary experiments with encouraging results.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a function whose domain is a graph. The authors adapt classic online learning techniques resembling the perceptron algorithm to this setting. Their approach brings sequential learning methods to a problem where the relationships represented by the graph are central to understanding the learning task.

A main contribution is a set of simple algorithms with performance guarantees that can be interpreted through graph structure. The properties highlighted include algebraic connectivity and graph diameter. Connecting guarantees to these quantities gives the analysis a structural meaning: characteristics of the graph help explain what the learning method can achieve.

The authors also discuss modifications for active learning on graphs, where the learning procedure can play a role in selecting information to acquire. Preliminary experiments produce encouraging results. The paper's strongest stated foundation is the combination of simple methods and graph-dependent guarantees; its experiments provide initial empirical support, rather than an extensive claim of demonstrated superiority across graph-learning applications.
summary.tldr: Perceptron-like online algorithms learn functions on graphs with guarantees tied to graph structure and possible active-learning extensions.

title: Online learning over graphs

abstract: The aim of this paper is to show that machine learning techniques can be used to derive a classifying function for human brain signal data measured by magnetoencephalography (MEG), for the use in a brain computer interface (BCI). This is especially helpful for evaluating quickly whether a BCI approach based on electroencephalography, on which training may be slower due to lower signalto-noise ratio, is likely to succeed. We apply RCE and regularized SVMs to the experimental data of ten healthy subjects performing a motor imagery task. Four subjects were able to use a trained classifier to write a short name. Further analysis gives evidence that the proposed imagination task is suboptimal for the possible extension to a multiclass interface. To the best of our knowledge this paper is the first working online MEG-based BCI and is therefore a “proof of concept”.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether machine learning can turn brain signals measured by magnetoencephalography, or MEG, into commands for an interactive computer interface. The researchers train classifiers on signals recorded while people imagine movements. The central question is whether the learned distinction can support actual online interaction, rather than only classify previously collected recordings.

The study applies RCE and regularized support vector machines to experimental data from ten healthy participants. Four participants subsequently used a trained classifier to write a short name. This provides a concrete demonstration that the recorded signals and learned classifiers could work together in an operating interface for some participants.

The authors also position MEG as a way to assess whether an electroencephalography interface might succeed, since training with the latter may be slower because of lower signal quality. Their analysis suggests that the chosen imagery task is suboptimal for extending the interface to multiple classes. They describe the system as a proof of concept and, to their knowledge, the first working online MEG interface.
summary.tldr: A MEG-based brain interface let four of ten participants write a short name using learned classifiers of imagined movements.

abstract: Inference tasks in Markov random fields (MRFs) are closely related to the constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) and its soft generalizations. In particular, MAP inference in MRF is equivalent to the weighted (maxsum) CSP. A well-known tool to tackle CSPs are arc consistency algorithms, a.k.a. relaxation labeling. A promising approach to MAP inference in MRFs is linear programming relaxation solved by sequential treereweighted message passing (TRW-S). There is a not widely known algorithm equivalent to TRW-S, max-sum diffusion, which is slower but very simple. We give two theoretical results. First, we show that arc consistency algorithms and max-sum diffusion become the same thing if formulated in an abstractalgebraic way. Thus, we argue that max-sum arc consistency algorithm or max-sum relaxation labeling is a more suitable name for max-sum diffusion. Second, we give a criterion that strictly decreases during these algorithms. It turns out that every class of equivalent problems contains a unique problem that is minimal w.r.t. this criterion.

paragraphs: The paper connects inference in Markov random fields with constraint satisfaction. Finding a maximum a posteriori assignment in an MRF is equivalent to solving a weighted max-sum constraint problem. This relationship brings together message-passing methods for probabilistic inference and arc-consistency methods, also called relaxation labeling, from constraint satisfaction.

The authors study max-sum diffusion, a simple but slower algorithm equivalent to sequential tree-reweighted message passing. Their first theoretical result shows that max-sum diffusion and arc-consistency algorithms become the same operation when expressed in an abstract algebraic formulation. This motivates naming diffusion max-sum arc consistency or max-sum relaxation labeling.

Their second result identifies a criterion that strictly decreases during these algorithms. Moreover, each class of equivalent problems contains one unique problem that is minimal according to this criterion. This supplies a precise account of the progress the algorithms make and a unique minimum within the corresponding equivalence class. That minimum concerns the stated criterion on equivalent problems, rather than a claim that the original discrete inference problem is always solved exactly.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies max-sum diffusion with arc consistency and identifies a strictly decreasing criterion with a unique minimum in each equivalence class.

title: What is decreased by the max-sum arc consistency algorithm?

abstract: We present a unified framework for learning link prediction and edge weight prediction functions in large networks, based on the transformation of a graph's algebraic spectrum. Our approach generalizes several graph kernels and dimensionality reduction methods and provides a method to estimate their parameters efficiently. We show how the parameters of these prediction functions can be learned by reducing the problem to a one-dimensional regression problem whose runtime only depends on the method's reduced rank and that can be inspected visually. We derive variants that apply to undirected, weighted, unweighted, unipartite and bipartite graphs. We evaluate our method experimentally using examples from social networks, collaborative filtering, trust networks, citation networks, authorship graphs and hyperlink networks.

paragraphs: This paper presents a common framework for predicting links and edge weights in large networks. Its central idea is to transform a graph's algebraic spectrum, a mathematical representation of graph structure. Different transformations produce different prediction functions, allowing several graph kernels and dimensionality-reduction approaches to be understood within the same framework.

The authors show how to learn the parameters of these functions by reducing parameter estimation to a one-dimensional regression problem. The runtime of that regression depends only on the method's reduced rank. The regression can also be inspected visually, making the learned transformation easier to examine. This efficiency claim concerns the reduced estimation problem rather than every stage of processing a network.

The paper derives variants for undirected, weighted, unweighted, unipartite, and bipartite graphs. Experimental evaluations span social networks, collaborative filtering, trust, citations, authorship, and hyperlinks. This range demonstrates the breadth of settings considered. The central contribution is a shared, efficiently parameterized way to learn spectral prediction functions across different kinds of network data.
summary.tldr: Learning transformations of graph spectra unifies several network-prediction methods and reduces parameter fitting to a visually inspectable one-dimensional regression.

title: Learning spectral graph transformations for link prediction

abstract: In this paper, we propose an Active Learning (AL) framework for the Multi-Task Adaptive Filtering (MTAF) problem. Specifically, we explore AL approaches to rapidly improve an MTAF system, based on Dirichlet Process priors, with minimal user/task-level feedback. The proposed AL approaches select instances for delivery with a two-fold objective: 1) Improve future task-specific system performance based on feedback received on delivered instances for that task, 2) Improve the future overall system performance, thereby benefiting other tasks in the system, based on feedback received on delivered instances for a particular task. Current AL approaches focus only on the first objective. For satisfying both goals, we define a new scoring function called Utility Gain to estimate the perceived improvements in task-specific and global models. In our experiments on standard benchmark datasets, we observed that global AL approaches that additionally take into account the potential benefit of feedback to other tasks in the system performed better than the task-specific approach that focused only the benefit of the current task.

paragraphs: An adaptive filtering system can learn from feedback on the instances it delivers to users or tasks. When several tasks share a learning system, that feedback may help more than its immediate recipient. This paper develops an active learning framework for a multi-task adaptive filtering system based on Dirichlet Process priors, aiming to improve performance with limited feedback.

The selection strategy has two objectives. It seeks feedback that improves the current task's future predictions, while also considering how that same feedback could improve the overall system and benefit other tasks. The authors introduce a scoring function called Utility Gain to estimate these improvements in task-specific and global models.

Experiments on standard benchmark datasets show that selection approaches accounting for benefits to other tasks perform better than an approach focused only on the current task. The finding supports treating feedback as a potentially shared resource: the value of delivering an instance depends not just on its local learning benefit, but also on its expected contribution elsewhere in the system.
summary.tldr: Selecting feedback for its benefits across tasks improves multi-task adaptive filtering over selection focused only on the current task.

title: Active Learning for Multi-Task Adaptive Filtering

abstract: In this paper, we review the problem of matrix completion and expose its intimate relations with algebraic geometry and combinatorial graph theory. We present the first necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions for matrices of arbitrary rank to be identifiable from a set of matrix entries, yielding theoretical constraints and new algorithms for the problem of matrix completion. We conclude with algorithmically evaluating the tightness of the given conditions and algorithms for practically relevant matrix sizes, showing that the algebraic-combinatoric approach can lead to improvements over state-of-the-art matrix completion methods.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we review the problem of matrix completion and expose its intimate relations with algebraic geometry and combinatorial graph theory. We present the first necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions for matrices of arbitrary rank to be identifiable from a set of matrix entries, yielding theoretical constraints and new algorithms for the problem of matrix completion. We conclude with algorithmically evaluating the tightness of the given conditions and algorithms for practically relevant matrix sizes, showing that the algebraic-combinatoric approach can lead to improvements over state-of-the-art matrix completion methods.

paragraphs: Matrix completion asks how to recover missing matrix entries from the entries that are available. When the matrix has low rank, its entries obey shared structural constraints. A central question is identifiability: whether the observed information determines the matrix sufficiently to make recovery possible. This question concerns the information available before choosing a particular recovery algorithm.

The paper connects this problem to algebraic geometry and combinatorial graph theory. It presents what the authors describe as the first necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions for identifiability for matrices of arbitrary rank. Necessary conditions describe requirements that must be met; sufficient conditions establish when identifiability follows. Together, these conditions provide theoretical constraints and motivate new completion algorithms.

The authors also evaluate the tightness of their conditions and the associated algorithms at practically relevant matrix sizes. Their results show that this algebraic and combinatorial approach can improve on existing matrix completion methods. The contribution therefore links a structural account of recoverability with computational methods that can benefit practical reconstruction.
summary.tldr: The paper gives combinatorial conditions for matrix identifiability and uses algebraic structure to develop potentially better completion algorithms.

title: A Combinatorial Algebraic Approach for the Identifiability of Low-Rank Matrix Completion
